Photographers can save hundreds of dollars on an expansive range of Sony mirrorless cameras, from budget-friendly APS-C models all the way to flagship full-frame bodies.

Sources indicate that starting with the APS-C camera deals, photographers can save $50 on Sony’s best APS-C interchangeable-lens model, the a6700. With its 26-megapixel Exmor R BSI CMOS sensor and 4Kp120 recording, the a6700 is a versatile and fully featured camera. While there’s no instant discount on it right now, unlike the rest of the cameras in this story, there is a $50 cashback campaign running through December 31, 2026. The camera is $1,498, but the $50 back later is nice.

With the 24.2-megapixel Sony ZV-E10, which comes in both black and white colorways, the $50 savings is upfront. The video-focused camera, designed for content creators, is $748 thanks to ongoing holiday savings. That's $450 less than its successor, the ZV-E10 II, which costs $1,198 and isn't discounted. That's massive savings.

In a recent development, the Sony a6400 isn't quite as advanced as the a6700, but the 24-megapixel model remains a very capable APS-C mirrorless camera. It's also significantly more accessible, especially after its $200 instant holiday discount. At $898, this is among the best values in Sony's APS-C lineup.

On the full-frame side of things, there are a ton of great discounts right now, including up to $600 off a Sony a7 III. While it has been succeeded by the a7 IV and, most recently, the a7 V, the Sony a7 III is still a capable camera, able to capture high-quality 24-megapixel photos and 4Kp30 video. At $1,398 after its $600 discount, it's the most affordable way into a fresh Sony full-frame camera right now. There's also a $50 cashback campaign for this camera.

According to recent reports, speaking of the newer a7 IV, that's on sale, too. In fact, it's $500 off—plus the $50 cashback campaign. It's $1,998 today before the $50 back later. It has a 33-megapixel sensor, 4Kp60 video recording, and some autofocus bells and whistles its predecessor lacks.

Well, the even newer a7 V is on sale, too! The discount is a bit smaller at just $200, plus $50 back after purchase, but it's still something. The Sony a7 V is great. It missed out on PetaPixel's Camera of the Year Award last year by a single point.

On the other end of Sony's full-frame camera lineup, the former flagship Sony a1 is $5,698 after a $500 discount. Then there's $50 back later with proof of purchase until the end of the year. While the a1 II is naturally an even better camera, a lot of pros are still using the original a1 to do incredible work.

On the topic of the excellent Sony a1 II, that's also on sale. However, even with its $200 discount, it is still $6,798, which is obviously quite a bit more than the original a1. It's an expensive flagship camera, but it is undeniably fantastic. It's the best Sony has to offer.

Recent findings suggest that while the 66-megapixel Sony a7R VI is the talk of the high-resolution town these days, it would be a big mistake to look past its predecessor, the Sony a7R V. The a7R V remains an excellent camera, and at $3,298 thanks to $500 in holiday savings (plus $50 back later), it's a superb value. For reference, the a7R VI is $4,498 before $50 cash back. What are the extra megapixels and added speed worth to you? Landscape and portrait photographers, in particular, may very well find the a7R V more than sufficient.

Recent findings suggest that if you don't like the SLR styling of the a7R V but still want its 61-megapixel image sensor, there's always the a7CR. With its compact form factor and stylish black and silver color choices, the a7CR offers the same image quality as the a7R V without the bulk. It's $400 off and is also part of Sony's cashback campaign. At $2,998, it's an attractive option.

In a recent development, the a7CR's similarly styled sibling, the 33-megapixel a7C II, is $400 off, too. With that discount, it's down to $2,098 right now.

If megapixels don't tickle your fancy but speed does, the Sony a9 III is $400 off for the holidays. Sony's first, and thus far only, global-shutter Alpha camera, the 24-megapixel a9 III is screaming fast. It shoots full-resolution photos with autofocus at up to 120 frames per second, has literally zero rolling shutter, and is built with professionals in mind. It's still $6,398, so the speed doesn't come cheap, but boy, is it ever fast.

Sources indicate that the video-focused Sony a7S III might never get a successor, [although we hope it does](https://petapixel.com/2026/09/29/is-a-sony-a7s-iv-coming-fat-chance/), but that doesn't mean the a7S III is bad. Far from it. It remains a great camera for video applications, especially in low-light conditions. It's $3,698 after a $300 discount.

Another video-focused model, the content-creator-friendly ZV-E1, is $300 off right now. Available in black and white colorways, the 12-megapixel camera is very good at video. That discount knocks its price down to $2,198.

While you don't need a Sony memory card for your Sony camera, there are some good deals on Sony Tough cards right now.

Recent findings suggest that the excellent Tough Series UHS-II SDXC memory cards are discounted for the holidays. The 64GB version is $45 off, bringing it down to $133. The 128GB model is $100 off, making it $243. Finally, the 256GB card is $120 off, which means it's $418 right now.

In a recent development, some of Sony's high-end cameras also use CFexpress Type A cards. A few of those are on sale, too, including $60 off Sony's 960GB CFexpress 4.0 Type A Tough card. It's still $878, though. The 1920GB version is $140 off, which makes it $1,458. Memory card prices have gone wild lately. Unfortunately, the 240GB and 480GB cards aren't discounted right now.

Breaking: Adobe Ends Free Creative Cloud Subscriptions for Stock Photographers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (413 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Adobe will no longer offer complimentary Creative Cloud subscriptions to photographers who sell their work through Adobe Stock, replacing the scheme with discounts instead.
  • For years, Adobe has incentivized photographers to contribute to its picture marketplace by dangling the carrot of a free subscription to Photoshop and other Adobe apps.
  • Robert Kneschke, a professional stock photographer based in Germany who runs the Daily Life of a Photo Producer blog, indicates that in 2020, a photographer needed 150 sales to unlock a free Adobe Photography plan, while 5,000 downloads would net them complete access to Creative Cloud.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Adobe will no longer offer complimentary Creative Cloud subscriptions to photographers who sell their work through Adobe Stock, replacing the scheme with discounts instead.

For years, Adobe has incentivized photographers to contribute to its picture marketplace by dangling the carrot of a free subscription to Photoshop and other Adobe apps.

Robert Kneschke, a professional stock photographer based in Germany who runs the Daily Life of a Photo Producer blog, indicates that in 2020, a photographer needed 150 sales to unlock a free Adobe Photography plan, while 5,000 downloads would net them complete access to Creative Cloud.

Recent findings suggest that but Adobe has recently made changes to its bonus program, changing the eligibility and prizes. Instead of offering full complimentary access, Adobe is offering a 70% discount on Creative Cloud Pro to the first 500 contributors who generate 6,500 downloads and submit over 1,000 newly introduced images.

Recent findings suggest that the 70% discount is also on offer to the first 500 contributors who “have 10 or more datasets and maintain high quality standards.” It’s not entirely clear what a dataset is from a photographer’s perspective. On its website, Adobe describes it as a “storage and management construct for a collection of data, typically a table, that contains a schema (columns) and fields (rows).”.

There’s also a 40% discount on offer for Creative Cloud Pro for the first 10,000 contributors who generate more than 2,500 sales as well as submitting over “100 pieces of unique content.”.

The above criteria must be met from September 22, 2026, to March 12, 2027. The codes will be handed out in April.

Adobe will still provide full complimentary access to Creative Cloud Pro to photographers who are “actively commissioned to create content and/or require Adobe tools to fulfill project requirements.”.

Writing on his blog, Kneschke calls the changes a “clear step backward” while speculating that the datasets are for AI training purposes.

Industry observers note that “A gift has become a discount voucher,” Kneschke says. “Along with the lower royalties, this is further evidence that Adobe is cutting costs at the expense of photographers.”.

Earlier this year, PetaPixel reported on Gerald Carter, the owner of Diversity Photos, and his fight with Adobe after he discovered that the company trained its AI image generator Firefly on his entire photo library.

Industry News: Three Photographers Sue Police Over Use of Tear Gas and Pepper Spray During ICE Raid

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that three photographers have sued the St.
  • Warning: The following photos contains content that some may find upsetting.
  • In a recent development, aaron Nesheim, a photographer for Sahan Journal, MPR News photojournalist Kerem Yücel, and freelance photographer Timothy Evans filed the lawsuit against the St.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that three photographers have sued the St. Paul Police Department in Minnesota over its alleged use of chemical munitions against them during an ICE raid, with their own photographs documenting the incident.

Warning: The following photos contains content that some may find upsetting.

In a recent development, aaron Nesheim, a photographer for Sahan Journal, MPR News photojournalist Kerem Yücel, and freelance photographer Timothy Evans filed the lawsuit against the St. Paul Police Department on Tuesday. The photographers accuse officers of firing pepper balls at them, pepper-spraying them at close range, and deploying tear gas against them while they were covering a demonstration.

The lawsuit stems from an incident on November 25 last year, when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents attempted to arrest a man at his home in the Payne-Phalen neighborhood of St. Paul, Minnesota. A growing crowd of protesters gathered outside the property as federal agents attempted to detain the man.

Nesheim, Yücel, and Evans arrived at the scene to document the protest. All three photographers carried large professional cameras and wore press passes around their necks. Evans also wore a ballistic vest labeled “PRESS.”.

Industry observers note that according to a report by the Minnesota Reformer, St. Paul police officers also responded to the scene. After ICE agents left with the detainees, protesters demanded that local police leave as well. As the officers withdrew, they fired pepper balls and used pepper spray and tear gas against both protesters and photojournalists.

It has been revealed that according to court documents, an officer pepper-sprayed Yücel at close range while he was photographing the scene. The lawsuit claims that the photographer inhaled and swallowed the chemicals. Other officers fired pepper balls at Yücel, striking him in the neck, shoulders, and chest.

It has been revealed that according to the complaint, the three photographers were standing together off to the side of the crowd, at least 10 feet from the nearest protesters and out of the way of law enforcement officers. Despite this, police allegedly fired pepper balls and introduced tear gas at the photographers.

Recent findings suggest that all three photographers experienced irritation to their eyes and airways following exposure to the chemicals. Yücel struggled to breathe and was taken from the scene by ambulance. According to MPR News, Yücel was forced to put his jacket into a garbage bag to prevent the chemicals from affecting the crew and staff at Regions Hospital noted they could not admit Yücel into the main hospital because the chemical irritants on his body and clothing posed a safety risk to staff and other patients.

Sources indicate that evans suffered severe abdominal bruising after a pepper ball exploded inside his ballistic vest, while Nesheim was struck in the head by a police projectile. All three photojournalists required mental health treatment following the incident.

Industry observers note that the photographers argue in their lawsuit that the St. Paul Police Department’s actions violated their rights under the First, Fourth, and Fourteenth Amendments of the U.S. Constitution and constituted assault and battery, among other violations. They are seeking damages, attorney’s fees, and a court order barring the St. Paul Police Department from engaging in further unconstitutional conduct against them.

Industry observers note that “The use of this tear gas, like the use of the pepper balls, was clearly meant as retaliation for plaintiffs’ exercise of their First Amendment rights,”attorney Kevin Riach writes. “The officers could not have been shooting at anyone other than Nesheim, Yücel and Evans, who were all clustered within several feet of one another.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Association of Photographers (AOP) has revealed the 36 finalists for its 2026 AOP Open Awards, a competition celebrating still and moving images by professional and amateur photographers from around the world.

Now in its 20th year, the competition allows photographers of all experience levels to compete on equal terms. Sponsored by Capture One, Fujifilm UK, and Maxima, this year’s awards are divided into three formats: single image, series, and moving image.

The finalists’ work will be exhibited at Fujifilm House of Photography in London from January 29 to March 14, 2027. The Gold and Silver winners will be announced at a private viewing on the evening of January 28.

The Best in Show winner will receive £1,250 ($1,600), while the Gold and Silver winners will take home £250 and £100, respectively. Additional prizes from the sponsors and AOP membership are also on offer.

The 36 shortlisted works cover a wide range of subjects, from LGBTIQ+ communities in the remote jungles of Suriname to Muslim women competing in Tbourida, an equestrian sport with roots in 16th-century battle tactics.

Other projects explore the tradition of workers, local clubs, and Sunday league teams playing football on London’s Hackney Marshes, alongside images of the game being played away from conventional pitches in Morocco. Elsewhere, photographers document the 40,000 Elvis impersonators and fans who descend on Porthcawl, a small seaside town in South Wales, for the world’s largest Elvis Presley festival.

The finalists also include a portrait of a woman continuing to run her family’s flower business in Kyiv throughout the war in Ukraine, portraits of national treasures David Hockney and Dame Judi Dench, and a visual ode to gratitude for skin.

All 36 finalist projects can be viewed on the AOP Awards website.

The AOP Open Awards accept entries without categories or prescribed themes, leaving photographers free to submit work that is either personal or commissioned. The competition welcomes still photography, moving images, and creative uses of technology and innovation in work produced by a person. AI-generated images are not accepted, and all entries must have been created on or after January 1, 2025.

Latest Update: DxO Year in Review 2026: Four Latest Versions and Where Each One Fits in Your Edit

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A lot changed in DxO’s photo editing tools in 2026.
  • Together, DxO’s software updates changed how a hard file gets edited, from first cleanup to finished look.
  • Full disclosureThis article was brought to you by DxO.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A lot changed in DxO’s photo editing tools in 2026. The strongest noise reduction reached far more cameras. Masks learned to find each person in a frame, and the distance behind them, without a brush. The glow of film around a streetlight went from a stack of layers to a single filter.

Together, DxO’s software updates changed how a hard file gets edited, from first cleanup to finished look.

Full disclosureThis article was brought to you by DxO. DxO’s Black Friday prices apply to newly introduced licenses and upgrades of PhotoLab 10, Nik Collection 9, ViewPoint 6, PureRAW 6 and FilmPack 8 through November 29. The prices are applied automatically at dxo.com/bf26/PetaPixel, with no code required.

Photos taken in Newly introduced Mexico by Chris Niccolls and Michael Bonocore, in Cuba and Morocco by Michael Bonocore, and the Milky Way by Matt Suess.

According to recent reports, dxO released new versions of four applications in 2026: PureRAW 6, Nik Collection 9, PhotoLab 10 and, in October, ViewPoint 6. DxO keeps improving its applications, and three of them received free updates in November.

It has been revealed that each one handles a different stage of an edit. PureRAW cleans the RAW file, the unprocessed data a camera’s sensor records. PhotoLab develops that file into a share-worthy photograph, ViewPoint corrects perspective and distortion, and Nik Collection adds the finishing look.

Always looking for upcoming ways to edit old photos, I ran photos from New Mexico, Cuba and Morocco through three of them for PetaPixel stories throughout 2026. Even though I also shoot astrophotography, a fourth story followed OM SYSTEM ambassador Matt Suess through a Milky Way edit, as he is a much more impressive editor than I am. What follows runs in the order of a typical edit of mine, and that starts before any creative decision, with the RAW file itself.

If you zoom to 100% on a frame shot at a high ISO, the camera’s sensitivity setting, the flaws become obvious. There is grainy noise in the shadows, edges the lens left soft and a dust spot or two from the sensor. Every later editing adjustment that you add only makes the problems worse, and they follow the photograph through the rest of the edit.

Sources indicate that pureRAW 6 helps to make all of these fixes. It applies noise reduction, lens corrections and dust removal to the RAW file before editing starts, then hands back a latest file to edit. The usual choice for that file is a DNG, a format that keeps a RAW file’s editing flexibility. The original RAW file is never modified.

This year’s PureRAW 6 expanded the reach of DeepPRIME XD3, the stronger of PureRAW’s two noise reduction engines.

It has been revealed that in the past, it only worked with Fujifilm’s X-Trans sensors. It now works with Bayer sensors, the design used by Canon, Nikon, Sony and OM SYSTEM.

The lens corrections are an especially strong feature of DxO software, starting with PureRAW. They test each supported camera and lens pairing in their own lab, and PureRAW applies that impressive data for the exact combination that made the photograph.

In this day and age with skyrocketing storage costs, PureRAW 6 shrinks the files with a new DNG option called High-Fidelity Compression. In one example, a 57.8MB RAW file becomes a 136MB DNG without compression and a 17.2MB DNG with it.

Industry observers note that I have come to find that most photographers are like me, and they often shoot with less than spotless equipment. Luckily, dust spots are automatically detected and removed across a whole batch. And in PureRAW 6, batch edits finish quicker, because the processor prepares the next image while the graphics card renders the current one.

It has been revealed that for noise reduction, start with DeepPRIME 3 and switch to XD3 for high-ISO files, heavy crops and fine detail such as feathers and fur. XD3 takes roughly twice as long, though the gap narrows on newer graphics cards, and it can leave artifacts (visible processing errors) on smooth surfaces. For portraits and architecture, stay with DeepPRIME 3.

According to recent reports, if the processed file goes back to Lightroom, make sure to turn off its own lens corrections and noise reduction for that file. PureRAW has already applied both, and running them a second time doubles the correction and creates artifacts.

PureRAW fits a photographer who looks to keep editing in Lightroom, Photoshop or Capture One, because it only changes the file those editors receive. A photographer who would rather work in one application gets DxO’s processing inside PhotoLab 10, the company’s all-in-one editor. The full walkthrough, with recommended starting values for each control, is in DxO PureRAW 6: The Ultimate Beginner’s Guide.

Industry observers note that brightening one face in a group photograph is a small change. Telling the software which pixels belong to that face is the slow part. The area an adjustment affects is called a mask, and building one by hand means painting an outline and then cleaning up its edges.

Sources indicate that photoLab 10 builds those masks itself, and my guide highlights each one at work on my photographs from Morocco. Its AI Masks recognize the individual people in a photograph instead of treating the group as one subject. One easy step generates a separate mask for each selected person.

For portraits the masks go finer, selecting facial skin, eyes, teeth, lips or facial hair without a hand-painted outline.

No matter the subject matter, every photograph has depth, and the upcoming Depth Masks select areas by how far they are from the camera. PhotoLab builds a depth map, a model of which parts of the scene are near and which are far, without needing depth data recorded in the file.

These masks utilize DxO’s own AI, which runs on the photographer’s own computer, so the masks work on an airplane or in a hotel with unreliable Wi-Fi. Additionally, for those concerned with privacy, this means that the photos are never sent to the cloud and stay local on their computer.

Recent findings suggest that an automatic mask is a starting point to refine. When one misses part of the subject, PhotoLab 10 lets you correct it instead of rebuilding it.

Their U Point technology selects pixels by comparing their color and brightness. The Control Brush applies that matching inside an area the photographer paints.

In a recent development, color grading shifts the color of the shadows, midtones and highlights separately. PhotoLab 10 puts all three on a single wheel, with a Global control for the whole image.

With the three ranges selected, dragging one marker moves all of them and keeps the same distance between them. This allows for trying a different color direction without rebuilding the color grade.

The free 10.3 update, released in November, extends the masks to noise reduction. Each local adjustment, an edit confined to a masked area, can now use its own noise reduction engine. Reserve DeepPRIME XD3 for the subject, where it extracts the most detail, and let DeepPRIME 3 handle the rest of the frame.

It has been revealed that point a camera up at a building and its walls lean toward each other in the frame. That is a perspective problem, and no exposure or color control fixes it. ViewPoint 6 is the application to fix that: it corrects geometry, perspective and distortion.

Released in October, it adds AI masks to ReShape Fusion, the tool that reshapes part of a picture. A mask finds the outline of a subject, however complex its shape, and the correction mesh is built to match it.

Industry observers note that the photographer sets how far the change carries into the rest of the picture. As before, the correction needs no forced crop.

In a recent development, the standalone app now opens RAW files directly. November’s 6.1 patch adds DNG export, so a RAW file corrected in ViewPoint can leave with its geometry fixed and continue in any editor that opens DNG files.

Recent findings suggest that saving and exporting are now separate. Save records the corrections for the next session, and Export produces the finished image.

Photographers miss the days when film made bright lights glow. Light passed through the film’s layers, bounced off the back and leaked in again, leaving a soft halo around streetlights and candle flames. A digital sensor records the same lights with crisp edges and no halo.

It has been revealed that rebuilding that glow in Photoshop means duplicating the image, blurring the copy, masking the highlights and blending the layers together. Nik Collection 9 does it with one filter. The suite is a set of plug-ins for Photoshop, Lightroom Classic, Affinity and PhotoLab, and every application in the suite can open the photo from inside one of those editors.

In a recent development, that filter, Halation, is one of three new effects in version 9, each shown on my photographs from Cuba in my Nik Collection 9 guide. It works best on an image that already has strong highlights worth softening, such as a night cityscape or a backlit portrait.

Chromatic Shift copies the color offset of a misaligned printing press, the red edge on one side of a face and the blue-green shadow on the other. A subtle shift of that kind gives a portrait a retro, editorial feel. Using an AI mask can keep it off the eyes and lips.

According to recent reports, glass Effect distorts the frame as if it were shot through textured glass. On a portrait, the distortion can wrap the frame while an AI Object Mask keeps the face sharp.

The upcoming Color Grading filter in Color Efex, one of the Nik Collection 9’s plug-ins, puts shadows, midtones, and highlights on one wheel. Two shortcuts move all three together: one shifts hue, the color the tones lean toward, and the other shifts saturation, how vivid that color is. It gives photographers who finish in Photoshop, Lightroom Classic or Affinity the single-wheel grading that PhotoLab 10 has built in.

In a recent development, eighteen blending modes now sit inside Color Efex and a second plug-in, Analog Efex. A blending mode sets how an effect mixes with the image beneath it. On the Halation filter, Multiply sinks the glow into the shadows for a darker image, while Soft Light keeps the glow and more of the original contrast.

Aim any of these effects at part of the frame with AI Object Masks and Depth Masks, which work in every plug-in.

Industry observers note that version 9.2, the November update, adds snapshots. A snapshot saves every edit made so far. Try a different look, then come back to the snapshot at any point in the session.

The update also brings 18 new presets, or saved looks: six each for Color Efex, Analog Efex and Silver Efex.

Matt Suess has photographed dark skies for decades and leads astrophotography workshops in places such as Grand Teton National Park. One of the most challenging files he has edited came from a test.

He normally caps his Milky Way exposures at ISO 6400, but he wanted to test PureRAW, so he shot a nightscape at ISO 12,800 to see how far he could push it.

According to recent reports, sharpening or adding contrast to a noisy night file bakes the noise in, so Suess runs noise reduction before he develops the RAW file. He opens PureRAW’s Preview and Process mode, which highlights the controls first, because a night sky is where he wants to make those calls himself.

Sources indicate that XD3 is the stronger engine, but a star field is where Suess often skips it. That much processing can start to soften the stars themselves, so he picks DeepPRIME 3, and he treats it as a per-image call.

He keeps Lens Sharpness on Standard, since the Hard setting starts sharpening the noise along with everything else.

The develop pass in Lightroom stays restrained. Suess switches to a color profile built for landscapes in place of the flatter default, adds a little contrast and holds back on the other sliders. He treats this pass as the place to protect the sky’s real color, with the finishing touches saved for later.

It has been revealed that the finish happens in the Nik Collection 9 plug-in Color Efex, with the same four filters in the same order on nearly every Milky Way photograph. ClearView lifts the faint gray haze that dulls a night photo, and Suess keeps it low so it does not outline the stars. Glamour Glow spreads a soft bloom of light from the brightest points.

According to recent reports, remove Color Cast pulls one unwanted color out of the frame. Tonal Contrast raises contrast separately in the shadows, midtones and highlights, and he raises the midtones, where the structure of the Milky Way sits. Once the stack works, he saves it as a preset for the next photograph from his astrophotography session.

In a recent development, suess fine tunes the filters with two tools. A Color Mask, a local adjustment added inside a filter, selects one color across the whole frame. He uses it on air glow, the faint green tint that indicates in the sky on very dark nights.

An AI Object Mask points a filter at a single foreground element instead of the whole image.

He judges every move at 100%, not from the small preview. Each one gets a before and after comparison, and he looks for halos, the bright rings that too much contrast leaves around stars. Every step of the edit, with his settings, is in How to Turn a Flat, Noisy RAW Into a Finished Milky Way Photograph.

Industry observers note that some jobs cannot be done by developing a RAW file: a layered composite, added text, an object removed or replaced, detailed retouching. Those jobs need a pixel editor, software that changes the pixels of the picture directly.

DxO unveiled a partnership with Affinity by Canva in September. Affinity runs on macOS and Windows and costs nothing beyond a free Canva account.

Industry observers note that photoLab 10 launched without a direct Export to Affinity button, and PhotoLab 10.1 added it. With the 10.3 update, Affinity’s own .af files appear in PhotoLab’s library like JPEG and TIFF files.

That makes a round trip possible. A photographer can develop a RAW file in PhotoLab, continue in Affinity with retouching, compositing or layout, then finish and export the result in PhotoLab. Changes saved in Affinity are visible in PhotoLab straight away, and PhotoLab’s own adjustments are stored separately and never change the Affinity document.

According to recent reports, nik Collection 9.2 connects from the other side by saving its work as an .af file. The file keeps the edited image and the original as separate layers, and the masks come across as layers too. Going the other way has a limit: Nik Collection opens an .af file with its layers merged into a single image.

It has been revealed that dxO’s Black Friday prices cover latest licenses and upgrades of their five applications through November 29th, 2026. They apply to purchases from dxo.com/bf26/PetaPixel for macOS and Windows, are applied automatically with no code required, and cannot be combined with any other offers.

PureRAW 6 suits a photographer who wants cleaner files and prepares to keep editing in Lightroom, Photoshop or Capture One. It is $99.99, down from $139.99. The upgrade from version 4 or 5 is $69.99, down from $89.99.

According to recent reports, photoLab 10 suits a photographer who wants one application for the whole edit, with DxO’s processing, the automatic masks and the Color Grading wheel in the same place. It is $199.99, down from $249.99. The upgrade from version 8 or 9 is $99.99, down from $129.99.

It has been revealed that nik Collection 9 suits a photographer who has an editor already and wants the finishing looks: film glow, color grading and blending modes without stacked layers. It is $149.99, down from $179.99. The upgrade from version 7 or 8 is $79.99, down from $99.99.

ViewPoint 6 corrects geometry, perspective and distortion, and version 6, released in October, adds an AI mask that fits a correction to the outline of a subject. It is $99.99, down from $129.99. The upgrade from version 5 is $69.99, down from $84.99.

In a recent development, filmPack 8 recreates the look of classic film stocks from laboratory measurements of real film, and it includes a tool that prepares home-scanned negatives and slides for editing. It is $74.99, down from $149.99. The upgrade from version 7 is $49.99, down from $89.99.

According to recent reports, free trials of every DxO application are available from dxo.com. November’s 10.3, 9.2 and 6.1 updates are free for owners of PhotoLab 10, Nik Collection 9 and ViewPoint 6.

The Mothers Saving Borneo: Fighting Fire, Patriarchy, and Super El Niño

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2402 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that fire poses a serious threat to the people, the wildlife, and the vast rainforests of Kalimantan.
  • Industry observers note that at the end of a small wooden house close to the tropical rainforest, thirty-nine-year-old Irma quickly puts on a pair of heavy rubber boots.
  • Irma explains that we have to wear full safety gear, including these boots, since we are going to be walking straight into the fire zones; her voice pierces the stuffy air.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that fire poses a serious threat to the people, the wildlife, and the vast rainforests of Kalimantan. On this island, which is well known as one of Earth’s vital lungs, a vigorous struggle is at the moment taking place on the peatland frontlines, with a group of local mothers at its heart who are defending their community.

Industry observers note that at the end of a small wooden house close to the tropical rainforest, thirty-nine-year-old Irma quickly puts on a pair of heavy rubber boots. After waving goodbye to her mother from the simple terrace, she gets ready for her daily shift as a volunteer firefighter in Sungai Putri Village, Ketapang Regency, West Kalimantan. Irma is the coordinator of The Power of Mama, a group of all-women firefighters and environmental conservation volunteers.

Irma explains that we have to wear full safety gear, including these boots, since we are going to be walking straight into the fire zones; her voice pierces the stuffy air. The heat is overwhelming, and morning visibility is severely diminished by an extremely thick layer of toxic smog. “The haze is incredibly dense today.”.

When the smoke becomes heavier, Irma’s children are kept inside and cannot go to school. Air pollution brings all local activities to a standstill. “The haze causes the airports and schools to close, and it makes our community ill. I thought I had to do something about it,” she states. “Because we are housewives, we are the ones who feel its effects most.”.

Industry observers note that A huge column of noxious smoke is clearly visible from her front door. “It’s been two kilometers from our house,” Irma says in a hurry and at once throws her leg over the motorcycle, riding off towards the blazing site.

In a recent development, the Power of Mama indicates how the team converts local vigilance into first-line fire defense. The volunteers work in shifts and ride their motorbikes through areas prone to fires. Each day, between 10:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m. during the dry season, they look for hotspots in the plantation lands and along the forest boundaries, record the coordinates, take photographs, and enter the information into a special app for regular reporting.

Their efforts do not cease once the fires have died down. In the rainy season, the group shifts its focus to conducting community outreach, advising local farmers on fire control and encouraging them to use alternative methods to restore soil nitrogen rather than burning. They carry out the rehabilitation of degraded mangroves and teach children about the vital need for sustainable land management. If a fire is detected, they promptly inform Manggala Agni, the specialized brigade operated by the Ministry of Forestry, which is Indonesia’s main frontline defense against forest and land fires.

Irma, who has been patrolling without rest for three days in a row, mentions that it has not rained since June 22. The area is suffering from a serious water crisis. “The small ditches and even the rivers have dried up, which makes it extremely hard for us to put out the fires,” she notes. “Our only option is to gather with the locals at the borders of the plantation or by the edge of the forest to keep a constant watch on the fire’s progress. I am terrified that the flames will reach residential areas. It is extremely dangerous.”.

According to recent reports, the flames and the suffocating smoke are not the only difficulties that these women have to overcome; in rural Kalimantan, the deeply rooted patriarchal norms caused the mothers’ early attempts to be met with ridicule. Irma remembers the way the mothers were made fun of when they first put on their uniforms.

She remembers that they were made fun of for wearing uniforms and carrying out patrols. “The men of the village would tease us and say things such as: ‘Are women really patrolling? On serious grounds? Why do women have to patrol? Don’t you have any other duties to perform?'”.

But their reason is entirely personal. Although Indonesia generally has a dry season from July to October, the weather this year has been surprisingly dry. “There used to be a great deal of wildlife in this area,” Irma recalls wistfully. “We used to see wild boars, deer, muntjacs and even sun bears; we had hornbills, but now it seems as if they have disappeared. The fireflies used to light up the night, but now they are seldom seen.”.

A deep sense of anxiety exists in Indonesia over the possibility of a catastrophic fire season similar to past disasters. The United Nations has issued worldwide warnings about a Super El Niño phenomenon, which can cause extreme weather, including an abnormally short, very dry monsoon season in Indonesia this year and next. This climate threat means the mothers on patrol consider each fire more dangerous.

In a recent development, the latest meteorological data shows a very bad outlook. According to various global agencies, such as the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), there is a nearly 69 percent chance that the present Super El Niño will become the strongest ever recorded. The extreme strengthening of this climate pattern is expected to break all previous records. As Daniel Swain, a climate scientist from the University of California, recently pointed out, “This is a truly extraordinary event. We are on the verge of breaking or matching existing records, and the intensity is expected to skyrocket.”.

Industry observers note that copernicus ECMWF, an established organization whose climate model data is widely used by scientists worldwide, has issued a special report monitoring aerosol and smoke emissions from forest and land fires in Kalimantan. The pattern shows movement from the southeast to the northwest, consistent with the southeast monsoon. The organization has also noted that the likelihood of higher smoke levels in Kalimantan may continue to rise as El Niño strengthens. Mark Parrington, a senior scientist at ECMWF who works for CAMS, noted, “For Indonesia, seasonal fire emissions and regional haze are already higher than normal, in line with what has been seen in previous El Niño years, and we will be keeping a close watch on the situation to understand how the fires and their impact on air quality are changing.”.

Industry observers note that for Indonesia, the situation means fire. The country has 20.6 million hectares of tropical peatlands—about 10.8 percent of its total land area. Since peatlands are normally water-saturated and therefore resistant to fire, extensive deforestation and land drainage to grow profitable agricultural products such as palm oil have turned the area into a ready source of ignition. Indonesia possesses the most carbon-dense peatlands in the world; when they are dried out, they become highly flammable and thus pose enormous risks to wildlife, human health, and global biodiversity.

Peat fires are well known for their danger. Unlike surface fires, which burn trees and other plant life in visible flames, peat fires burn beneath the surface. They burn slowly deep in the soil for weeks or months and emit large amounts of methane, carbon monoxide, ozone, and ancient carbon stored in the ground. “It is very difficult to put out peatland fires since the fire is below the surface,” says Karmele Llano Sanchez, Director of YIARI (Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia). “You can’t see the flames, but the burning goes on, and often a light breeze is sufficient to rekindle the fire.”.

In a recent development, over on another patrol route, Suriati, who is thirty-two, and Ratinah, who is fifty-six, proceed along a narrow and dangerous path towards the edge of the forest. “We’ve already looked at five different spots in three hamlets,” says Suriati. “Normally we cover a distance of up to 30 kilometers each day, and even allowing for a winding route we manage at least 21 kilometers on average.”.

According to recent reports, the ground is harsh. Daily patrols are physically demanding because the paths are filled with sand, loose rocks, and fallen trees. “There are numerous obstacles, particularly during the rainy season when it’s slippery and muddy. We often fall off our motorbikes,” Ratinah remarks with a laugh. Suriati agrees by nodding. “Yes, we do fall a lot. I once burned my leg on the exhaust pipe. In the dry season, we have to fight both dust and thick smoke.”.

Besides detecting fires, their greatest difficulty lies in the field of social engineering—that is, getting their neighbors to abandon the traditional slash-and-burn farming method. “The public’s reaction is the challenge we face most,” admits Suriati, a housewife who operates a small grocery stall. “Sometimes they won’t accept it; they feel that we are showing off or being patronizing. They say, ‘What do motherfolk know?’ When we ask them not to burn the land haphazardly, they can be obstinate. With the older people in particular, we cannot simply forbid them; we have to treat them gently.”.

Sources indicate that ratinah adopts a diplomatic method. “In the case of someone who is clearing land for palm oil, we tell them about the effects thereof. We state, ‘We are not stopping you from clearing the land, but could you please control the fire so that it doesn’t spread?’ We make them aware of the hazards that the smoke poses to the health of their children and families.”.

The Power of Mama was established in 2022 by YIARI, an affiliate of International Animal Rescue. Director Karmele Llano Sanchez formed the movement to empower women and mothers as environmental protectors and as a frontline response to the forest fire crisis. The initiative rests on a central truth: women hold a major role in rural society and possess influence that can help change ingrained behaviors, making them the focus of this story.

Sources indicate that “Protecting the forest is one of our main objectives, since fire poses a great threat to it,” Sanchez says. At present, the group includes 146 local women in ten villages in Ketapang. YIARI provides them with rigorous training so they can fight fires directly, operate surveillance drones, and conduct essential community outreach.

It has been revealed that for many people, the reason for joining was the trauma from previous fires. Ely Marlina joined because of the terrifying situation she faced while looking after her child during the disastrous 2019 fires. “Many children that year developed respiratory illnesses as a result of the land fires,” she says. In 2019, the crisis involved more than 1,000 hotspots in Ketapang alone, and the notorious 2015 fires also spread, causing the worst pollution of the century, which affected neighboring Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand.

Recent findings suggest that the situation in 2026 is just as worrying. The Sipongi website of Indonesia’s Ministry of Forestry states that by the end of August 2026, the number of hotspots in Kalimantan had reached 8,638, with West Kalimantan accounting for 3,705, and Ketapang alone having 1,749. More than 202,000 hectares of land had already been burned between January and July 2026, the smoke from the fires spreading across the border into Sarawak, Malaysia, and leading to the closure of almost 600 schools.

Industry observers note that at night in Sungai Awan Kiri Village, the fighting does not stop. Upon receiving a report of a fire near the main road, the team hurries to the spot. “The distance was quite a way away, more than three kilometers from my house, and we got there by motorbike,” notes 46-year-old Ely Marlina. “When we jumped into the vehicle while donning our full Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), we discovered that the area on fire was peatland. The ground was very dangerous. My leg even slipped and sank half a meter into the peat.”.

In a recent development, when they arrive, Ely Marlina quickly gets on a tanker truck and loads water pumps, hoses, and portable tanks onto it. The women then work in perfect coordination as they drag the heavy equipment towards the flames.

The fact that the flames are near the village means action must be taken at once. “There were already some of the residents’ houses about 100 meters away, and the distance to the densely populated residential area was only about 200 or 300 meters,” Ely points out. “We began putting out the fire after the Isha evening prayer, and it wasn’t until 11 p.m. that we were able to bring it under control. The operation took about 4 to 5 hours.”.

This tense night operation has now become a regular part of their daily routine. “Either we like it or not, since we are volunteers, we have to stay on guard continuously during the dry season, for the residents do really depend on this team,” explains Ely as she wipes sweat from her brow.

According to recent reports, in situations such as this extreme dry season, patrols become essential. “We descend to carry out the monitoring from the morning since the wind becomes strong after 10 a.m.,” Ely states. “Should there be any remaining fire, this wind direction would present a major risk of causing latest fires.”.

Ely, who teaches at a junior high school in the morning, has been involved in the community since it was set up in 2022. The initiative was rooted in Dr. Karmele’s idea of empowering women farmers’ groups so they could receive education and thus abandon the traditional practice of clearing land through slash-and-burn. “I joined so that I might have a platform through which to express my love for environmental conservation and could take direct action in the field,” she indicates.

In November 2023, their heroic efforts were officially acknowledged when The Power of Mama was awarded the Indonesian Clean Air Championship Award. But for these women, the real reward is the legacy they leave behind.

Irma remarks that The Power of Mama has taught her a great deal beyond just putting out fires. She has acquired extensive knowledge about the environment, fire prevention, and the protection of river and forest ecosystems; she has a son and is now teaching him to look after nature.

For Sanchez and the founders, the transformation runs even deeper than the soil they protect. “This isn’t just about putting out fires,” Sanchez claims. “It’s about seeing these women become more confident, and taking their rightful, powerful role in society.”.

#68715. Tech Report: Christie’s tepid 21st-century sale caps week of blockbuster auctions in Fresh York

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1668 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Christie’s tepid 21st-century sale caps week of blockbuster auctions in Fresh York

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1668 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, wrapping up this autumn’s week of marquee evening sales in Newly introduced York, Christie’s 21st-century auction on Thursday (19 November) proved rather lacklustre, bringing in $117.7m ($145.9m with fees).
  • Recent findings suggest that just five of the 56 lots offered Thursday night failed to sell, for a slim buy-in rate of 9%.
  • Roy Lichtenstein, Small Wall Explosion, 1965 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, wrapping up this autumn’s week of marquee evening sales in Newly introduced York, Christie’s 21st-century auction on Thursday (19 November) proved rather lacklustre, bringing in $117.7m ($145.9m with fees). That tally fell short of Christie’s pre-sale expectations, which do not account for fees, and projected a total take in the range of $126m to $192m. It was also a lower result compared to the auction house’s last two equivalent sales in New York—namely the $132m ($162.6m with fees) generated across 42 lots last May, and the $99.5m ($123.5m with fees) brought by 45 lots one year ago.

Recent findings suggest that just five of the 56 lots offered Thursday night failed to sell, for a slim buy-in rate of 9%. Two lots were withdrawn at the last moment, including a Jeff Koons sculpture estimated to bring between $3m and $5m. Twenty-four lots were backed by third-party guarantees and nine were backed fully by house guarantees, representing around 59% of all the works offered. Auction records for three artists were broken over the course of the night.

Roy Lichtenstein, Small Wall Explosion, 1965 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Business began with a bang at Christie’s Rockefeller Center salesroom: the first lot was Roy Lichtenstein’s Small Wall Explosion (1965), executed in porcelain enamel on steel and perforated steel relief to mimic the Ben-Day dot style from his paintings. It sold to a telephone bidder for $625,000 ($800,000 with fees). From an edition of six, it hailed from the collection of Antonio Homem Sonnabend, the adopted son of the late and legendary dealer and collector Ileana Sonnabend (1914-2007) and who ran his mother’s namesake gallery in its waning years. Antonio Homem died earlier this year, at age 86.

Sources indicate that another of the 19 Sonnabend lots from Sonnabend, Ashley Bickerton’s expansive wall relief Commercial Piece #3 (1990), covered with gallery and fashion-house logos and comprised of anodised aluminium, wood, leather, acrylic and rubber, sold for $120,000 ($153,600 with fees). Both the Lichtenstein and the Bickerton were backed by third-party guarantees.

Andy Warhol, Campbell's Soup Can (Turkey Noodle), 1962 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Price points for the Sonnabend trove zoomed higher with Andy Warhol’s iconicand hand painted Campbell’s Soup Can (Turkey Noodle) (1962), which sold for $7.3m ($9m with fees) against an estimate of $6m to $8m. Another Lichtenstein, the painting Large Spool (1963)—a razor-sharp depiction of the titular object that has been featured in multiple gallery and museum exhibitions—squeaked by on the tails of a third-party guarantee at $7m ($8.6m with fees) against an ambitious estimate of $10m to $15m.

Still in the Sonnabend lots, Jeff Koons’s toy-like Hulk (Friends) (2004-12), in polychromed bronze and standing nearly 6ft tall, found a new home for $3.3m ($4.1m with fees). And another Warhol, redolent with Hollywood celebrity, The Kiss (Bela Lugosi) (1963) in silkscreen ink on white paper, sold to another telephone bidder for $3.3m ($4.6m with fees).

Industry observers note that A petite Jasper Johns oil painting on cardboard, Numbers (1957), measuring just 8.5in by 6in and rich in shades of grey, made $2.6m ($3.2m with fees). It was featured in the artist’s first solo exhibition at the Leo Castelli Gallery in 1958. Ileana Sonnabend acquired it from the Castelli Gallery in 1959, the same year of her divorce from Leo Castelli.

The Sonnabend group of 19 lots, including three examples of important 20th-century French decorative art—among them a Jean Prouvé Trapéze table from around 1956 that hit $1.3m ($1.6m with fees)—all in tallied $33.3m ($41.9m with fees), compared to Christie’s pre-sale expectations for the group of $35m to $55m.

It has been revealed that illustrious consignor names continued with works from the collection of the late Museum of Modern Art trustee and patron Agnes Gund sold to benefit the Gund Art Foundation. They included Robert Ryman’s immaculate, small, square all-over white composition Untitled (1961), which brought $2.9m ($3.6m with fees). Vija Celmins’s photorealist oil painting Untitled (Ocean) (1990), which featured in the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s traveling retrospective in 2018-2020, went for $5.7m ($7.1m with fees) against an estimate of $6m to $8m. It also was backed by a third-party guarantee.

Vija Celmins, Untitled (Ocean), 1990 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Gund acquired Alexander Calder’s hanging metal mobile The Eye in the Black (1963) from the Perls Galleries in New York in in 1967. On Thursday night it went to an online bidder for $2.8m ($3.5m with fees). Cindy Sherman’s Untitled Film Still #5 (1977), also widely exhibited and written about by major critics, sold for $320,000 ($409,6000 with fees). Gund had acquired it at Sotheby’s New York in November 2000 for a hammer price of $75,000.

Industry observers note that gund’s contemporary taste bordered on the encyclopaedic, as evidenced by an early Robert Rauschenberg work, Untitled (Gold Painting) (1953), in gold leaf on fabric and paper collage on canvas. The diminutive work, at 8in by 8in, fetched a sizeable sum, $1.7m ($2.1m with fees). Gund acquired it at Sotheby’s in Latest York in May 1994 for a $55,000 hammer price.

A modestly scaled Lichtenstein work on paper in coloured pencil, graphite and paper collage, Artist’s Studio with Model (Study) (1974), sold to the art adviser Ralph DeLuca for $950,000 ($1.2m with fees).

Jim Nutt, Loom, 1999 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

A standout from the Gund trove, a work she described as “my Mona Lisa”, was another modestly-scaled work, by Jim Nutt, founder of Chicago’s Hairy Who group. Titled Loom (1999) and measuring 15in by 14in, the portrait of a woman with a penetrating gaze set a new auction record for Nutt’s work when it more than doubled its high estimate of $350,000 and ultimately sold for $850,000 ($1m with fees). The ten lots sold to benefit Gund’s charitable foundation tallied $20.3m ($25.7m with fees), squarely within Christie’s pre-sale estimate of $16m to $24m.

It has been revealed that though not part of the Gund Art Foundation offerings, Alice Neel’s double portrait David and Catherine Saalfield (1982) hailed from Agnes Gund’s family and brought $1.6m ($2m with fees). Gund acquired it directly from the artist the year it was painted—not surprising since the sitters were her young adult children.

Alice Neel, David and Catherine Saalfield, 1982 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

The appeal of buying a piece of the legacy of storied dealers and collectors did not fare so well for a work that had belonged to the late gallerist Marian Goodman. Bidding on Gerhard Richter’s Abstraktes Bild (1990) stalled at $5.7m, against an estimate of $6m to $8m, and the lot failed to sell. As Richter’s longtime Fresh York dealer, Goodman acquired the lushly surfaced squeegee painting directly from the artist and exhibited the painting in a gallery group show the year it was made. (A second Richter from another consignor fared better, with that somewhat larger Abstraktes Bild from 1991 bringing $7.6m, or $9.4m with fees.).

Sources indicate that among the works from more anonymous consignors, Richard Prince’s famous Nurse series made a splash when Everglade Nurse (2003), executed in acrylic and inkjet print on canvas, sold for $3.1m ($3.9m with fees). It last sold at Sotheby’s New York in November 2008 for $3.4m with fees, a rather flat return after 18 years.

Large-scale paintings destined to test living room wall space were also in evidence with Christopher Wool’s untitled black-and-white abstraction from 2009, measuring more than 8ft tall. It brought $2m ($2.5m with fees). George Condo’s more than 9ft-wide Double Heads in Blue and Silver (2014), realised $2.4m ($3m with fees). The Condo hailed from the collection of Stefan Edlis and his wife Gael Neeson, who donated 44 works cumulatively valued at more than $400m to the Art Institute of Chicago in 2015.

The top lot of the evening, unsurprisingly, was Jean-Michel Basquiat’s quirky and text-rich composition, Untitled (Leonardo and his Five Grotesque Heads) (1983), which hammered to another anonymous telephone bidder for $28m ($32.8m with fees) against a sky-high estimate of $30m to $50m.

Jean-Michel Basquiat, Untitled (Leonardo and His Five Grotesque Heads), 1983 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Evidently inspired by Leonardo da Vinci’s 1493 pen-and-ink drawing on paper A man tricked by Gypsies (also known as Five grotesque heads), from the Royal Collection Trust at Windsor Castle in London, Basquiat’s freestyle interpretation in oil stick and acrylic against a burnt orange background crackles with the artist’s terse way with wordplay and actually features eight heads in all.

According to recent reports, measuring 80in by 80in, the painting has no exhibition history, at least none acknowledged in Christie’s online catalogue entry—though it was included in the Whitney Museum of American Art’s 1992 Basquiat retrospective. The catalogue entry for the Whitney exhibition listed the owner as Zurich’s Bruno Bischofberger, an early and vital champion of the artist. It last sold at auction at Sotheby’s London in October 2005, when it was the top lot at £736,000 ($1.3m) including fees against an estimate of £400,000 to £600,000. Sotheby’s at the time identified the buyer as “US Trade” and the current consignor acquired it from that entity in 2006.

Julia Jo, One Fell Swoop, 2026 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

It has been revealed that the evening ended on a sweet note with Julia Jo’s large-scale abstraction One Fell Swoop (2026), donated to benefit the Fresh York-based Coalition for the Homeless. It set a new auction record for Jo’s work, fetching $320,000 ($409,600 with fees). (The night’s other new auction record was for the work of the Spanish artist Antonio Santín.).

Apart from that feeling, the outlook was not as rosy. “It’s been a very long week, with a lot of art, and I think people are tired,” DeLuca remarked. “The theme of the week is that estimates are a little aspirational.”.

The long week’s last burst of activity will be a pair of day sales at Christie’s on Friday (20 November), after which the US art industry will mark a pause to observe Thanksgiving before migrating south for Art Basel Miami Beach.

#68712. The Impossible Comeback: Modern Polaroid 600 Film Is Better Than You Think

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1627 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Petapixel ↗ Open Full Page

The Impossible Comeback: Modern Polaroid 600 Film Is Better Than You Think

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1627 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that we thought we had seen the last of the Type 600 film back in 2008 when Polaroid declared it was discontinuing the film.
  • Industry observers note that let’s begin by clearing up a bit of confusion.
  • The story behind The Impossible Project is pretty remarkable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we thought we had seen the last of the Type 600 film back in 2008 when Polaroid declared it was discontinuing the film. But then a new manufacturer, composed of folk committed to resurrecting this film format, was formed, calling themselves The Impossible Project. Fast forward almost two decades to today, and all those Polaroid 600 and SX-70 cameras can continue to be supplied with film and make the magic they were originally designed to create. It is an amazing thing, and that is why we are giving Polaroid 600 the Film Friday treatment; it truly is magical stuff.

Industry observers note that let’s begin by clearing up a bit of confusion. The firm now known as Polaroid is not the original Polaroid company. What happened is that The Impossible Project acquired the rights to use the Polaroid name in 2017 and rebranded themselves Polaroid Originals. A year or so after that, they dropped “Originals” and rebranded back to the original, and recognizable, Polaroid name. In short: The Impossible Project became Polaroid Originals, which became Polaroid.

The story behind The Impossible Project is pretty remarkable. When Polaroid confirmed they were closing up shop in terms of film production, a trio of individuals, Florian Kaps, Marwan Saba, and André Bosman, formed The Impossible Project, which leased one of the old Polaroid plant buildings in the Netherlands and bought a bunch of the old equipment. They then hired ex-Polaroid engineers to help them build a replacement film for the discontinued Polaroid films. They focused on the integral films such as 600, SX-70, and Spectra. Sadly, they were not able to bring back any of the pack films that Polaroid had made.

It has been revealed that that early film was pretty awful stuff, but they were attempting to recreate a complex chemical process that Polaroid themselves had spent decades perfecting. Nonetheless, when those first Impossible films hit the market, they quickly proved to be very ephemeral (fading out quickly), extremely finicky (you had to shield the film when it ejected or it would wash out), and highly inconsistent.

It has been revealed that but it was a start, and to Impossible’s credit, they continuously revamped the film technology, rolling out multiple successive generations of film. More than a bit unfairly, though, those early generations of the film earned Impossible a negative reputation with many that took years to shake and still persists today. Photographers often talk about issues that Impossible films generated in past iterations but have since been fixed as if they are still happening. What we are getting at, and one of the first things worth discussing with this film, is that the current product far exceeds the often low expectations placed upon it.

Here’s how we describe the current Polaroid film in general. It is not the original Polaroid film, nor is it a resurrected version of it. It is best thought of as its own thing. It definitely has a vintage analog look to it. Whereas Fuji Instax is known for crisp, bright, sharp colors, Polaroid film is a fair bit different.

Let’s start with the Polaroid 600 B&W film. The current generation of this film has a nice amount of contrast to it as well. Shadows can be very crisp and deep, but the highlights are not as clean as those found on Instax. Polaroid 600 B&W has become fairly neutral in its monochrome rendition but still has a touch of an ivory warmth to it. Naturally, as an ISO 640 film, there is a decent amount of visible grain to these images. We feel like the grain of the B&W emulsion is more noticeable than that of the Color emulsion, but, having said that, it is a nice-looking film grain. The developing time for the 600 B&W is stated as 5-10 minutes, with ambient air temperature being one of the biggest factors in an increase or decrease over this time.

The Polaroid 600 Color film, meanwhile, has pretty rich colors but can unpredictably throw in some color casts here and there. The contrast of the Color 600 feels higher than that of the B&W 600. The shadows in Color 600 are deeper and more blocked up. Highlights tend to have a warmer, creamy cast to them as opposed to being a stark white. There is an element of serendipity to the film as well. It is nowhere near as inconsistent as it used to be, but your results will vary from shot to shot. This is part of its charm, in our opinion. Even if the film were perfect, you’d still be running it through old Polaroid cameras that were scavenged at Goodwill or the thrift store. Embrace the element of chance that often arises when using such analog technology. The Color 600 emulsion has a longer developing time than that of the B&W, with a stated range of 10-15 minutes (influenced by ambient temperatures).

According to recent reports, of course, the film’s biggest selling point is its instant nature. There are not many places you can go in the analog world of photography and enjoy seeing your images instantly. For decades, the ability to snap a photo and watch it develop in front of your eyes has charmed people worldwide. It allows you to make a portrait of that interesting passerby and let them walk off with a developed result. Or to get a shot of that special someone and memorialize it in the iconic Polaroid frame. And don’t overlook the fact that each shot is a one-of-a-kind creation. There is no reprinting of the negative; you’ve made a limited-edition series of one. There is a quote by Polaroid’s inventor, Edwin Land, that sums this up beautifully: “[A Polaroid camera] places before you a thing that is more of the thing than the thing was.”.

Industry observers note that before closing, we do have some general tips when shooting with Polaroid 600. The first is to remember that it is an ISO 640 film (as opposed to SX-70, which is ISO 160). This makes Polaroid 600 the better choice for instant photography in slightly dimmer conditions. Most Polaroid 600 cameras have built-in flashes, but not all of them do, so the extra film speed may help. Also, since it is a faster ISO, be more careful when flying with it. Polaroid recommends avoiding airport X-rays at all costs. If you are traveling with Polaroid 600 film, it is best to avoid packing it in your checked luggage (which goes through more powerful X-rays) and to request a hand check at security.

There is also the matter of shielding the film right after it has ejected from the camera. Polaroid film maintains some sensitivity to exposure after it has ejected. The best practice is to immediately tuck it away out of light for the required developing time. It is fine to peek at it now and again, but leaving a developing Polaroid exposed to bright light will result in a faded, washed-out result.

According to recent reports, the final point to make in regard to Polaroid film is that it uses the array of cameras made by Polaroid over the several decades that the organization was fully invested in the development of this film. There are dozens of different cameras, oodles of accessories, and all sorts of other fun paraphernalia from the 1970s, ’80s, ’90s, and ’00s to dig up and pair with a box of the modern Polaroid films. One of our staff has a tri-image filter for his Polaroid 600. It’s goofy and definitely very ’80s, but he has a ton of fun with it. So, if you are going to shoot Polaroid, make sure to do some research into the history of the cameras and products made for this film and see what toys you can find to experiment and have fun with! There have also been various Polaroid 600 editions with creative borders, such as the Round Frame. This fun edition operates like normal, but the resulting image is encapsulated in a circular frame instead of a square. Over the years, Polaroid has produced 600 film with various colored borders too.

Lastly, while our entire write-up has been focused on Polaroid 600 film, we can’t sign off without mentioning Polaroid’s i-Type film. Polaroid i-Type film has the same chemistry formulation as Polaroid 600 film, which means it is also a 640 ISO film. The main difference is that Polaroid 600 film includes a built-in battery within the pack. Most vintage Polaroid cameras had no battery of their own, using the battery in the film pack to power the camera and thus ensuring a fresh battery every time you loaded film. Polaroid has now issued modern takes on those vintage OneStep cameras as well as their completely new I-Series. These modern Polaroid cameras have internal rechargeable batteries. So, Polaroid released a less expensive, battery-less version of 600 film called i-Type specifically for these new-generation cameras.

Sources indicate that that is what we have for you today. We’re bringing you both films today at a discounted rate, so head over to our website to shop for both Polaroid 600 and i-Type film, both Color and B&W. While supplies last, of course!

It Should Have Been Zuiko

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (956 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I remember exactly where I was when I heard what the fresh name for the camera brand spun off from Olympus was going to be.
  • Recent findings suggest that it wasn’t possible to keep Olympus, since the parent tech giant this fresh company would be spun off from would be retaining and using that brand name.
  • OM System feels like a name decided around a corporate roundtable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I remember exactly where I was when I heard what the fresh name for the camera brand spun off from Olympus was going to be. I remember sitting at my desk at my old house, looking at the press release, dumbfounded. There was no way they actually picked that, right?

Recent findings suggest that it wasn’t possible to keep Olympus, since the parent tech giant this fresh company would be spun off from would be retaining and using that brand name. Something else needed to be chosen.

OM System feels like a name decided around a corporate roundtable. OM makes a ton of sense as it had been a part of the Olympus brand history for years, so I can see how the suits decided it would be great to keep it as part of the newly introduced organization’s name. OM actually comes from Olympus Maitani, in honor of Yoshihisa Maitani who was a very important camera designer at the company. So by choosing OM, they would intrinsically keep part of the Olympus name, albeit mostly hidden since the average person doesn’t know this history.

Recent findings suggest that and it’s not just one product, it’s a system of cameras and lenses! OM System, on paper, makes logical, rational sense. I don’t have any matter with OM Digital Solutions as the corporate name, but OM System for a product? That’s where you lose me.

In a recent development, it’s uninteresting and, frankly, comes with some serious downsides. What makes it worse is that there is a spectacular brand name that they could have chosen (and still can) that they own as part of the spinoff: Zuiko.

Industry observers note that before becoming Olympus Corporation, the organization was known as Takachiho Seisakusho, named after Mount Takachiho, the peak where mythology notes the Japanese gods descended to Earth. When the company expanded from microscopes into Western export markets in 1921, it adopted the trademark Olympus as a Greek mythological parallel to Mount Takachiho.

It has been revealed that takachiho Seisakusho developed its first photographic lens at the Mizuho Optical Research Laboratory in 1936. They needed a name for the upcoming optic, so they combined two kanji characters from the facility’s name: 瑞 (Zui) from Mizuho and 光 (Ko) from Kogaku. The word that was formed from there was Zuiko, which most directly translates to “auspicious light” or “holy light.”.

More loosely translated, it can mean “light of the gods.”.

When Olympus shifted to mirrorless cameras with Micro Four Thirds, it added an “M” to the front of Zuiko to distinguish it from its Four Thirds DSLR lenses. It still uses M.Zuiko today. OM Digital Solutions acquired the Zuiko name entirely as part of its exit from Olympus and still owns it.

Nikon. Canon. Sony (Alpha). Lumix. Sigma. Pentax. Ricoh. Zuiko.

Japanese camera brand names are short, two-syllable words that are easy to fit on the front of cameras and steeped in rich meaning. Sony itself is already two syllables, but Alpha was inherited from Minolta which picked the name because it symbolized peak performance and the beginning of a new era. Canon is adapted from the Buddhist bodhisattva of mercy, Kwanon. Nikon is a contraction of Nippon Kogaku, the original name of the company. Lumix is a shortened version of luminance, or light.

Sigma comes from the mathematical symbol that means “the sum of parts.” It also was very important to Michihiro Yamaki (father of Sigma’s current president Kazuto Yamaki) that a short, two syllable word be the name, as that simplicity would mirror the contemporaries like Canon, Nikon, and Pentax.

Speaking of Pentax, that is a combination of the DSLR pentaprism and the Contax name. Ricoh is very similar to Nikon in that it is a contraction of Riken Kogaku, the pre-war name of the company.

All of these names are strong, quick, and easy to say. They all follow this formula because it a strong foundation and a proven success. Zuiko was right there, bringing with it the entire history of the brand’s power in imaging along with one of the most badass translations among any camera brand. Light of the Gods? My goodness, that’s strong. Fierce, even!

Sources indicate that OM System not only has too many syllables, it’s physically too long. The tops of OM System cameras look downright crowded trying to fit those words on there. Embracing Zuiko across its cameras and lenses (and they can drop the M now that the company only makes one type of optic) would have felt like a powerful, intelligent coalescence of the brand’s move into the future by embracing its rich past.

In a recent development, it gets worse when you have OM as part of the company name and the camera names. OM System OM-1 sounds redundant. There is a better way.

Recent findings suggest that there is no reason OM Digital Solutions has to keep OM System. They can rebrand anytime they like. I argue they should. I know that might sound crazy considering how recently OM System was chosen, but continuing to use it would only be falling into the sunk cost fallacy (the mistake of continuing to invest time, money, and effort into something just because you already spent time on it, even when abandoning it would clearly be the better option).

OM Digital Solutions just threw off the shackles of private equity a few months ago. They are charting a new path now. There is no better time to put a stamp on that decision and fly a new flag: Zuiko.

Pentagram rebuilds Poetry Foundationâs brand identity around a redrawn Pegasus mark, central-axis type stacks, and two-color covers.

Seventy black silhouettes sit in neat rows on off-white paper, tracing how Pentagram stripped a century-old winged horse down to one sharp mark. Since 1912, the Pegasus has belonged primarily to Poetry magazine, the Chicago journal that early on printed Gwendolyn Brooks, Carl Sandburg, and T. S. Eliot. Pentagramâs brief was to turn that single emblem into a unified brand identity for the entire Poetry Foundation. It isnât treated like a fragile crest locked in a corner. On the black lockup sheet, the Pegasus rides between wide-tracked POETRY and FOUNDATION lettering, tops 2026 Pegasus Awards, shrinks into an inline paragraph bullet, and tucks beside the numerals 61. One silhouette carries the organization across every scale.

Industry observers note that photography steps out of the frame here. As Pentagram notes, poetsâ words become the artwork, anchored by a central-axis stacking motif built so the internal team can assemble layouts swiftly. The black scale diagram maps that range from a clean Meet Our Grantee-Partner: header into a dense mission block where tiny uppercase lines weave between oversized serifs. The cover system doesnât hide the writing inside. On the cobalt-blue matter, hot-pink display type pulls KB Brookinsâs line, Give me more to immortalize, straight to the front beneath a pink orb â nodding to the magazineâs founding âOpen Doorâ policy. Across fourteen consecutive spines from January 2026 through May 2028, each issue pairs two contrasting inks with a tiny Pegasus at the base, while the brown back cover centers electric-blue poet names above a five-Pegasus arc.

Beyond print, the brand identity loosens up without losing structure. On a white wall clock set over wood paneling, twelve black Pegasus silhouettes replace the hour numerals in mid-flight poses. Everyday objects follow suit. A natural canvas tote stacks The poets have emerged! in chunky black serifs beneath a small MAGAZINE lockup, and an oatmeal cap with a forest-green corduroy brim tucks an embroidered Pegasus and Poetry above the bill. Inside, open spreads like Koko Taylor Is the Healer of Wounded Women give poems calm serif pacing and wide margins, while the Poetry Off the Shelf podcast tile brings the rust-red mark onto mobile. Itâs a working kit built to move from clock face to canvas tote without crowding the verse.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that earlier this year, photographer and creator Mr.
  • Unlike the Micro Four Thirds-based camera Mr.
