📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that earlier this year, photographer and creator Mr. 50mm built a DIY digital rangefinder camera using parts he salvaged from a FED 5 Soviet-era rangefinder and a Panasonic GF3 Micro Four Thirds camera. Mr. 50mm is back with an even better DIY digital rangefinder, and this time it’s APS-C.

Unlike the Micro Four Thirds-based camera Mr. 50mm dubbed the “RGM-79” earlier this year, the new “C7M” uses a larger APS-C image sensor. Mr. 50mm is using the imaging pipeline from the original Canon EOS M mirrorless camera, which Canon unveiled way back in 2012.

The Canon EOS M features an 18-megapixel APS-C CMOS image sensor, up from the 12.1-megapixel Micro Four Thirds sensor Mr. 50mm salvaged from a Panasonic GF3.

A DIY digital rangefinder requires two donors, though. Rather than the FED 5 rangefinder Mr. 50mm used before, he’s sticking with two Canon cameras this time around. The donor rangefinder is the Canon 7, a rangefinder series that started in 1961 with the original Canon 7 and ended in 1967 with the Canon 7sZ.

Recent findings suggest that although Mr. 50mm hasn’t finalized everything or released a build video yet — it’s in the works — the C7M sure does look impressive thus far. Mr. 50mm is especially impressed with the Canon 7’s finder, which he describes as a “marked upgrade compared to a Fed camera.”.

“The bar wasn’t that high, but the Canon 7 does a lot of things very, very well. You get a brighter finder, you get projected and selectable frame lines, and they’re parallax-corrected,” the builder explains.

It has been revealed that further, the Canon 7 uses a Leica M39 screw mount, which is great news for Mr. 50mm. It’s a widely used mount with a ton of lens options on the market.

It has been revealed that while the Canon 7 doesn’t have many controls, that isn’t a downside for Mr. 50mm.

According to recent reports, “It doesn’t have that many dedicated controls, which helps reduce the amount of controls I need to either port or figure out if I’m okay to live without. In the end, the digital camera really just has to be able to do two things. It has to accommodate the rangefinder that I’m gonna put on top, and it has to be able to accommodate the mount that I’m using,” he explains.

There are plenty of challenges, though.

“Unfortunately, it isn’t just as easy as disassembling an EOS M and then jamming on new parts,” Mr. 50mm explains. “There [were] quite a few modifications that needed to be done to the camera to make this work, which I’ll discuss probably in depth in another video.”.

Ultimately, as the video above shows, he solved the biggest challenges. He notes the C7M is “mostly done” and, impressively, it only took a couple of weeks to build from start to finish. Despite a damaging drop during the build, it came together pretty well.

Industry observers note that there’s always a catch, though. There are some rangefinder calibration concerns left to figure out, and not everything aligns perfectly yet. Mr. 50mm notes he needs to trim back some more material from the EOS M’s parts, although he isn’t sure how much they have left to give.

“Eventually, once things get a bit more ironed out, I’ll draft up a tutorial on how you can actually make your own,” the photographer notes.

Sources indicate that so while the C7M isn’t totally finished yet, it looks very cool and even more promising. Digital rangefinder cameras are expensive, but building one using donor parts and 3D-printed components makes the format significantly more accessible, assuming someone is comfortable with the build process itself.

It has been revealed that although there isn’t a build tutorial yet, it’s still worth considering the potential cost to build a C7M. The Canon EOS M body is around $260 used, not much more than a Canon 7 rangefinder body. If someone has access to a 3D printer, printing the other parts won’t cost much. That’s much less than a brand-newly introduced Leica digital rangefinder, for sure.

Picture this: you're settled into your seat on a United flight out of LAX, the Pacific stretching endlessly outside your window, and you know — you genuinely know — that the person next to you paid $400 for this exact seat while you paid **7,500 miles**. That's the Hawaiian sweet spot, and it's one of the most quietly powerful redemptions available to anyone building a travel rewards strategy. Hawaii has always been the aspirational American vacation. It's the honeymoon destination, the bucket-list family trip, the anniversary getaway. And because of that demand, flights from the mainland — especially during spring break, summer, and the holidays — rarely go on sale. A round-trip economy ticket from Los Angeles to Honolulu will routinely run **$400–$700**, and during peak travel windows, prices can push past $1,000 for a family of four. That's real money. FI-community money. Now consider what Turkish Airlines Miles & Smiles charges for that same seat: **7,500 miles one-way**. At the low end of cash pricing ($200 for a one-way), you're extracting **2.7 cents per point**. At the high end ($500 during peak season), that same 7,500 miles is worth **6.7 cents per point** — a figure that makes even seasoned travel rewards enthusiasts do a double-take. For context, most people in the points world consider 1.5–2 cents per point a solid redemption. **Getting 6.7 cents per point is extraordinary.** It's not a fluke or a loophole — it's a structural pricing inefficiency baked into the Turkish award chart, which treats all short-haul domestic U.S. flights (including Hawaii, which is technically a domestic route) at the same rock-bottom rate. This is the fundamental insight behind every great travel rewards redemption: **loyalty programs price awards based on their own logic, not cash fares.** Turkish Miles & Smiles sees LAX→HNL as a short Star Alliance partner flight. The fact that cash fares on that route are elevated because of destination demand is irrelevant to their award chart. That gap — between what Turkish charges in miles and what the market charges in dollars — is exactly where you save. For a ChooseFI community member who already holds Citi ThankYou Points, this redemption is within reach right now. You don't need to fly Turkish. You don't need to connect through Istanbul. You just need availability on United, 7,500 miles, and about 20 minutes.

Industry observers note that the magic here comes down to one core concept: Star Alliance partner pricing on a domestic U.S. route.

Turkish Airlines is a Star Alliance member, and like most alliance programs, they allow their members to book award flights on partner airlines — including United. Where Turkish gets interesting (and generous) is in how they price those partner awards. Their award chart uses a fixed, distance-based or zone-based structure, and for short-haul U.S. domestic flights, the price bottoms out at 7,500 miles one-way in economy.

According to recent reports, here's the pricing inefficiency in plain language: Turkish Miles & Smiles doesn't care that Hawaii is an aspirational, high-demand destination. To their award chart, LAX→HNL is just another short domestic United flight. Meanwhile, United's own MileagePlus program charges significantly more for the same route — often 13,000–22,500 miles one-way depending on the fare bucket. Turkish is pricing the same seat at less than half what United charges its own members. That's the gap you're exploiting.

No fuel surcharges — ever. This is a critical detail that makes Turkish a standout program. Many European programs (we're looking at you, Lufthansa Miles & More) pile on hundreds of dollars in fuel surcharges that nearly erase the value of the award. Turkish charges zero fuel surcharges on any award flight, including partner redemptions. Your out-of-pocket cost when booking this redemption is taxes and fees only — typically $5–$15 for a domestic U.S. itinerary.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that five historic Christian artefacts were restituted to the Ethiopian Heritage Authority in a ceremony at the country’s London embassy on Wednesday (18 November).
  • Sources indicate that mcCarthy, an American financier who used to live in London and now resides in East Asia, has long been a serious collector of European medieval art.
  • Recent findings suggest that ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that five historic Christian artefacts were restituted to the Ethiopian Heritage Authority in a ceremony at the country’s London embassy on Wednesday (18 November). The process was part of a wider initiative by the American collector Robert McCarthy and the Toledo Museum of Art in Ohio that is expected to see many more objects returned to Ethiopia.

Sources indicate that mcCarthy, an American financier who used to live in London and now resides in East Asia, has long been a serious collector of European medieval art. He broadened his collection in the 1990s to include Ethiopian art, at a time when there was less concern about provenance. In 2023-24 he lent objects to the exhibition Ethiopia at the Crossroads, which was presented in venues in Baltimore, Salem in Massachusetts and Toledo. It was at Toledo that he began discussions with Sophie Ong, assistant director of strategic initiatives, about the future of his collection.

Recent findings suggest that ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa. Photo: Stephen Chung for Toledo Museum of Art and Embassy of Ethiopia.

According to recent reports, this eventually led to the upcoming, complex arrangement. Toledo will acquire McCarthy’s 375 Ethiopian objects, one of the largest such private collections. Two thirds will be donated and the remainder bought. Some of this material will be exhibited when the museum’s galleries reopen in autumn 2027 after a major reinstallation of its permanent collection.

According to recent reports, the museum then intends to return much of the collection to Ethiopia, in tranches over the next 20 years. Any items deemed to have left Ethiopia illegally or inappropriately will be restituted. Details have not been released, but it is assumed that this will include looted material seized by British troops at the 1869 battle of Maqdala and which later came onto the international art market.

Objects judged to have been exported properly will remain at the Toledo museum. Stewardship of items with an indeterminate status will be decided jointly by the Toledo museum and Ethiopian officials. It is thought that ultimately half of McCarthy’s 375 items may be returned.

The unusual tripartite arrangement between McCarthy, the Toledo museum and the Ethiopia authorities could prove to be a template for dealing with restitution claims by other African countries. At the handover, Alula Pankhurst, speaking on behalf of the Ethiopian Heritage Authority, described it as “a fresh model of partnership”.

This week’s restitution of five objects to the government’s Ethiopian Heritage Authority is slightly different, in that they have been directly returned by McCarthy. The Toledo museum was unwilling to accession them because of records suggesting that they had left Ethiopia after the 1970 Unesco convention.

In a recent development, the items are two 15th-century illuminated manuscripts and three processional crosses. All are believed to have been improperly removed from Ethiopian churches.

The earliest of the two manuscripts is a Book of Revelation with a Horologium (daily cycle of prayers). It includes seven full-page illuminations, dating from around 1400. The volume was recorded in the late 20th century as being in the Saqqā Madḫānē Ālam Church in Šawā Province.

The other manuscript is a large mid-15th century Gospels, which includes full-page images of the Four Evangelists. The scholar Diana Spencer noted in a 1974 article that she saw it at the church of Emmaus Giyor near Wafa Yasus.

Industry observers note that ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa. Photo: Stephen Chung for Toledo Museum of Art and Embassy of Ethiopia.

Sources indicate that the three brass processional crosses being returned date variously from the late-18th to early-20th centuries. Each has incised inscriptions which may make it possible to determine which church they came from.

The five returned objects are now being sent from London to the National Museum of Ethiopia in Addis Ababa, where a fresh display of restituted material is scheduled to open in December. Most of the rest of the display will be material which had been looted at Maqdala.

However, the forthcoming Addis Ababa display may feed into a debate over whether religious items that can be identified with a particular location should be retained in the National Museum or returned to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, I was young and in need of guidance.
  • I would speak to Gary every morning when he assigned me jobs for the day, talking me through what was expected and the specific set of photos I needed to produce.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Long before I worked on the PetaPixel news desk, I was an agency photographer covering breaking news, features, and sports.

According to recent reports, I was young and in need of guidance. I found that in the form of my photo editor, whom I’m going to call Gary.

I would speak to Gary every morning when he assigned me jobs for the day, talking me through what was expected and the specific set of photos I needed to produce.

After I wired him the photos, he would let me know whether I had done a good job or a terrible one.

He would often edit my photos, reframe them slightly, change the crop, cull some of them, or call me up and ask if I had a different angle.

But Gary did far more than that. He was a leader in the newsroom, worked closely with the news editor to shape stories and come up with ideas, and was an excellent salesman.

In a recent development, his vivacious personality helped. He invented nicknames for me and the other photographers, made silly jokes, and was just generally good for staff morale. Not everyone liked the owners, but everyone liked Gary.

It has been revealed that after I had worked there for a few years, the agency was bought out, and Gary moved to a latest hub hundreds of miles away. Our relationship was never the same. The new regime was different, and I left soon after.

I thought of Gary this week when the Associated Press officially cut all eight of the remaining photo editor positions in the U.S.

It has been revealed that AP has moved the positions to its hub in Noida, India. The agency indicates it has plans to grow the Indian operation to 100 staff members, including video producers.

AP photo editors are legendary: Consider the famous Napalm Girl photograph, for example, when Horst Faas and Hal Buell overruled Carl Robinson’s decision not to wire Nick Ut’s photograph.

Photo editors have played a crucial role in the fortunes of photographers for a very long time, advocating for us while seeing the bigger picture.

It’s not a question of whether talented photo editors exist in India. Of course, they do. But there’s something valuable about having an editor who understands the local news environment, knows the photographers personally, and can build relationships over years of working together.

And look, I get it: the press industry is tough. Agency bosses were once raking in vast sums of money — these days they face lousy picture rates from a fractured industry.

Sources indicate that photo editors do not attend a news story in person the way photographers do; therefore, they could theoretically be anywhere. This is a globalized, technologized world: workers in developing countries are technically in competition with workers from the U.S.

But while these massive decisions make sense from a financial point of view, what are the long-term consequences?

Photographers, like my younger self, have fewer opportunities to benefit from a leading light like Gary.

Nowadays, photographers are increasingly expected to be fully formed; the bosses need someone they can rely on to do a good job no matter what. And while there are plenty of great photographers out there who can do that, they all had to cut their teeth somewhere.

As with many other things in life, it feels like the ladder for the younger generation is being removed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Black and White Photo Awards 2026 winners have been unveiled. Photographers competed across six categories, each vying to be named Black and White Photographer of the Year.

Speaking of which, this year’s significant winner is Shengwei Dai, who took the top spot for a spectacular shot of a man jumping between two moving trains, with dozens of passengers looking on.

Dai earned a €1,500 cash prize for the win, the largest single award in the competition’s five-year history.

Alongside Dai’s overall win, competition judges selected winners across six categories: Architecture, Fauna and Flora, Landscape, Portrait, Street, and the new Open Theme.

“The new category aims to welcome photographs that, through their artistic, narrative, or conceptual approach, do not fit neatly into any of the traditional disciplines,” the Black and White Photo Awards explains.

Each category also includes Golden, Silver, and Bronze mentions, which serve as runner-up and honorable mention distinctions. Category winners each receive a €200 cash prize.

Photographer Qian Shen won the Architecture category with a striking shot of the Suzhou Olympic Sports Center in China.

Recent findings suggest that mohammad Mirza’s photo, Silent Majesty, earned the top spot in the Fauna and Flora category. The image captures a white rhinoceros emerging through the mist and trees in Kenya’s Solio Reserve, a private wildlife sanctuary.

According to recent reports, jie Fischer’s Flamingo in Flight 2 bested the competition in the Landscape category. The nearly abstract aerial shot captures a flock of flying flamingos from a top-down perspective against a high-contrast, pattern-filled terrain.

Happy Mukherjee’s portrait, Behind the Silence, depicts a young girl and invites viewers to wonder about her expression and gaze.

Cow Watching by Chongfeng Wu won the Street category. Unlike most street photos captured in urban environments, Wu’s pastoral shot is much quieter.

The inaugural Open Theme winner is Lloyd Lane, whose image, Convergence, captures a flock of starlings over Brighton Palace Pier in England.

The judges also selected finalists across all six categories, and their work can be viewed on the Black and White Photo Awards website.

The Black and White Photo Awards is already looking forward to its sixth annual competition in 2027, with entries opening on January 1.

Van Gogh’s record-breaking ‘Blossoming Chestnut Trees’: the $190m sale and the restitution claim that nearly upended it

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1331 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees sold at Sotheby's Fresh York on Wednesday night (18 November) for $190.4m, including fees.
  • In a recent development, the auction of the Van Gogh opened at $135m, two telephone bidders coming in.
  • Before the auction, Sotheby’s had not confirmed a formal estimate range, but instead suggested that the painting should fetch a hammer price of around $180m (before fees).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees sold at Sotheby's Fresh York on Wednesday night (18 November) for $190.4m, including fees. Auctioneer Oliver Barker began the sale by stating that “the work is being offered for sale pursuant to an agreement between the seller and the heirs of the Hedwig and Samuel Fischer family”. The Fischer family had sold the painting in 1936.

In a recent development, the auction of the Van Gogh opened at $135m, two telephone bidders coming in. A third bidder, in the saleroom, won the contest after less than four minutes, at a hammer price of $165m. He is the New York dealer William Acquavella, presumably acting for an unidentified client.

Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (May 1890).

Before the auction, Sotheby’s had not confirmed a formal estimate range, but instead suggested that the painting should fetch a hammer price of around $180m (before fees). This may have been slightly optimistic, since it was far more than any Van Gogh has ever made. Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (May 1890) is a fine landscape, although not among his very best. And the other 11 pictures in last night’s auction of the Blaquier-Arrieta collection generally sold for around, or even below, their lower estimates.

The uncertainty last weekend over a possible Nazi-era claim for the Van Gogh may have discouraged some potential bidders, but the $190m (including fees) was nonetheless an astonishing result. This was for an artist who had failed to sell during his own lifetime. Van Gogh completed nearly a thousand paintings in his career, with only a single recorded sale: The Red Vineyard (November 1888, Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts, Moscow).

Only three artworks have ever sold for more at auction: Leonardo’s Salvator Mundi (around 1500, $450m, Christie’s, 2017), Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1916, $236m, Sotheby’s, 2025) and Andy Warhol’s Shot Sage Blue Marilyn (1964, $195m, Christie’s, 2022).

It has been revealed that the previous record price for a Van Gogh was $117m (including fees) for Orchard with Cypresses (April 1888), which Christie’s sold in 2022. The Blossoming Chestnut Trees price was 62% more.

Sources indicate that sotheby’s has been open about Blossoming Chestnut Trees’s Nazi-era (1933-45) provenance. Following our inquiries, we reported in our 2 October blog post: “It was purchased four years later [in 1926] by the Berlin-based publisher Samuel Fischer, and on his death in 1934 it passed to his daughter Brigitte. Although the family was persecuted because of their Jewish heritage, a Sotheby’s spokesperson confirmed to us that, based on recent research, the family was free at all times to dispose of the painting.”.

Literaturport.de via Wikimedia Commons.

News of a possible Nazi-era claim emerged only five weeks later. Berlin-based Gunnar Schnabel, who describes himself as a “looted art researcher” specialising in the Nazi period, told the Newly introduced York Times that he first heard about the sale on 7 November, when he was “lying on a sofa in his vacation home”. His letter to Sotheby’s calling for the sale to be delayed was sent on 12 November, just six days before the auction. Obviously this put Sotheby’s in a very awkward situation: should the sale be postponed or go ahead?

In a recent development, in response, Sotheby’s stated: “We are aware of the persecution experienced by the Fischer family. After the Anschluss in 1938, the family fled Austria, and the Gestapo confiscated their Vienna home, library and remaining art collection. But the circumstances around this transaction were different”. The auction house also added that after the war, no claim was ever made for the Van Gogh.

Urgent negotiations were held with the representatives of the Fischer family. The key question at stake was whether their ancestors had been the victim of a forced sale at a lower than market value. By June 1936, when the Van Gogh was sold, the family had just moved to Vienna. They had consigned the painting to the Cassirer gallery in Amsterdam several years earlier, in 1932-33. The price eventually paid in 1936 by the buyer, Paris-based collectors Henriette and Marcel Kapferer, was $22,000.

Recent findings suggest that comparisons with other Van Gogh sales around the time are telling. In 1935, the year before the Fischer sale, Orchard with Cypresses had sold for $15,000 at the New York auction house Parke Bernet (this was the painting which later fetched a record Van Gogh price in 2022). That makes the $22,000 seem reasonable.

Sources indicate that then there is the Sunflowers (August 1888), which had been sold to London's National Gallery in 1924 for the equivalent of $5,800. Although this sale took place 12 years before Blossoming Chestnut Trees and Jo Bonger, Vincent’s sister-in-law, probably reduced the price for a major museum, it is now regarded as Van Gogh’s greatest masterpiece. This again suggests that the Fischers received a reasonable sum for their picture.

Following yesterday’s Sotheby’s auction, Schnabel told The Art Newspaper that the Fischers had also been supported by the Commission for Looted Art in Europe's co-chair Anne Webber. He added that the family is delighted that Blossoming Chestnut Trees “which hung in the Berlin home of Samuel and Hedwig Fischer for a quarter of a century, has now found a new owner”. They hope this case “may offer some encouragement to other families who have faced persecution during the Nazi era, and that they, too, may find a path toward the recognition of their rightful claims.”.

Recent findings suggest that the terms of the 17 November settlement between the heirs of the Fischer family and the Blaquier-Arrieta family remain confidential. Presumably some sort of financial compensation has been paid. The agreement opens the door for the Fischer heirs to make claims for further paintings which had once been in their family if they come onto the market in the future.

Title page of the Leicester Galleries exhibition Artists who Died Young, with an image of Blossoming Chestnut Trees.

As a postscript on the 1930s story of Blossoming Chestnut Trees, soon after the Kapferers bought the picture they lent it to an exhibition in London, Artists who Died Young at the Leicester Galleries in 1938. A year after the London exhibition, war broke out. Blossoming Chestnut Trees had been sent to the United States a few months earlier to New York dealers Wildenstein & Co and, after passing through two American private collections, it went to Argentina in 1975, to the Blaquier-Arrieta family. Following the Sotheby’s sale, it remains a mystery where the Van Gogh will ultimately reside.

Sources indicate that martin Bailey is a leading Van Gogh specialist and special correspondent for The Art Newspaper. He has curated exhibitions at the Barbican Art Gallery, Compton Verney/National Gallery of Scotland and Tate Britain.

Martin Bailey’s recent Van Gogh books.

In a recent development, martin has written a number of bestselling books on Van Gogh’s years in France: The Sunflowers Are Mine: The Story of Van Gogh's Masterpiece (Frances Lincoln 2013, UK and US), Studio of the South: Van Gogh in Provence (Frances Lincoln 2016, UK and US), Starry Night: Van Gogh at the Asylum (White Lion Publishing 2018, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale: Auvers and the Artist’s Rise to Fame (Frances Lincoln 2021, UK and US). The Sunflowers are Mine (2024, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale (2024, UK and US) are also now available in a more compact paperback format.

His other recent books include Living with Vincent van Gogh: The Homes & Landscapes that shaped the Artist (White Lion Publishing 2019, UK and US), which provides an overview of the artist’s life. The Illustrated Provence Letters of Van Gogh has been reissued (Batsford 2021, UK and US). My Friend Van Gogh/Emile Bernard provides the first English translation of Bernard’s writings on Van Gogh (David Zwirner Books 2023, UKand US).

To contact Martin Bailey, please email vangogh@theartnewspaper.com.

Please note that he does not undertake authentications.

Breaking: Between Moonlight and Aurora: Photographing East Greenland After Dark

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1847 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that photographing East Greenland at night is an exercise in preparation, observation, and adaptation.
  • Industry observers note that during a recent photography expedition in East Greenland, hosted by Secret Atlas this last October 2026, I spent several evenings leading the photographic project targeting enormous icebergs illuminated by the rising moon, alongside the Northern Lights appearing above the surrounding fjords and ice.
  • Sources indicate that some photographs begin long before the camera is taken out of the bag.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that photographing East Greenland at night is an exercise in preparation, observation, and adaptation. The landscape is immense, the conditions can be demanding, and the opportunities to make a particular image may be limited to a few minutes. Towering icebergs, drifting sea ice, fog, low clouds, and the changing Arctic sky create an environment in which light can completely transform the way a scene is perceived. Yet having spectacular scenery in front of you does not necessarily mean you will come away with a strong photograph. The challenge is to recognize what makes a moment worth capturing, understand how the available light interacts with the landscape, and make the right decisions before that moment disappears.

Industry observers note that during a recent photography expedition in East Greenland, hosted by Secret Atlas this last October 2026, I spent several evenings leading the photographic project targeting enormous icebergs illuminated by the rising moon, alongside the Northern Lights appearing above the surrounding fjords and ice. These two subjects offered very different photographic challenges and a particular one-of-a-kind night operation.

Sources indicate that some photographs begin long before the camera is taken out of the bag. The moonrise series was one of those projects. Across four days, I followed the changing opportunities to photograph the rising moon among the enormous icebergs of East Greenland. The objective was not simply to record the moon above the horizon, but to find a relationship between the moonlight, the architecture of the icebergs, the sense of exploration, and the surrounding landscape.

Industry observers note that the first opportunity to photograph the sequence came around 8 p.m. on day three of our expedition, when the timing and the available light finally began to align. In the Arctic, twilight can retain considerable ambient light even as the moon rises. This transition creates an interesting balance: the landscape may still hold detail, while the moon begins illuminating the ice from a different angle.

It has been revealed that A rising moon and a monumental iceberg are impressive subjects individually, but putting them together is not enough. Their positions, relative sizes, illumination, and separation from the background all influence how the image is read. Anticipating these relationships is essential, particularly when the window for making the photograph is short.

Industry observers note that photographing from a Zodiac adds another dimension to the process. Polar bear presence in East Greenland limits our possibility to operate on land during low-light conditions. Unlike working from stable ground, the shooting position is not necessarily fixed, and even small movements can affect the framing, particularly when using a long focal length.

In a recent development, the objective was to find a viewpoint from which the iceberg formations could be separated visually and the rising moon incorporated without losing the sense of scale. Icebergs are difficult subjects to photograph because their dimensions can be hard to communicate.

Recent findings suggest that focal length plays an key role in communicating scale. A wide-angle lens can emphasize the surrounding environment, while a longer lens can compress the scene and bring distant formations visually closer together.

Exposure requires similar care. A gradually brightening moon against a dark sky can make it difficult to preserve highlights without losing detail in the shadows. Rather than trying to make every part of the photograph equally bright, I aim to retain the texture of the illuminated surfaces while allowing darkness to remain part of the image, preserving my highlight and shadow information.

In a recent development, the Northern Lights create a very different set of challenges. The moon’s position can be anticipated, allowing me to plan around a relatively predictable source of illumination. This is great for subject illumination, though distracting when the moon appears in the frame. The aurora, by contrast, can change rapidly in brightness, shape, color, and movement.

Recent findings suggest that from our main vessel, we navigate through the fjord in search of a good-looking iceberg to frame our shot. We carefully position the ship to achieve the greatest possible stability while maintaining the flexibility to adjust our orientation depending on where the aurora is expected to appear. The moment the Northern Lights emerge, close coordination via VHF radio with the bridge team becomes essential. As we prepare to photograph from the ship’s outer deck, the vessel is brought to a complete standstill, reaching zero speed over ground. This allows us to capture the scene with maximum stability, even using exposures of around half a second, while the iceberg and the dancing aurora create the perfect natural composition.

Aurora photography involves a series of compromises between shutter speed, aperture, and ISO. A longer exposure collects more light, which can help when the display is faint, but it can also blur the finer structures of a rapidly moving aurora. A shorter exposure preserves more detail in the curtains and patterns but requires enough light to produce a usable image. There is no universal exposure for the Northern Lights. The right settings depend on the brightness and speed of the display, the available ambient light, the lens, and the amount of detail I want to retain. I adjust according to the behavior of the sky rather than relying on a fixed recipe, as shown below with this powerful curtain of light.

Sources indicate that as the sun began to set, we left the comfort of our main vessel and ventured out aboard our Zodiacs for a reconnaissance ride through the surrounding waters. Our mission was to explore the landscape, identify one or two particularly striking icebergs, and select the perfect setting for what we hoped would become an unforgettable night of aurora photography. Capturing the Northern Lights is as much about patience and preparation as it is about being in the right place at the right time. With exposures ranging from half a second to four, five, or even six seconds, stability becomes essential. Even the slightest movement can compromise an image. Out here, surrounded by the vastness of the polar landscape, finding a way to create a stable photographic platform would be one of the greatest challenges of the night.

Sources indicate that our idea was to return after dark, launching the Zodiacs from the main vessel and navigating through the freezing waters in search of newly formed sea ice near one of the selected icebergs. This young ice, approximately one centimeter thick, offered the possibility of carefully positioning the bow of a Zodiac against its edge, allowing us to wedge ourselves into place and create the stability required for long exposures. Finding a sufficiently wide area of newly formed ice would also give us the freedom to reposition ourselves as the auroras shifted and danced across different parts of the sky. But this was about more than simply finding a stable platform. It was about finding the right perspective, in pitch darkness surrounded by the freezing Greenlandic waters.

It has been revealed that when planning an operation like this, I always look for ways to approach an iceberg while maintaining a safe distance and shooting from as low an angle as possible. I want the iceberg to become a powerful element in the composition, rising beneath the aurora and giving the image a strong sense of scale and depth. The newly formed sea ice often adds another dimension to the scene. Its delicate patterns, textures, and natural leading lines can guide the viewer’s eye toward the main subject, transforming an already extraordinary landscape into a compelling photographic composition.

By 11 p.m., it was time. We left the main vessel and began our night mission. Alongside my teammates Signe-Maria and Myriam, I led our group of photographers toward the giant icebergs and the newly formed sea ice. Behind us, the ship’s powerful searchlight illuminated our chosen iceberg, providing a guiding beacon across the darkness as we made our way toward our destination. Once we reached the area, we carefully positioned the Zodiacs against the edge of the newly formed ice. Every movement had to be deliberate. We wanted to achieve the stability needed for photography while maintaining a safe distance from the iceberg and the surrounding ice.

It has been revealed that fortunately, we had prepared for this moment long before leaving the ship. During the day, we had already assembled, adjusted, and practiced our photographic setups, making sure everyone knew exactly what to do. Now, under the darkness of the polar night, there was no time to waste. We secured our tripods against the Zodiac’s pontoon and tilted them forward, carefully adjusting their position to keep every part of the Zodiac out of the frame. One by one, our photographers settled into their compositions, pointing their cameras toward the magnificent icebergs.

According to recent reports, everything was ready. I picked up the radio and called the ship’s bridge team, asking them to switch off all the lights. And suddenly, everything changed. The powerful beam that had guided us across the darkness disappeared. We were now completely immersed in the polar night, resting on the newly formed sea ice, facing a gigantic iceberg beneath an extraordinary celestial spectacle. Above us, twenty billion stars seemed to fill the sky. A half-moon gently illuminated the frozen landscape, revealing the magnificent shapes and textures of the iceberg, while the auroras began dancing overhead, bringing movement and color to an otherwise silent world.

Sources indicate that for a moment, everything seemed to stand still. There we were, floating between the ocean and the ice, surrounded by one of the most extraordinary landscapes on Earth. Cameras were clicking, shutters were opening and closing, and each long exposure was capturing a fleeting moment of this ever-changing spectacle. It is difficult to describe the feeling of witnessing such a scene. You can proposal every detail, prepare your equipment, study the conditions, and carefully orchestrate the entire operation, but nature always has the final word. And when everything finally comes together, the experience goes far beyond photography. That night, we were fortunate enough to experience something truly exceptional. A moment in which preparation, teamwork, adventure, and nature converged beneath the dancing auroras. The photographs will remain on our SD cards, but the feeling of being there, surrounded by the icebergs, the stars, and the silence of the polar night, will remain with us forever.

Industry observers note that there is a tendency to describe photographs of the Arctic as the result of being in the right place at the right time. Luck certainly plays a role. The moon must rise in a favorable position, the weather must allow the landscape to be seen, and the aurora must develop in a way that creates an interesting composition. None of these conditions can be guaranteed. But being present when a spectacle occurs is only part of the process. The photographer must recognize the potential of the scene, decide where to position the camera, choose a focal length, balance the exposure, and determine which elements belong in the frame. Preparation does not control nature; it makes it possible to respond when an opportunity appears.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Johnson Banks rebuilds RIBA for its 200th birthday: the RIBA brand identity turns negative space into a bold typographic mark.
  • Sources indicate that the first thing you see is the space between the letters.
  • Johnson Banks started from a Philip Johnson line, that all great architecture is the design of space that contains, cuddles, exalts, or stimulates the people in that space, and let the negative space inside the four letters carry the idea.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Johnson Banks rebuilds RIBA for its 200th birthday: the RIBA brand identity turns negative space into a bold typographic mark.

Sources indicate that the first thing you see is the space between the letters. RIBA arrives as four solid capitals on a pale wall, each letter built from the gaps around it, the R split into a bowl and a leg, the B into two stacked bowls, the A into a triangle over a flat base. It is a mark about architecture made from architecture itself, walls and openings rather than a drawn symbol, and it holds at every size, from a tote bag to a building banner.

The type does the work. Johnson Banks started from a Philip Johnson line, that all great architecture is the design of space that contains, cuddles, exalts, or stimulates the people in that space, and let the negative space inside the four letters carry the idea. The mark can sit on top of a photograph, cut into it, or anchor a corner or an edge, and the same logic runs through a set of drop capitals, letters drawn to open a page like a doorway.

The old identity, letters drawn by Eric Gill beside a highly detailed symbol, had drifted over twenty-five years into hundreds of sub-brands with no house style holding them together. The fresh system pulls them back into line, with related identities for RSAW, the Royal Society of Architects in Wales, and RIBAJ, the institute journal, each sitting inside the same approach, and clear guidelines built on accessible fonts so the brand stays useful and durable.

In a recent development, colour went back to the beginning. The historic red, the shade the public knows from RIBA signboards, returns front and centre, running across the tote bag, the drawing stencil and the vertical banner on a brick facade. Against it, the palette stays quiet, stone grey, pale blue, black, so the red reads as a signal rather than a decoration, and the crest, the two lions, survives in a simplified, softened form as a quiet sign-off, debossed in black on black.

The system proves itself on the objects architects use. Book spines carry RIBA, RSAW and RIBAJ in red, white and blue on a wooden shelf. A red stencil ruler cuts the letters into a drawing tool. A poster for the Domestic Building Contract pairs a giant yellow D with a red architectural photograph. And the illustration style, flat geometric shapes in red, blue and green with small cut-out figures, gives the brand a way to talk about people without a photograph.

#68693. Layered Compositions Will Level Up Your Landscape Photography

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2982 w)

Layered Compositions Will Level Up Your Landscape Photography

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2982 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A landscape can look dramatically different in person than it does in a photograph, particularly when a scene loses its sense of depth and scale.
  • In a recent development, creating depth in landscape photography starts with understanding how different parts of a scene relate to one another.
  • Industry observers note that getting those elements to work together takes more than placing an interesting subject in the foreground or pointing the camera at a dramatic mountain range.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A landscape can look dramatically different in person than it does in a photograph, particularly when a scene loses its sense of depth and scale. Explore how thoughtful layering brings distant views to life by connecting nearby details with the features that make a location memorable.

In a recent development, creating depth in landscape photography starts with understanding how different parts of a scene relate to one another. Foreground details establish scale, middle-ground features connect the viewer to the wider landscape, and distant elements provide context. When these elements complement one another, they give the photograph greater dimension and draw the viewer through the frame.

Industry observers note that getting those elements to work together takes more than placing an interesting subject in the foreground or pointing the camera at a dramatic mountain range. Camera position, focal length, overlapping shapes, and changing light all influence how layers appear and how easily the viewer can distinguish them. This guide explores how to apply these techniques in the field—from recognizing natural layers and arranging them within the frame to avoiding visual clutter.

Industry observers note that the foundation of a layered landscape composition is the relationship between its foreground, middle ground, and background. These three zones provide a visual structure that communicates distance and gives the viewer a sense of moving through the scene. The foreground is the area closest to the camera, the middle ground occupies the space between the viewer and the distant scenery, and the background typically contains the farthest elements, such as mountains, hills, or the sky.

Industry observers note that each layer serves a distinct purpose. The foreground anchors the immediate setting and gives the viewer an entry point. The middle ground bridges that starting point to the rest of the landscape, while the background provides context, scale, and a sense of distance. When these elements work together, the photograph feels far more dimensional than a composition built around a single distant subject.

Not every landscape needs three clearly defined layers. A photograph of a mountain reflected in a lake, for example, might rely on two dominant planes, while a forest scene could contain several overlapping layers of trees. The goal is not to force every scene into a rigid formula, but to recognize the distinct planes of distance within it and decide how each contributes to the composition.

Sources indicate that before setting up the camera, take a moment to identify what occupies each part of the view. Look for elements that naturally lead the eye through the frame, as well as areas that might compete for attention. Taking this step helps determine whether the scene already has a strong visual structure or whether changing your position could reveal a more effective arrangement.

Recent findings suggest that A strong foreground gives a landscape photograph an immediate point of entry. Rocks, grasses, wildflowers, fallen trees, shoreline details, and other nearby features establish a sense of place while making the distance feel more pronounced. Rather than simply filling the bottom of the frame, the foreground should serve a clear purpose in the composition.

Recent findings suggest that look for foreground elements that relate to the larger scene. A line of rocks leading toward a mountain, a patch of wildflowers beneath a distant ridgeline, or a weathered tree framing a valley can connect the viewer to the landscape beyond. These details establish scale and make an expansive scene feel more tangible.

Camera position has a considerable effect on how prominent the foreground becomes. Lowering the camera gives nearby objects greater visual weight, often exaggerating their apparent size relative to the background. This can create a dramatic sense of depth, particularly when using a wide-angle lens. However, getting too close can make a foreground object overwhelm the rest of the photograph. Move the camera forward and backward while checking how much space the foreground occupies and whether it remains connected to the distant view.

Pay attention to the edges of the frame as well. A partially cropped rock, branch, or other object along the border can look accidental if it draws attention without adding to the composition. Sometimes shifting the camera just a few inches is enough to position the foreground more deliberately. If there is no suitable foreground element, resist the urge to include something merely to fill the space. A clean, uncomplicated foreground is often more effective than one that distracts from the landscape.

The middle ground is often the most overlooked part of a landscape composition. Photographers frequently concentrate on finding an interesting foreground and capturing a dramatic background, leaving the space between them without a clear visual role. Yet this middle zone is essential because it bridges near and distant elements, helping the photograph feel cohesive.

Middle-ground subjects can include rolling hills, tree lines, rivers, fields, valleys, waterfalls, or clusters of rocks. These features smooth the transition between planes of distance and can create a natural path through the image. A river winding between a foreground shoreline and distant mountains, for example, gives the viewer a route through the landscape. A series of hills can create successive bands that gradually recede toward the horizon.

Industry observers note that look for shapes and lines that link different parts of the scene. A sloping hillside might echo the angle of a nearby rock formation, while a line of trees could guide attention toward a distant peak. Repeating forms also help unify a composition; a series of ridges or tree-covered slopes creates a visual rhythm that reinforces depth.

Industry observers note that if the middle ground feels empty, consider whether changing your position reveals more of the landscape between the foreground and background. Moving laterally along a trail or shoreline can shift the relationship between overlapping features and expose details that were previously hidden. You may also find that a slightly longer focal length brings distant layers together more effectively, especially in landscapes with repeating hills or ridgelines.

The background gives a landscape its broader context, but distant elements can easily lose definition when they blend together. A mountain peak that merges with a similarly toned ridge, for example, may lose its shape and visual impact. Creating separation between background features preserves their individual forms and reinforces the sense of distance.

Industry observers note that light and weather often provide natural separation. Sidelighting reveals the contours of distant mountains, while low-angle sunlight casts alternating bands of brightness and shadow across hillsides. Fog, mist, and atmospheric haze also distinguish successive layers by reducing contrast as the landscape recedes. These conditions produce subtle tonal transitions that make distant features appear farther away.

A post shared by Kate / Torva Terra (@torvaterra).

Industry observers note that camera position matters, too. A slight change in elevation or angle can separate a mountain from the ridge behind it or reveal a gap between two overlapping peaks. Before taking the photograph, examine the outlines of distant features and look for places where they merge. Moving even a short distance can create enough separation to make the shapes easier to read.

It has been revealed that exposure also affects how well those details are retained. Bright skies behind dark mountains often create a wide dynamic range, particularly at sunrise and sunset. Check the histogram and highlight warnings to avoid losing vital sky detail. If necessary, use exposure bracketing or a graduated neutral density filter to manage the difference in brightness. Preserving tonal detail across the scene helps maintain the distinction between distant layers.

Overlap is one of the most direct ways to communicate depth in a landscape photograph. When one object partially obscures another, the viewer immediately recognizes that the two elements occupy different planes of distance. A foreground tree overlapping a distant ridge, for example, creates a clear spatial relationship even though the photograph is a two-dimensional image.

Look for natural arrangements where landscape features overlap cleanly. Successive mountain ridges, layers of trees, and rolling hills are particularly useful because they provide repeated shapes at different distances. The viewer can follow these forms as they recede into the background, creating a sense of depth without requiring a prominent foreground subject.

Sources indicate that how much elements overlap also matters. If one element completely hides another, the relationship between them becomes less obvious. If the objects barely touch, their outlines can merge into an awkward visual intersection. Small changes in camera position can reveal more of one feature or create a cleaner separation between them.

It has been revealed that this is especially notable when photographing forests or densely layered landscapes. Branches and tree trunks can easily intersect in ways that make the image feel tangled. Rather than trying to include every interesting tree, look for openings where individual trunks and branches remain distinguishable. A slight shift to the left or right may separate one tree from another and make the overall arrangement easier to read.

Focal length directly influences how distance and scale appear in the finished photograph. Wide-angle lenses are useful when the foreground is an important part of the composition. Their broad field of view captures nearby details alongside distant scenery, while perspective exaggeration between close and far objects emphasizes depth.

When using a wide-angle lens, foreground placement becomes particularly notable. An object close to the camera can appear much larger than everything behind it, sometimes dominating the frame. This can be effective when the foreground has a strong shape or texture, but it can also make the composition feel unbalanced. Pay attention to how close you are to the nearest subject and whether its scale supports the relationship between layers.

Telephoto lenses offer a different approach. Rather than emphasizing the distance between foreground and background, longer focal lengths narrow the field of view and make distant features appear closer together. This visual compression can emphasize repeated layers of mountains, hills, trees, or other landscape elements. A scene that looks relatively open through a wide-angle lens may reveal a more graphic arrangement when photographed with a telephoto lens.

Industry observers note that neither approach is inherently better. A wide-angle lens communicates the scale of an expansive landscape, while a telephoto lens isolates a series of distant forms and emphasizes their relationship. If a scene has several interesting layers, try photographing it at different focal lengths before deciding which version best captures the scene.

Light makes layered landscapes more distinctive by revealing shapes, textures, and tonal differences across planes of distance. The same scene may look relatively flat under even midday light but become far more dimensional when low-angle sunlight creates alternating bands of illumination and shadow.

Sidelighting is particularly useful for emphasizing the contours of hills, mountains, and other landforms. As the sun sits low on the horizon, ridges catch the light while valleys remain in shadow. This creates visual separation between successive layers and gives the scene a stronger sense of form. Backlighting can also be effective, especially when photographing trees, grasses, or other translucent elements in the foreground.

A post shared by Kate / Torva Terra (@torvaterra).

Atmospheric conditions provide another way to distinguish distance. Mist and fog soften the contrast of distant hills and mountains, creating a series of progressively lighter layers. After a storm, breaks in clearing clouds often spotlight individual sections of a landscape while leaving others in shadow. These changing conditions produce natural divisions between foreground, middle ground, and background without requiring strong compositional elements in every part of the frame.

Sources indicate that when photographing in changing weather, be prepared to work promptly. Use a tripod when shutter speeds are slow, but avoid relying on one fixed composition if the light is moving across the scene. Take multiple exposures as conditions evolve, particularly when sunlight briefly strikes a distant ridge or a break in the clouds reveals a latest layer. These short-lived lighting conditions can make a substantial difference to the finished image.

Adding layers can create depth, but it can also introduce too much visual information. A foreground full of rocks, a middle ground crowded with trees, and a background filled with overlapping mountain peaks may leave the viewer unsure where to look. The challenge is deciding which elements contribute to the photograph and which ones make it harder to read.

Industry observers note that start by identifying the primary subject or visual feature. This does not have to be a single object — it might be a mountain range, a winding river, or a series of repeating ridgelines. Once you know what should attract attention, consider whether the other layers support it. A foreground element that pulls the eye away from the main subject may need to be repositioned or excluded from the frame.

Simplifying a composition does not always mean removing entire layers—it often means adjusting how much visual weight each one carries. A smaller foreground can establish context without competing with the background, while an open middle ground gives the viewer’s eye room to travel through the scene. Switching to a longer focal length can also help trim distracting edges or unrelated elements.

Watch for bright highlights, stray branches, and high-contrast objects that pull attention away from the subject. These distractions become more disruptive in a layered composition, where the viewer’s eye is already navigating multiple planes. Scan the entire frame before pressing the shutter—paying close attention to the corners and edges—for anything that interrupts the visual flow. Often, shifting the camera slightly or tightening the crop is enough to clean up the frame.

Recent findings suggest that even a minor shift in camera position can alter the relationship between every layer in a landscape. Moving forward or backward changes the scale and placement of foreground objects, while stepping laterally can reveal or conceal distant features. Camera height also dictates how much of the ground plane is visible and how smoothly the foreground transitions into the background.

Rather than immediately setting up a tripod at the first scenic overlook, take time to explore the area. Walk along a ridge, follow a shoreline, or look for a slightly elevated vantage point that opens up the landscape. Observe how foreground elements align with distant peaks, trees, or ridges. Often, the strongest composition sits just a few steps away from the obvious viewpoint.

A post shared by Kate / Torva Terra (@torvaterra).

Once you find a promising spot, a tripod helps you fine-tune height and framing deliberately. Lowering the tripod emphasizes nearby textures, while raising it reveals more of the middle ground. If your tripod has an adjustable center column, extend it sparingly as raising the column too high reduces stability, especially in windy conditions.

Recent findings suggest that perspective control is also worth considering in scenes with strong vertical lines. Tilting the camera upward causes trees, cliffs, or buildings to converge toward the top of the frame. While that converging effect can work creatively, keeping vertical lines straight requires leveling the camera and adjusting your composition by stepping back or switching to a wider lens. What matters most is whether the perspective reinforces how you want the layers to relate.

Sources indicate that building a layered landscape composition becomes much easier when you approach a scene methodically. Start by identifying the anchor of the view—whether that is a distant peak, a line of trees, a winding river, or light sweeping across a valley. From there, work backward toward the camera to see which nearby elements can serve as an entry point without overpowering the main subject.

It has been revealed that once you have identified potential layers, move around to test different arrangements. Look for foreground features that lead naturally into the middle ground, and check how distant shapes overlap. Watch the gaps between objects so unrelated elements do not merge into awkward outlines. If the scene feels overly busy, simplify with a tighter framing or a longer focal length rather than trying to include everything.

Sources indicate that your camera settings should support both the field conditions and the intended depth of the photograph. For a static landscape requiring front-to-back sharpness, a mid-range aperture such as f/8 or f/11 is a reliable starting point. Focus roughly one-third of the way into the scene, then zoom in on your review screen to verify that both the nearest and farthest key elements are sharp. Optimal focus distance depends on focal length, aperture, and proximity to the foreground; if a very close foreground and distant background cannot both be rendered sharply in a single frame, focus stacking is a reliable alternative when the scene is still.

Keep your ISO low when practical, but do not let the pursuit of a noise-free file force an overly slow shutter speed. Wind moving through grasses or foliage often calls for a faster exposure, even if that requires raising your ISO. A tripod eliminates camera shake, but it cannot freeze motion within the landscape itself.

Before leaving a location, photograph the scene using several different focal lengths and compositions. Start with a wider frame that emphasizes the foreground, then try a tighter composition that compresses repeating layers or gives greater weight to the background. I also like revisiting locations under different light and weather, as shifts in atmosphere or time of day can completely transform a scene’s character and yield a more dramatic photograph. Comparing these variations helps reveal which arrangement and conditions best capture the landscape.

Industry observers note that ultimately, layered landscape photography is about building intentional relationships between elements in a scene. Foreground, middle ground, and background offer a reliable structural framework, but their impact depends on how well they connect, overlap, and remain visually distinct. By paying close attention to camera position, focal length, light, and visual balance, you can create landscapes with genuine depth and clarity.

Finding, acquiring and showing off: how rich buyers use social media to build art collections

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (787 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

💡 Key Takeaways
  • How do major collectors use social media to help them navigate the art world?
  • While the most common routes into collecting according to the report were the influence of family (28% of respondents) and cultural exposure through visits to museums, galleries, and fairs (22%), a surprising 13% discovered art collecting independently through online channels or social media.
  • In a recent development, the data also indicates that those who started their art collecting journey online had higher levels of engagement with in-person exhibitions and events, both locally and overseas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How do major collectors use social media to help them navigate the art world? The latest Art Basel & UBS Survey of Global Collecting 2026 report, which surveyed 3,100 high net-worth individuals (HNWIs) who collect art, demonstrates that social media platforms—and Instagram in particular—are an increasingly key tool for discovering art and artists, buying works and promoting collections. Here is how online platforms are being used and what the art world can learn from it.

While the most common routes into collecting according to the report were the influence of family (28% of respondents) and cultural exposure through visits to museums, galleries, and fairs (22%), a surprising 13% discovered art collecting independently through online channels or social media. Interestingly, online channels were a less common route into collecting for Gen Z collectors (10%) than for Gen X (16%), “running against any assumption that younger collectors might be more likely to find their way to collecting through digital channels”, the report states.

In a recent development, the data also indicates that those who started their art collecting journey online had higher levels of engagement with in-person exhibitions and events, both locally and overseas. “While being introduced to art through family or cultural exposure may reflect a more passive route into collecting, those who started out online were typically more active in seeking out art content,” the report says. “This suggests a more deliberate, self-directed collecting journey that carries forward into greater engagement with events later on.”.

When it comes to collecting, 58% of respondents said they had used digital resources for advice with 32% of collectors citing either Instagram or X (formerly Twitter) as sources when it came to making purchases. Nineteen percent used recommendations from Instagram (up 2% year-on-year), including 22% of Gen Z respondents, and women were more likely to use them than men. The platform X—which has seen decreased usage in recent years due to controversies around its ownership and usage—was used by 18% of the sample, and this was again highest among Gen Z (23%).

A collectors’ likeliness to use social media recommendations for collecting also depended greatly on where a person was from: collectors in Hong Kong, the US and the UK were most likely to use social media for advice while those in Mainland China were less likely, undoubtedly due to the restrictions of social media platforms in the country.

Contrary to popular belief around the slow uptake of artificial intelligence (AI) in the art world, the study also revealed that collectors trusted AI tools for art recommendations twice as much as those from social media and influencers, and also slightly more than in-store advisors and editorial content.

Sources indicate that the importance of ​​online and social media platforms in reaching collectors is growing. According to the survey, 27% of HNWIs’ total expenditure was made through such external platforms, up by 5 percentage points year-on-year and from 17% in 2024. The share of collectors buying directly from artists also grew to 69%, with 38% of works bought via Instagram, highlighting the benefits of a strong, independent social media presence for artists. It is also interesting to note that artist-direct spending through Instagram was higher among newly introduced collectors than more experienced ones: 8% for those in the market for two years or less, versus just 2% for those collecting for 20 years or more.

But can seeing a work online really seal the deal? Apparently so—among the 75% of respondents who had purchased a work directly from a dealer in 2025/2026, 53% had bought via Instagram without viewing the work in person, up from 43% in 2024.

The report interestingly states that the youngest generation of collectors—Gen Z—are not the ones using social media the most in their collecting journeys. “The generation raised on social media is, it turns out, the one most inclined to keep its collecting close,” the report indicates. While the data showed that Gen Z were the highest-spending generation surveyed and had the most wide-ranging collecting habits, their awareness of digital footprints leads them to seek greater control and privacy over their "personal and cultural identities".

“Anonymous accounts and smaller, niche social networking platforms allow them to communicate in ways that feel less pressurised and performative,” the report states. “With social media feeds heavily controlled and populated by algorithms rather than personal networks, Gen Z consumers are increasingly interested in taking back control over who sees their personal content by sharing it with smaller, vetted and carefully chosen audiences.”.

When it came to sharing information about their collections with the wider public, only 25% Gen Z shared their own content publicly, compared with 36% of millennials and around one third of other older collectors.

A post shared by KitKat Australia & New Zealand (@kitkatanz).

Shisuo Design Office creates "surreal" rural house in China using salvaged steel

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jiang Deng Lu is a house in rural Anhui designed by Chinese studio Shisuo Design Office using stainless-steel offcuts salvaged from the client’s own factory.
  • Described by Shisuo Design Office as a “surreal rural house”, the compact building is raised partially on stilts to look as though it is floating above its sloped riverside site.
  • It sits beside the client’s ancestral home and serves as both a memorial for his late father and a separate dwelling where his elderly mother can host visiting relatives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Lv Xiaobin.

Jiang Deng Lu is a house in rural Anhui designed by Chinese studio Shisuo Design Office using stainless-steel offcuts salvaged from the client’s own factory.

Described by Shisuo Design Office as a “surreal rural house”, the compact building is raised partially on stilts to look as though it is floating above its sloped riverside site.

It sits beside the client’s ancestral home and serves as both a memorial for his late father and a separate dwelling where his elderly mother can host visiting relatives.

“The client wanted to build a house beside the old family home, providing a comfortable place for his mother and relatives to gather and share meals during holidays,” Shisuo Design Office told Dezeen.

“But beyond this practical need, there was a deeper emotional connection. The old house was left by his father, while the new one represented his own way of creating new memories for the family,” it continued.

“We hoped the house would bring the family together more often, beyond just festive occasions.”.

Jiang Deng Lu’s proportions were determined by the recycled stainless steel offcuts and unused windows salvaged for the project by the client, who is the owner of a stainless steel factory.

“The building’s geometry was strictly reverse-engineered from these salvaged materials,” said Shisuo Design Office.

“Instead of imposing a predetermined architectural form, we meticulously measured and mapped these specific surplus components. The building’s precise dimensions, roof pitches, and structural envelope were entirely reverse-engineered from this salvaged inventory,” added the studio.

“The resulting structure starkly contrasts the client’s modern, lightweight metal industry with the heavy, rooted legacy of his father’s masonry, translating familial love into a rigorous tectonic language,” the studio said.

It has been revealed that externally, the house is wrapped in a full stainless-steel facade, which the studio said deliberately contrasts with “traditional rural vernacular”. This is punctured by the salvaged windows, positioned to frame views of the river.

It has a rectangular blueprint, with a balcony that is suspended over the river on one side.

Inside is a living space, which sits raised above a dining area accessed directly from the foyer. A bathroom and shower room sit off this dining space.

Sources indicate that interior finishes are pared-back, with stone flooring and white walls complementing the cool-toned exterior of the home. Wooden furnishings and greenery seen through the windows add warmth to the space.

According to Shisuo Design Office, the highlight of the interior is a nine-metre-long window that cantilevers 2.2 metres outward, providing shelter for the terrace below.

Another house featured on Dezeen with a distinctive metal facade is Bondi House, a two-storey, two-bedroom dwelling by Nick Kent Design in Sydney.

Sources indicate that some institutional rape cases create a glut of content. Recent allegations against Cornell students led to the publication of the accused’s portraits, images of their text messages, and videos of their fraternity house. Tweets and articles flooded the internet, while a journalist’s attempt to identify Jane Doe introduced an entire Instagram campaign: Owners posted their own pictures with the hashtag #iamjanedoe to help shield the victim. On the other side of the spectrum, reported rapes in the military, the Catholic Church, and less wealthy communities around the world may be met with silence, handled privately, or otherwise fail to galvanize the digital realm.

Spanish photographer Laia Abril — whose larger project “A History of Misogyny” has also tackled feminicide, abortion, and endometriosis — faces a tricky mandate as she created On Rape and Institutional Failure, first shown in 2020 and now on view at the International Center for Photography. Her images have to be compelling without embracing spectacle, specific while addressing an enormous, global theme.

According to recent reports, the artist makes two key choices, one conceptual and one formal: She shoots objects instead of people, all in black-and-white. Honing in on her palette, Abril gets at the seemingly eternal nature of misogyny; her distilled images stoke a similarly condensed rage.

Breaking: The Ebullient Ecofeminism of Carolina Caycedo

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (435 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Hyperallergic

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ST LOUIS, MO — A pink lake under an avalanche of digital detritus; a neon rainbow behind a man in a hazmat suit; a gilt sky above a lone wind turbine.
  • Caycedo’s candy-colored drawings lure the eye only to disquiet the mind, exposing the contradictions of so-called clean energy, whose production often depends on environmentally destructive mineral extraction.
  • Such visual beguilement — and ecological exigency — anchors Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots, an exhibition of sculpture, video, printmaking, and drawing that explores the joyous, multisensory dimensions of the artist’s activism.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ST LOUIS, MO — A pink lake under an avalanche of digital detritus; a neon rainbow behind a man in a hazmat suit; a gilt sky above a lone wind turbine. These are among the surreal, meticulously rendered scenes in Carolina Caycedo’s series Mineral Intensive (2023–ongoing).

Caycedo’s candy-colored drawings lure the eye only to disquiet the mind, exposing the contradictions of so-called clean energy, whose production often depends on environmentally destructive mineral extraction.

Such visual beguilement — and ecological exigency — anchors Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots, an exhibition of sculpture, video, printmaking, and drawing that explores the joyous, multisensory dimensions of the artist’s activism.

Raised in Bogotá, Colombia, the Los Angeles-based artist devoted two years to collaborative research with botanists, plant taxonomists, and Native elders, informing her rendering of prairie and botanical life across the Mississippi River watershed. By turns bright and delicate, Caycedo’s Plant Portraits series (2021–ongoing) lends an ecofeminist bent to the larger show, merging feminine anatomy with botanical illustration.

Detail of Carolina Caycedo, "Neodymium Intensive" (2026), colored pencil, aluminum and variegated metal leaf on paper (left); Installation view of "Celestial Autonomy, the Dance of Big Dipper and North Star" (2023) at Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots at the Kemper Art Museum.

Like a heavenly necklace, “Celestial Autonomy, the Dance of Substantial Dipper and North Star” (2023) dangles in the center of the gallery. Constructed of Alaskan nets, buoys, and other fishing equipment — its title honors the indigenous communities in the region.

Across the Mississippi River, as part of the Counterpublic 2026 triennial, another sculptural installation, “Fiesta de la Raíces” (2026), vivifies the National Building Arts Center in Sauget, Illinois. A three-dimensional “portrait” of the area’s root systems, the sculpture resembles a shaggy chandelier of rope, beads, and natural fibers — beckoning admirers to bask in its festive opulence.

Recent findings suggest that at a time when ecological disaster feels ever imminent, art attuned to earthly precarity can often feel didactic or downright drab. Caycedo insists on an alternate vision: Humanity in sync with a resplendent planet — the ground beneath us trembling with riches, the sky adorned with unseen stars.

Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots continues at the Kemper Art Museum at Washington University in St. Louis (One Brookings Drive, St. Louis, Missouri) through January 4. The installation, "Fiesta de la Raíces," part of Counterpublic 2026, will be on view at the National Building Arts Center (NBAC) (2300 Falling Springs Road, Sauget, Illinois) through December 12. The exhibition at the Kemper was curated by Meredith Malone and "Fiesta de la Raíces" was curated by James McAnally.
