Canva's 'AI off switch' finally recognises the backlash from creatives

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (751 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the past couple of years, most of the press releases coming from software companies have contained announcements of latest AI features.
  • Canva is one of those companies, and it's introduced a bunch of generative AI tools to its design platform.
  • In a recent development, canva has added two AI controls for both Free and Pro consumers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the past couple of years, most of the press releases coming from software companies have contained announcements of latest AI features. Image, video and vector generation, removal tools, agentic workflows, AI assistants, and myriad other advances that can help artists do in seconds something that used to take hours.

Canva is one of those companies, and it's introduced a bunch of generative AI tools to its design platform. So the email I received yesterday made me do a double take. On the day that Anthropic completed the world's biggest IPO in history, it introduced an 'AI off switch'.

In a recent development, canva has added two AI controls for both Free and Pro consumers. The generative AI switch can be used to hide all of its generative AI tools, including Magic Write, Magic Design, Magic Expand, Dream Lab and Canva Code. It can be switched on or off at any time.

There's also an option to “See less AI content” on Canva's library of templates and design elements. This addresses complaints about the glut of AI-generated content making it harder to find quality work, something that's been causing problems on platforms as varied as Etsy and ArtStation.

Canva claims AI-generated content remains a "small portion" of its library and that such content is identified in its metadata. Turning on the fresh function isn't guaranteed to remove it completely, but it should put human-made templates and design elements first in search results and recommendations.

According to recent reports, the addition of a couple of toggles to the UI wouldn't normally be breaking news, so the fact that Canva feels this deserved its own announcement is telling. After heavily promoting AI tools, it's now presenting the ability to turn them off as a groundbreaking advance – and it is. This might be the first time that a major AI-forward creative software developer has recognised that a sizable portion of its user base just isn't into it.

"We believe AI has extraordinary potential to help people bring their ideas to life, and we're excited to keep pushing the boundaries of what's possible," Canva says. "At the same time, like so many of you, we know there's something special about the time, care, and creativity that goes into making something that's truly yours.".

According to recent reports, an 'AI off button' is something that some creatives have been calling for. Part of the difficulty in implementing one is that it needs a definition of AI. Programs like Adobe's Photoshop have used machine learning for many years; it just wasn't branded as 'AI'. Many artists welcome tools that speed up their work, but not ones that do the creation part for them, especially if they're powered by models that were trained on unlicensed work.

Sources indicate that canva's recognised that. The toggle only turns off generative AI tools, such as ones that generate latest imagery, text or code from prompts. Assistive editing tools like Background Remover or Magic Grab, which lets you select and move an object in an image will still be available. Using them won't cause your work to be shamed with metadata identifying it as AI-generated.

A 'no AI button' also requires a willingness from the provider. Since generative AI features are often charged on a per-use basis via credits, software companies generally want to encourage their customers to use them.

Adobe teased some impressive-looking AI-powered tools in the Adobe Max Sneaks presentation last week, but it's also clear that some customers detest generative AI, which has created a market for fresh tools like the artist-led Niva app, which is promoting itself as AI-free art software.

Will an AI-off button let Canva have its cake and eat it?

You can learn more about Canva on the website.

Sources indicate that hilma af Klint's painting “Ser III No. 5” (1920) sold for a record $12.7 million (SEK 128.9 million) at Bukowskis's modern art and design auction in Stockholm today, November 19, fetching over 16 times the upper end of its estimated price.

The first abstract painting by the Swedish artist and "mother of abstraction" to appear on the open market in 30 years, "Ser III No. 5" was one of the 85 geometric paintings the artist produced during a fervent months-long process in 1920. Theosophical symbols, triangles, and circles in "Ser III No. 5" provide insight into af Klint's last engagement with geometric abstraction before she turned to more naturalist watercolors in the last years of her life.

Nike Tuned Air "a huge stride forward" in air-filled trainer design says innovation lead

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (844 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, sportswear brand Nike has unveiled the 3D-printed air bags that will be used for its next generation of air-filled trainers.
  • According to recent reports, “I see it personally as a revolution, not an evolution,” McCartney told Dezeen from the LeBron James Innovation Center in Oregon.
  • In a recent development, tuned Air was designed to give Nike much greater control of how air is used within the midsole to provide cushioning and support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography courtesy of Nike.

According to recent reports, sportswear brand Nike has unveiled the 3D-printed air bags that will be used for its next generation of air-filled trainers. In this interview, the brand’s chief innovation, design & product officer Phil McCartney explains why it is a technological and performance advance.

According to recent reports, “I see it personally as a revolution, not an evolution,” McCartney told Dezeen from the LeBron James Innovation Center in Oregon. “It’s a huge stride forward.”.

In a recent development, tuned Air was designed to give Nike much greater control of how air is used within the midsole to provide cushioning and support. Using a combination of proprietary 3D printing and “selective lamination” allows Nike to create midsoles that perform in different ways under different parts of the foot.

Informed by the raised vibrant colours on magazine covers, the airbag is built up from layers of ink.

“We can engineer the structure and tune the structure in the heel differently to the forefoot,” said McCartney.

“We can also tune the height, so you can have a variety of different heights, and we can tune the structure inside.”.

Nike unveiled the technology and concept images for a running shoe today, and is planning for the first Nike Tuned Air trainer to be launched next year.

The trainers will be the first in what Nike sees as a third major generation of its air-filled shoes, since Nike CEO Phil Knight worked with inventor Frank Rudy to use a cushioning system filled with gas in the late 1970s.

Following the Nike Air Tailwind in 1978, Nike developed Air Max in the 1980s and Air Zoom in the 1990s.

In a recent development, “At its core, Air, for 50 years, has been this magical combination of lightweight, cushioned and resilient – it doesn’t break down over time,” said McCartney. “That’s why from day one when Phil [Knight] struck the deal with Frank Rudy, we’ve been so committed to it – it just delivers a really unique benefit.”.

“If Max Air is about maximal cushioning and impact protection, Zoom Air is more about responsiveness and snappiness,” he continued. “Tuned Air, because of this proprietary ink and selective lamination process, allows us to literally tune the sensation within the airbag, which enables us to sort of move free from the constraints of typical geometry and shape.”.

According to McCartney, this change in how the airbags are manufactured opens up possibilities, especially in customisation.

Sources indicate that “It is the first step in exploring all the different places that this will go,” stated McCartney. “The capability and what we’re able to do with this proprietary ink and the selective lamination allows us to really unlock the real potential of air.”.

“It also creates this canvas for all the design explorations that we’ve always wanted to do, but the limitations of the manufacturing process didn’t allow,” he continued.

According to recent reports, “So now the handcuffs are off in terms of it being a canvas – what expressions do we want to explore? What different visuals, geometries, and different ways to articulate the benefit can we explore? We’re looking at all of that. “.

While the air-filled midsole has been manufactured, the trainer is still in development. However, McCartney expects the shoe to look close to the concept render that was revealed today.

According to recent reports, “There’ll be a few modifications,” he said. “Knowing where the design is going to go. It’s pretty representative as an illustration, but it isn’t the final design.” He noted that the final air bag design will be close to the prototype.

“What we’re exploring now is how do we take the idea of lightweight cushioning and this idea of tuned [and find] what that looks like in an expression and an experience on the upper.”.

One key design element that will feature in the commercial release next year will be the full-length, visible air bag, which McCartney said is an “notable part of the design and important part of this platform”.

The midsoles are the latest innovation in Nike’s exploration of using air within footwear and apparel. While it has made millions of shoes containing air, it has also recently unveiled the inflating Air Milano Jacket at 2026 Winter Olympics and its Radical AirFlow t-shirts that counterintuitively use more material to make a wearer cooler.

In all the areas of innovation that McCartney oversees at Nike, air is where he sees the most potential.

“There’s a number of areas, but if I had to pick one, I think that [air] is the platform that intrigues us most, that drives our creativity the most, that also translates into the biggest athlete benefit. And I mean athlete in the broadest sense of the term – if you’ve got a body, you’re an athlete.”.

“We’re really intrigued and fascinated by the notion of being able to harness what’s all around us to further performance,” mentioned McCartney. “That started in footwear, obviously. This is the next revolution.”.

Photography courtesy of Nike.

Adobe software might still rule in many industries, but there's a growing number of alternatives, from Canva's free Affinity to open-source Krita, Maxon's Autograph for motion design and DaVinci Resolve for video editing. Into the fray, comes a new artist-led app who's main selling points include the fact that it DOESN'T have any generative AI tools.

Industry observers note that NIVA is clean and light, works in your browser and it's led by a conceptual artist rather than a software developer. After it was announced on Instagram this week, it picked up close to 30,000 users in 48 hours.

Like the recent AI-coded Adobe clones, NIVA was born out of a frustration with the direction of a certain Californian software giant. But it takes a very different approach. It wasn't vibe coded, and it doesn't attempt to replicate the look, feel or functions of any one existing program.

The project's led by Stuart Semple, an artist who previously annoyed Anish Kapoor by creating a very black shade of black.

Recent findings suggest that "With Adobe pushing AI further into its tools, I wanted somewhere people could still practise their craft and make things themselves. No AI doing it for them," he notes. "NIVA is very much our own thing that we've all built together.

Having previously made FREETONE, a free alternative to Pantone colours, with Culture Hustle, he started a Kickstarter for a project that was initially called Abode. He raised $240,000 from 3,000 backers, a few hundred of whom have been using the software regularly over a year and a half of beta testing. Around 10 people were involved more heavily in making the software, but Stuart says he largely built it himself "with help from some geeky friends from time to time when I've got stuck.".

Sources indicate that at some point the name changed, and the project became NIVA. "I can't say I woke up to a nasty letter from the lawyers representing Adobe for legal reasons, so I won't," Stuart comments.

NIVA has many of the core tools and functionalities of a program like Photoshop. There are brushes, a pen tool with boolean ops, cloning and healing tools, layers, curve adjustments and blend modes, type tools with kerning, layouts and gradients.

Industry observers note that but it's lighter, with a more minimalist UI and fewer menus despite providing the ability to draw vectors, manipulate photos and lay out text and pages all in a single app. People also get a portfolio page, and there's a visual asset library called Storehouse, where you can store, sort, search and share work. Work can be exported in formats including PDF and SVG.

It has been revealed that the pricing model is refreshing too. There's no subscription, and NIVA is free to use for an hour a day. You can buy full-day passes for $10 a time, or you can buy permanent access for $100. If you buy a day pass and later go permanent, the price of the day pass will be discounted. This allows a full opportunity to try the software before committing.

The response so far has been more enthusiastic than Stuart ever imagined. "I'm so excited and a bit freaked out", he admits, adding that what he finds most encouraging is that over half of the people who used NIVA in those first 48 hours made something with it within 40 seconds of getting access.

"We're finally at a stage where it's stable enough and good enough to share with the world," he adds. It's only version one, the start of something I hope will be great. I still have loads I want to do with it".

You can use the software online at NIVA.design.

He writes news, features and buying guides and keeps track of the best equipment and software for creatives, from video editing programs to monitors and accessories. A veteran news writer and photographer, he now works as a project manager at the London and Buenos Aires-based design, production and branding agency Hermana Creatives. There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.

In a recent development, the Center for Curatorial Studies at Bard College confirmed Laura Hoptman, executive director of the Drawing Center in New York, as the recipient of the 2027 Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence, a $25,000 prize. Hoptman's curriculum vitae reads like a roll call of NYC's major institutions: She started out as an assistant curator at the Bronx Museum in the 1980s and later held curatorial roles at the Museum of Modern Art and the New Museum.

So it is no surprise that, when asked what this recognition signified for her, Hoptman chose to invoke the network and community that her career has grown alongside.

Recent findings suggest that “The best kind of professional recognition comes from one's peers, and this is one of the many reasons why this award is so meaningful to me,” Hoptman told Hyperallergic in an email. “It also reminds me how damn lucky I have been to have spent the last 30 years around art and artists in one of the greatest cultural hubs in the world. After all this time, my vocation still fills me with joy.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earlier this month, Trump’s White House ballroom and military bunker laid its final structural steel beam, with politicians and critics weighing in on the scale of the project.

Recently taken images of the extension, which show the structure with massive concrete shear walls, steel beams, and columns, along with a partially enclosed roof structure, have drawn attention to the scale of the building.

No sign of its planned neoclassical ornamentation has yet been implemented.

Officially called the East Wing Modernization Project, the structure dwarfs the Executive Residence and West Wing.

Trump declared the laying of the last steel beam in the superstructure on 4 November, the day after the national midterm elections.

“This is a special structure,” Trump mentioned on a tour on 4 November, according to NBC News. “It’s going to be not only one of the biggest, but it’ll be the most beautiful ballroom, I think, anywhere in the world, and they’ve been trying to get it for 150 years.”.

In a recent development, it says everything about Donald Trump that his gilded ballroom dwarfs the size of the People's House—and it says everything about the American people that they repudiated him loudly and clearly last Tuesday. pic.twitter.com/ou23LpAes8.

Since then, there has been a renewed wave of criticism online over the project, ranging from outrage to humour.

Former senator and presidential candidate Hillary Clinton wrote on X (formerly Twitter), commenting on the size of the structure and noting the midterm election’s “repudiation” of Trump.

“It states everything about Donald Trump that his gilded ballroom dwarfs the size of the People’s House—and it says everything about the American people that they repudiated him loudly and clearly last Tuesday,” wrote Clinton.

Congressman Jim Clyburn took a similar stance in a statement on Facebook, noting that the ballroom was “much bigger” than the rest of the White House.

Sources indicate that architecture critic Kate Wagner took a more humorous approach, noting that the ballroom is not neoclassical in construction. Wagner compared it to a Ramada Inn, a chain of hotels in the US, that they will “glue pediments to”.

“[It’s] an outcome designed in a lab to make everyone angry. possibly the most trump building ever built,” wrote Wagner on X.com.

The ballroom has been controversial since Trump demolished the White House’s East Wing in October 2025. The National Capital Planning Commission approved the project in April.

It has faced legal challenges, with US District Judge Leon issuing a stay in response to a lawsuit led by the National Trust for Historic Preservation.

the fact that trump's ballroom is clearly not neoclassical in any way shape or form is possibly the funniest moment in architectural history.

In August, the Supreme Court allowed the project to continue, though the dissenting opinion said it was “likely unlawful”.

Despite the legal challenges, construction has continued, with Trump’s team leaning on the national security aspects of the underground bunker.

The administration has also floated plans to add a screening facility at Sherman Park – a small park to the southwest of the White House. Trump also installed a paved helipad on the White House lawn.

Working mothers face widespread discrimination in London’s commercial art world, report finds

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1205 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the contemporary art world has become increasingly adept at putting feminism, gender equality and the politics of care at the centre of its public-facing programming.
  • Not far at all, according to the first ever peer-reviewed study on motherhood and discrimination in London’s commercial art world, published today by the European Journal of Cultural Studies and The Art Working Parents Alliance.
  • According to recent reports, based on a survey of 50 art world employees working across the UK capital’s galleries and auction houses, including 12 in-depth interviews, research by Kate McMillan and Cleo Roberts-Komireddi exposes a workplace culture in which mothering children often comes at considerable professional cost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the contemporary art world has become increasingly adept at putting feminism, gender equality and the politics of care at the centre of its public-facing programming. Galleries mount exhibitions exploring women's experiences, champion female artists and engage with questions of representation and social justice. But how far do those values extend to the women working behind the scenes?

Not far at all, according to the first ever peer-reviewed study on motherhood and discrimination in London’s commercial art world, published today by the European Journal of Cultural Studies and The Art Working Parents Alliance.

According to recent reports, based on a survey of 50 art world employees working across the UK capital’s galleries and auction houses, including 12 in-depth interviews, research by Kate McMillan and Cleo Roberts-Komireddi exposes a workplace culture in which mothering children often comes at considerable professional cost. As the report puts it: “Becoming a parent is at the root of the glass ceiling, and for many, it represents the glass cliff.”.

It has been revealed that three-quarters of survey respondents say becoming a parent has negatively affected their career progression, while more than one in five say they had been explicitly denied promotion. One woman was told she was ineligible for promotion while on maternity leave—a breach of UK law. Just 54% received enhanced maternity pay, compared with a national workplace average of 74.1%.

Recent findings suggest that and these problems are not limited to smaller companies. “We assumed this would affect small art galleries with between five and 20 staff, but we found that massive, multi-national galleries are also failing,” McMillan states. As the report notes: “A lack of accountability pervades the sector.”.

Roberts-Komireddi believes that the “culture of secrecy” that enshrouds much of the art market—where financial transactions, benefits and networks are opaque and rarely disclosed—contributes to the discrimination women face when they become mothers. “Opacity really serves certain individuals and maintains this sense of fear, which was something I found particularly startling when we did our 12 in-depth interviews,” she claims. “Fear and perceived retribution pervade these workplaces and women’s relationships to these workplaces.”.

That fear is often felt as soon as women announce their pregnancies. The report documents, among other instances, a pregnant woman being made redundant while experiencing a high-risk pregnancy, an employer attempting to dissolve a pregnant employee’s role and use the money to hire a new salesperson and a woman who miscarried returning to her desk immediately after a hospital appointment because she feared taking time off would damage her career. One interviewee describes feeling that by becoming pregnant she was making herself “vulnerable and less valuable”.

According to recent reports, the findings also point to a deeper contradiction within an industry that publicly champions equality but often operates according to an unforgiving model of constant availability, international travel and after-hours networking. The art critic and curator Hettie Judah, who is a co-founder of The Art Working Parents Alliance, describes the colliding of 6pm private views with bedtime routines as the “witching hour” clash.

Recent findings suggest that the difficulties are not confined to maternity leave itself. For many, the return to work can prove more damaging. Interviewees describe coming back to find their responsibilities have been redistributed, their relationships with artists and clients disrupted, or their standing within the gallery diminished. One woman discovered that a colleague who had covered her maternity leave had been given half her role, along with the artists she had spent years representing. Another returned from leave to find there was no desk for her in the gallery’s newly introduced office.

Industry observers note that crucially, the report reveals the lack of formal HR structures across the commercial art sector. Only half of the respondents worked for galleries with dedicated HR staff, while just 30 of the 50 remarked their workplace had a specific maternity or parental leave policy. In some cases, employees were left to research their own entitlements, negotiate their packages and even draft policies themselves. The report’s authors say that a lack of professional HR expertise contributed to instances of discriminatory practice and breaches of the UK Equality Act.

According to recent reports, the consequences can be far-reaching. For many women, the choice has been stark: find a way to accommodate the demands of motherhood or compromise their careers. Three-quarters of the women interviewed made changes to their careers after becoming pregnant, with some moving into freelance or independent work, taking less senior positions or leaving the industry altogether. Only a third of survey respondents were offered flexible working on their return, while half were expected to be in the office four or five days a week. One interviewee described the culture as one in which “presentism is more key than doing the work”.

The role of class and wealth is key in shaping these experiences. The report notes how some senior figures have access to live-in nannies, au pairs and domestic help, leaving them less attuned to the financial and practical pressures facing employees who must balance childcare with demanding working hours. One interviewee stated that the management team “all had night nurses, and you know, people helping at night. So, for them to understand that you’d had three hours of interrupted sleep and were expected to be at an opening, and a dinner, get home at 12:30 and then get up at 4:30 again, was impossible”.

It has been revealed that for those on more modest salaries, the cost of childcare can make evening events and travel particularly difficult to sustain. The report suggests that the more junior and precarious the employee, the greater the likelihood of experiencing discrimination—and the fewer resources they have to challenge it.

According to recent reports, these divisions are not simply a question of wealth, however. They also complicate assumptions about gender solidarity within an industry where women make up a significant proportion of the workforce, but senior positions are often occupied by men. As Roberts-Komireddi points out, the assumption that women will necessarily support other women can be misleading—some of the more surprising testimonies in the report describe male directors showing greater sympathy towards pregnant employees than their female counterparts.

These accounts suggest that the treatment of working mothers is shaped not simply by the gender of those in positions of authority, but by a wider workplace culture in which employees have little power to challenge established practices. Indeed, the report argues that discriminatory treatment is widespread, identifying breaches of the Equality Act in the experiences of all the women interviewed. Yet legal cases rarely make it to an employment tribunal. “In the UK, up until 1 October this year, women only had three months to bring a case to tribunal, which is not a lot of time, particularly if you’re about to give birth,” Roberts-Komireddi states. “There’s a reluctance to go down that route because it’s a long, tiring, expensive process.”.

Sources indicate that looking ahead, the report’s authors hope to set best practice in the art industry. “If you look at huge corporations like Google, they have changed their policies in order to retain and attract mothers who make excellent staff—we could learn a lot from them,” Roberts-Komireddi says.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that nothing in visual culture is neutral, least of all the color wheel itself. Scholar Richard Powell explores this deceptively simple truth in his new book, tackling the theoretical entanglement of race and pigment and how Black painters have used color over time. Trailblazing art historian Lowery Stokes Sims, formerly a curator at the Met Museum and director of the Studio Museum in Harlem, parses his richly layered essays today, linking the critical theory of Josef Albers and Darby English to the practices of artists like Jacob Lawrence and Alma Thomas. The book, Sims writes, shifted the way she’ll look at art moving forward.

Meanwhile, on the other end of the spectrum: News broke that a 1920 painting by Hilma af Klint sold for $12.7 million. Yes, the same Hilma af Klint who described herself less as an artist and more as a channel for a higher power, who followed the guidance of spirits that took physical form through her paintings. But hey, at least the painting’s owner has a new addition to their investment portfolio?

In reviews, Alina Cohen spends time with the poignant, impactful photographs by Laia Abril, who evokes the systems of patriarchy and sexual violence through the quietly haunting garments and objects in their wake. As the Cornell 7 case continues and convicted abusers sit in office, Abril’s photographs “reject both the invisibility of some crimes and the all-too-visible nature of others.” More, as always, below.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books.

Industry observers note that I was aware of the place of color theory in the practice of art and knew the names of key theorists, from Johann Wolfgang von Goethe to Johannes Itten to Josef Albers. But otherwise, I presumed artists’ palettes were the result of personal predilection, technical explorations (i.e., the opening up of brushstrokes and form in the 19th century and the introduction of a wall of color in the 20th century), or cultural orientation. So it was therefore with great interest that I approached reading Richard Powell’s latest publication, Colorstruck!: Painting, Pigment, Affect (2026). | Lowery Stokes Sims.

Read more about all the winning design projects below:.

Design project of the year and graphic design of the year: V&A East Storehouse by Fieldwork Facility.

Design studio Fieldwork Facility was challenged with navigating visitors to the V&A’s storage vault, including 250,000 historic art, craft and design objects – especially a younger, more diverse crowd who might normally feel excluded from museums.

This fun and informative signage and wayfinding perfectly embraces the changing nature of the V&A East Storehouse.

The Hackney design studio looked to an unexpected source of inspiration when creating wayfinding for London’s V&A East Storehouse: Gen-Z apps and services.

“This fun and informative signage and wayfinding perfectly embraces the changing nature of the V&A East Storehouse,” said the master jury.

“As the displays change, the signage, captions and general wayfinding can be updated efficiently, embracing the adaptability and lack of formality of the museum.”.

Furniture design of the year: Dado Series by Allen Kaufmann Objects.

Berlin studio Allen Kaufmann Architekten won furniture design of the year for its Dado series of tables and shelves.

What is simple in appearance is underscored with a well-resolved and detailed construction made from a monomaterial.

The practice adapted a traditional woodworking joint to create a flat-pack range that can be assembled completely without tools nor glue, screws, brackets or other fasteners.

“What is simple in appearance is underscored with a well-resolved and detailed construction made from a monomaterial,” the judges stated. “The shelving is satisfying to assemble and demonstrates everything furniture needs to be, and no more.”.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Seating design of the year: Kino by Pablo Castillo Design.

Barcelona-based designer Pablo Castillo won seating design of the year for Kino, a cantilevered 3D-printed chair for Decibel.

Modern shapes meet zero-waste manufacturing; surely the future.

The designer’s aim was to create a recognisable chair silhouette, while also responding to the specificities of the 3D printing process.

Recent findings suggest that its entire form is printed from PLA, the most common bioplastic, although the material is reinforced with cellulose plant fibres. This increases its strength, enabling the cantilevered seat.

“The 3D printing of furniture is becoming more refined and this is a strong example of that,” stated the master jury.

According to recent reports, “The mono-material construction is sophisticated and has a strong aesthetic profile,” they continued. “Modern shapes meet zero-waste manufacturing; surely the future.”.

Collectible design of the year: Lima Charlie by Studio Laurids Gallée.

Austrian designer Laurids Gallée won collectible design of the year for Lima Charlie, a series of five colourful, sculptural lamps.

Mesmerising, intriguing and evocative, these lights are truly original and demonstrate a high level of care in their meticulous craftsmanship.

The lighting collection comprises five hand-cast resin light works and machined aluminium pieces.

In a recent development, first, the designer used digital processes to determine each composition. Then, casting solid blocks of the material before colouring, cutting and sculpting them into shape. Each piece was meticulously sanded and polished to arrive at the desired smooth surface.

“Mesmerising, intriguing and evocative, these lights are truly original and demonstrate a high level of care in their meticulous craftsmanship,” praised the judges. “Beautiful treasures to enhance any space.”.

Bespoke design of the year: Real Time Schiphol People’s Clock by Maarten Baas.

Dutch designer Maarten Baas won bespoke design of the year for The People’s Clock, a choreographed representation of the passage of time at Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport.

It was an ambitious undertaking to make the piece, which celebrates and gives ownership to the airport workers.

Baas recruited 1,000 participants – the majority being airport employees – to form the hands of The People’s Clock and move in sync, forming the hour and minute hands. The second hand comprises a single person running a lap of the circular perimeter each minute.

“This timepiece in Amsterdam’s busy airport momentarily takes customers away from the efficient functionality of the space by providing a reference to the time in a more playful and poetic way,” said the master jury.

“It was an ambitious undertaking to make the piece, which celebrates and gives ownership to the airport workers.”.

Lighting design of the year: Hoop Table Lamp by John Tree for Vaarnii.

Designer John Tree won lighting design of the year for the Hoop Table Lamp for Finnish brand Vaarni.

There is a confidence in the minimal use of materials and a cuteness in the ensuing form.

The monolithic light combines a block of solid pine wood – synonymous with the Finnish brand’s designs – with a hooped shade of thin pine veneer, sourced from a sustainably managed forest.

“We were all drawn to the simple and characterful gestures of this table lamp, which embraces warmth from a common timber,” the judges remarked.

“There is a confidence in the minimal use of materials and a cuteness in the ensuing form.”.

Architectural lighting design of the year: Cologne Cathedral by Licht Kunst Licht.

Lighting design studio Licht Kunst Licht won architectural lighting design of the year for its illumination of Cologne Cathedral’s historic facade.

This well-considered lighting scheme successfully highlights Cologne’s monumental cathedral as a jewel on the night skyline.

The lighting scheme used more than 700 surface-mounted LED luminaires to transform nighttime views of the world’s tallest cathedral without drilling a single hole in its delicate stonework.

“This well-considered lighting scheme successfully highlights Cologne’s monumental cathedral as a jewel on the night skyline,” the judges praised.

“The light sources are subtly integrated and have managed to reduce energy consumption while creating maximum impact for this city landmark,” they added.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Surface design of the year: Basic Third by Pretty Plastic.

Dutch manufacturer Pretty Plastic won surface design of the year for its Basic Third tiles.

There is an inherent beauty and honesty to the product, adding texture and depth to the architecture.

The cladding material was developed by the Pretty Plastic organization, started by architecture studios Overtreders W and Bureau SLA.

The tiles, which were made from 30,987 kilograms of post-consumer plastic waste, have been applied as cladding for Plus Ultra III, the first timber laboratory building in the Netherlands.

“Pretty Plastics has chosen to work with the worst kind of plastic – PVC – and found a way to repurpose the material into tiles,” said the judges.

“The material is already fire-compliant and UV stable, making it a worthy contender for the cladding of buildings,” they continued. “There is an inherent beauty and honesty to the product, adding texture and depth to the architecture.”.

Looking ahead, the judges noted “its impact will be proven by how easy it is to scale.”.

Textile design of the year: Bianni Wool Paper by Arudeko.

Mexican design studio won textile design of the year for Bianni, a paper-like material made from colourful waste wool.

With so much wool waste in the world, this new material adds value to the waste.

Sourced from the off-cuts of handmade carpets and cushions crafted by local weaving communities in Teotitlán del Valle, Mexico, Arudeko saw the potential to use the surplus material and save it from being discarded.

Bianni can be sculpted into everything from lampshades to room dividers.

“With so much wool waste in the world, this latest material adds value to the waste,” the judges commended.

“Furthermore, the processing provides employment to skilled locals, the outcome being an interesting and beautiful paper alternative to be applied to other products,” they said. “There is much potential for further exploration across the world.”.

Workplace design of the year: Area by Foster + Partners and Kettal.

Foster + Partners and Kettal won workplace design of the year for their modular Area table system.

There is an appealing monumentalism to this office desk and a tactility in the simplicity and richness of the material composition.

Designed to be durable and adaptable, Area combines aluminium columns, a panoply of tabletop options and concealed power. The aluminium columns anchor the design, serving as both structural support and discreet container for power cables and electrical components.

“There is an appealing monumentalism to this office desk and a tactility in the simplicity and richness of the material composition,” remarked the judges.

“There are sophisticated elements and thoughtful hidden details for integrating technology into an otherwise minimalist design,” they continued.

Product design (consumer design) of the year: Pedal 4 by Minimal.

British start-up Minimal won product design (consumer design) of the year for Pedal 4, an electric cargo bike with the carrying capacity of a small van.

A smart new vehicle typology that addresses the challenges of inner city deliveries.

The four-wheeled, pedal-assist cargo vehicle was built to take up less room on the roads and evade traffic even on London’s crowded and complex streets. It is now operating in London with delivery companies Royal Mail and Evri.

“A smart new vehicle typology that addresses the challenges of inner city deliveries,” praised the judges.

It has been revealed that “This is a great ‘last mile’ replacement for large polluting vans. The slender design manoeuvres easily in city streets while the electric motor emits no noxious pollutants,” they continued.

“The vehicles’ local assembly also allows it to be easily repaired.”.

Product design (health, wellbeing and wearables) of the year: CurifyLabs PharmaPrinter Aurum by Studio Aslak Siimes.

Industrial design firm Studio Aslak Siimes and Finnish startup CurifyLabs won product design (health, wellbeing and wearables) of the year for pharmaceutical compounding system, PharmaPrinter Aurum.

It’s refreshing to see something so functional having also been aesthetically considered.

The system is designed to improve the process of creating patient-specific medicine, born from the realisation that almost 30 per cent of all medication requires personalisation rather than being mass-manufactured, according to studio founder Aslak Siimes.

Industry observers note that “This device offers a real innovation in precision healthcare and decentralises the production of pills,” the judges mentioned. “Precise medical doses are prepared bespoke for each customer, reducing waste and eliminating human error.”.

“Furthermore, it’s refreshing to see something so functional having also been aesthetically considered,” they added.

Product design (bathroom) of the year: Dekoda by Kohler Health.

Kohler Health won product design (bathroom) of the year for Dekoda, a health tracker specifically for the toilet.

This is an innovative, early-diagnostic device for ongoing monitoring of health conditions.

Designed to be discreet and intuitive, the tracker clips to the side of the toilet bowl to give insights on gut health and hydration levels, and to detect the presence of blood.

According to recent reports, “This is an innovative, early-diagnostic device for ongoing monitoring of health conditions,” the judges noted. “The design of the device is discreet and visually passive, making it suitable for its function in the bathroom.”.

Installation design of the year: Einder for USB002 Tour by Boris Acket and Fred Again.

Visual artist Boris Acket won installation design of the year for Einder, which featured as the standout show design for DJ Fred again..’s USB002 Tour.

In a recent development, this lightweight and flexible installation uses minimum material to maximum effect, making it evocative while sustainable. More please!

The installation features a large suspended sheet of fabric which floats above the audience like a transparent, breathing roof.

Throughout the concert, the sculpture wafts and moves across the audience, creating smaller and larger spaces, static spatial gestures, storms, and water surfaces.

The judges summed up the project as “stunning, emotive, immersive, dynamic, simple”.

According to recent reports, “This lightweight and flexible installation uses minimum material to maximum effect, making it evocative while sustainable. More please!”.

Sustainable design of the year: Datecrete by Datecrete Studio.

Architect Sara Abu Farha and engineer Khaled Shalka won sustainable design of the year for Datecrete, a concrete-style material developed by Abu Farha and Shalka formed from crushed dates.

This is a necessary regional innovation, repurposing an abundant waste material (date pits) into a local construction material, and providing a welcome alternative to concrete.

Sources indicate that the project aims to demonstrate how the abundant regional byproduct can become part of an architectural material language. Patent-pending, Datecrete can be produced as floor and wall tiles, cladding, furniture, lighting elements and smaller design objects.

“This is a necessary regional innovation, repurposing an abundant waste material (date pits) into a local construction material, and providing a welcome alternative to concrete,” said the master jury.

“The processing of the pits is decentralised, so it has the potential to scale in communities across the date-growing region.”.

Material innovation of the year: Mimmik Tile by Front.

Dutch sustainability platform Front and biotechnology company Biomason won material innovation of the year for Mimmik, a low-carbon, concrete-like floor tile strengthened by bacteria.

This tile design is genuinely pushing innovation forward in its creation; collaborating with bacteria as a sustainable alternative to concrete.

Front believes Mimmik is the first bacteria-grown tile to be industrially produced, making a sustainable technology available to a wide market of specifiers looking to reduce the carbon footprint of their commercial projects.

“This tile design is genuinely pushing innovation forward in its creation; collaborating with bacteria as a sustainable alternative to concrete,” praised the judges.

Sources indicate that “As such, the embodied carbon is greatly reduced,” they noted. “The production is scalable and could shift the dial in the future production of tiles and paving.”.

How long have you been working in this space?

Describe an average day in your studio.

Sources indicate that I work from my apartment. The most predictable parts of my studio day start with putting on my sunscreen and painting clothes. It’s a very small space that I paint in, so I usually have to push stuff aside when I start, like my painting cart, stool, and trash bin. I, then, turn on my air purifier, open the lids of my palettes, scrape paints from the previous session, and play either TV indicates I’m familiar with or podcasts hosted by comedians in the background. The day usually ends with my cleaning the palette, emptying and wiping my brush cleaning tank, and diligently washing my brushes. Then I wash my face and go to sleep.

#68670. Latest Update: GTA 6's environmental storytelling is hidden in the details you might never notice

Latest Update: GTA 6's environmental storytelling is hidden in the details you might never notice

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (505 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The best environmental storytelling in video games doesn’t always hit you in the face and demand you stop to look, and GTA 6 has perfected that.
  • Rockstar’s developers say that kind of discovery is central to Grand Theft Auto 6, a world designed to reward players who take their time.
  • In a recent development, “The life is in the detail of Grand Theft Auto VI,” says Adam Cochrane, Vice President of Art: Environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best environmental storytelling in video games doesn’t always hit you in the face and demand you stop to look, and GTA 6 has perfected that. Sometimes it’s a carefully dressed room, an overgrown garden, or a detail you spot out of the corner of your eye while heading somewhere else.

Rockstar’s developers say that kind of discovery is central to Grand Theft Auto 6, a world designed to reward players who take their time. After three weeks of playing GTA 6, I'd say the world-building is some of the best, most detailed, and most nuanced I've experienced. It can be as small as mud on a character's trainers, a branded coffee mug, or a car decal.

In a recent development, “The life is in the detail of Grand Theft Auto VI,” says Adam Cochrane, Vice President of Art: Environment. “The subtle sway of trees or bunting swaying in the wind. A puddle of bin juice around the bottom of a dumpster, or an overgrown garden in a property that is unoccupied.”.

It’s the sort of detail that makes a place feel inhabited rather than assembled for a game. Cochrane points to the personalisation of homes and businesses, and the little vignettes the teams have added for players to discover. Some offer in-game rewards; others are there simply to be found.

In a recent development, “Then you zoom out, and you look at the sheer scale of the world, and you realise that the detail you’ve been discovering on such a small scale is quite literally everywhere across the vast landscape of this world,” he says. “Then you realise that it’s all been curated, considered, and created by a human hand, and you can’t quite believe it.”.

That thinking extends beyond what you can see. Steven Messinger, Senior Design Director: Open World, explains that Rockstar has built deep backstories for things players may only glimpse. The game’s gang compounds, for example, have a fully mapped drug network, from supply routes to street-level buyers.

“Players will only pick up on bits and pieces of this,” Messinger says, “but having that structure in the background as something we consistently refer to helps everything feel more real, like this substantial machine is always running even when players aren’t there.”.

It’s a huge amount of work for details many players may miss. That’s rather the point.

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. Tech Report: The Real Miami Museums and Artists Behind GTA VI’s Vice City

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (646 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hyperallergic

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After 13 agonizing years of waiting for Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6), gamers worldwide wasted no time tearing up the streets of the game's fictional state of Leonida after it was released yesterday, November 19.
  • According to recent reports, as fans embed themselves in GTA 6's immersive landscape, many have recognized real-life locations across South Florida making unexpected cameos.
  • “It was totally unexpected to see Grand Theft Auto VI reimagine The Bass as the ‘Vice City Museum of Art,’” said Silvia Karman Cubiñá, executive director of the Bass Museum of Art, in an email to Hyperallergic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After 13 agonizing years of waiting for Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6), gamers worldwide wasted no time tearing up the streets of the game's fictional state of Leonida after it was released yesterday, November 19. The South Florida-inspired game environment is heavily influenced by the culture, environment, and architecture of Miami — from its Art Deco resorts, white-sand beaches, Cuban quarter, and strip clubs, right down to its museums and arts venues.

According to recent reports, as fans embed themselves in GTA 6's immersive landscape, many have recognized real-life locations across South Florida making unexpected cameos. One such case is the Vice Museum of Art, which Rockstar Games confirmed is modeled after the Bass Museum of Art in Miami Beach.

“It was totally unexpected to see Grand Theft Auto VI reimagine The Bass as the ‘Vice City Museum of Art,’” said Silvia Karman Cubiñá, executive director of the Bass Museum of Art, in an email to Hyperallergic.

“It’s a wonderful reminder of how art and architecture can become part of popular culture,” she continued. “Now, I’m just curious: will the Vice City Museum of Art get more visitors than we do?!”.

While not listed as a landmark like the Vice Museum of Art, another building in Downtown Vice City appears to be directly modeled after the Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM). Situated near the Vice City Arts Center, which is heavily based on Miami's Adrienne Arsht Center for Performing Arts, the PAMM-inspired building sits right on the water's edge just as the museum does in real life.

“We were as delighted as anyone else to find PAMM in what feels like the biggest video game of all time,” noted Alexa Ferra, PAMM's senior director of marketing and communications, in an email to Hyperallergic.

Ferra attached a photo someone sent her from the game showing the PAMM dupe and some gummy bear-inspired sculptures installed in the shallow water.

“It's a testament to our stunning Herzog & de Meuron building, and goes to show if you stick around long enough, you'll pop up in the unlikeliest — but inevitable — of places.” Ferra added.

Other references to Miami's arts and culture scene include Leonida's Stockyard neighborhood, which directly channels the street murals and warehouse-lined roads of the Wynwood Arts District. It was reported earlier this summer that Rockstar Games had hired over 50 real street artists to design the in-game murals across Stockyard. Owners shared they've spotted the works of street artist Ahol Sniffs Glue (David Anasagasti), among others.

In a recent development, miami-raised contemporary photographer Josh Aronson also took notice of GTA 6's inclusion of his installation at the Catalina Hotel & Beach Club in Miami Beach during Miami Art Week 2024, which Rockstar Games incorporated in Vice City's own Catalina Hotel. From Aronson's Florida Boys (2020–) photo series, the photo “Spring” (2024) was made into an enormous sublimated fabric print that hung from the second-story window of the hotel.

The same printed photo, which features a group of cheerful young men photographed from above while floating in water, is shown at Vice City's Catalina Hotel.

Recent findings suggest that “Florida Boys is my own imagined version of Florida, so I love that it gets to live on in another imagined Florida,” Aronson told Hyperallergic. “The installation at the Catalina was temporary, but in Vice City, someone might stumble upon it years from now. It’s a reminder of the wild ways we encounter art today, and how a work can find new life long after it comes down.”.

GTA6's pre-holiday release comes just before Miami Art Week begins early next month. Those dropping in can find some of Aronson's installations on view beyond Vice City at the Vizcaya Museum and Gardens and the Museum of Contemporary Art, North Miami, and also pay homage to the cultural venues and districts that inspired Leonida.

#68668. National Gallery of Canada receives major gift of modern and contemporary glass art

National Gallery of Canada receives major gift of modern and contemporary glass art

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (739 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the National Gallery of Canada (NGC) in Ottawa is embarking on a fresh chapter in its collecting history with a promised gift of 56 modern and contemporary glass works from Canadian American businessman and philanthropist Charles Bronfman and his late wife, Andrea Bronfman.
  • It has been revealed that “This is the gallery’s first gift of modern and 20th-century glass,” Jean-François Bélisle, director and chief executive of the NGC, tells The Art Newspaper.
  • The gifted Bronfman Collection spans more than a century of glass experimentation, with works by 29 artists from Canada, Europe, the United States and Asia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the National Gallery of Canada (NGC) in Ottawa is embarking on a fresh chapter in its collecting history with a promised gift of 56 modern and contemporary glass works from Canadian American businessman and philanthropist Charles Bronfman and his late wife, Andrea Bronfman. Accompanied by an endowment to establish the institution’s first curatorial position dedicated to decorative arts and design, the donation will help broaden the museum’s collection and increase its scholarly contributions.

It has been revealed that “This is the gallery’s first gift of modern and 20th-century glass,” Jean-François Bélisle, director and chief executive of the NGC, tells The Art Newspaper. “It significantly expands our understanding of art history, bringing together artistic expression and material and technical innovation.”.

The gifted Bronfman Collection spans more than a century of glass experimentation, with works by 29 artists from Canada, Europe, the United States and Asia. The collection traces the medium’s evolution from the sinuous forms of Art Nouveau and Arts and Crafts to the streamlined aesthetics of Art Deco and Modernism. Early 20th-century examples by Tiffany Studios, Émile Gallé and the renowned studio Daum demonstrate how artists pushed glass beyond traditional decorative applications.

Daum Frères, Lamp, around 1905. Collection of Charles and the late Andrea Bronfman Photo: NGC.

Recent findings suggest that the works also chart the emergence of studio glass as an independent discipline in the post-war period. Additional artists with works in the donation include Dale Chihuly, whose gravity-defying installations are in museums worldwide, as well as the studio glass pioneer Toots Zynsky and the well-known Canadian American artist Laura Donefer.

A selection of pieces from the collection is currently on view in the NGC’s European galleries (until 30 April 2027). Highlights of the installation include Edward Hald’s The Fireworks Bowl (around 1921), alongside architectural works by Tiffany and Frank Lloyd Wright.

Sources indicate that “Harvey Littleton’s Red Crossed Form (1990) is another notable work that reflects the development of studio glass as an independent artistic medium,” says Anabelle Kienle Ponka, the NGC’s senior curator of European, American and Asian Art. “The presentation brings together very different approaches to glass, from the decorative traditions of the early 20th century to the formal and technical experimentation of contemporary artists.”.

Industry observers note that tiffany Studios, Lamp, around 1900. Collection of Charles and the late Andrea Bronfman Photo: NGC.

The international scope of the donation highlights the exchange of technical traditions, particularly the influence of Venetian glassmaking on successive generations of artists, Kienle Ponka indicates. Together, the works demonstrate the medium’s versatility across sculpture, architecture and ornamentation.

Equally significant for the NGC is the accompanying endowment, which will fund the museum’s first curatorial position dedicated to decorative arts and design. The NGC has not shared the sum of the endowment, but notes that the post will support research, exhibitions and future acquisitions, establishing a foundation for sustained institutional engagement with the field.

Industry observers note that “[The donation’s] significance extends well beyond this gift,” Bélisle says. “The position will allow us to pursue further acquisitions, develop exhibitions and scholarship, and build relationships with artists and institutions.”.

Sources indicate that installation view of works by Lino Tagliapietra and Harvey Littleton from the Bronfman Glass Collection, National Gallery of Canada, Ottawa, until 30 April 2027. Photo: National Gallery of Canada, Ottawa.

The donation builds on a long history of the Bronfman family’s philanthropy in Canada's cultural sector. “My late wife Andy and I were admirers of the art of glass making and wanted to share this love with other Canadians,” Charles Bronfman remarked in a statement. “With the planned celebrations marking the upcoming 100th birthday of my sister, Phyllis Lambert, founder of the Canadian Centre for Architecture, and the 50th anniversary of the Canada Council for the Arts’ Saidye Bronfman Award, named after my mother, I am truly delighted to be contributing in this meaningful way to the national collections.”.

According to recent reports, the NGC has received other transformative gifts in recent years, including a 2025 donation of 61 contemporary works valued at C$22.8m ($16.8m) from collector Bob Rennie and his family. “The Bronfman gift is significant in a different way,” Bélisle claims. “Its importance lies not only in the quality and range of the works, but also in the accompanying endowment, which will provide the expertise and resources to develop decorative arts and design as a sustained area of collecting and scholarship.”.

  • In a recent development, AUBURN, Alabama — In Lowndes County, Alabama, less than an hour from Gee’s Bend, a group of women meet weekly to quilt together in a community center across from Mt.
  • According to recent reports, sew Their Names: Quilting, Creativity, and Activism at the Jule Collins Smith Museum of Fine Art at Auburn University culminates a three-year partnership between the university and the Hopewell Project.
  • It has been revealed that “A lot of the time, when institutions are trying to connect with communities, they’re parachuting artists into a place that already has art and culture there,” Randi Evans, the former Manager of Public Practice and Community Partnerships at the Museum, explains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, AUBURN, Alabama — In Lowndes County, Alabama, less than an hour from Gee’s Bend, a group of women meet weekly to quilt together in a community center across from Mt. Willing Baptist Church. In 2021, they began to carefully stitch the names of formerly enslaved congregation members into their work. What started as a project to preserve and commemorate these forgotten figures of history soon grew into a broader collaboration across Alabama.

According to recent reports, sew Their Names: Quilting, Creativity, and Activism at the Jule Collins Smith Museum of Fine Art at Auburn University culminates a three-year partnership between the university and the Hopewell Project. The exhibition showcases a series of handmade quilts by Yvonne Wells, Wini McQueen, and Mercedes Braxton, alongside fellow Lowndes County artists including Bill Traylor, Noah Purifoy, and Charlie Lucas, highlighting the region's rich artistic tradition.

It has been revealed that “A lot of the time, when institutions are trying to connect with communities, they’re parachuting artists into a place that already has art and culture there,” Randi Evans, the former Manager of Public Practice and Community Partnerships at the Museum, explains. “We were really cognizant of our role, to work away from that narrative and work in collaboration with what was already happening at these sites.”.

Industry observers note that A transplant herself, Evans hoped to learn about the traditions of Southern artists when she attended the quilt symposium “Every Stitch a Story,” hosted on Auburn’s campus. After Evans heard about the “Sew Their Names” project through a presentation by Judge Susan Walker, she thought it might be a good fit for the Museum in Motion initiative at the Jule. Previously, this initiative supported the 2022 exhibition Spell, Time, Practice, American, Body: The Work of RaMell Ross; Evans herself spearheaded partnerships across Hale County, where Ross’s film Hale County This Morning, This Evening (2018) was made.

Workshops at Auburn University's Rural Studio, November 2024 (both photos Mike Cortez).

“Since Auburn is a land grant institution, we see that part of our mission is taking the museum beyond our walls and reaching out to other parts of the state,” says Christy Barlow, the Museum’s Assistant Director of Education, Engagement, and Learning. Supported by resources from the Jule, “Sew Their Names” traveled around the state, pairing a showcase of quilts by commissioned artists with a series of workshops that allowed community members to participate in the quilt-making process.

Sources indicate that the first workshop took place in November 2024, as the exhibition traveled to Hale County, where Auburn’s Rural Studio, an off-campus architecture program focused on rural housing development, is located. The quilts were exhibited at a variety of local venues — what Evans termed a “quilt trail” — including Newbern Library, a project by Rural Studio; Sumac Cottage, an art gallery in Greensboro; and the Safe House Black History Museum, which foregrounded the exhibition’s focus on historical reckoning.

The exhibition then traveled to the Project Threadways Symposium in Florence, Alabama. Founded by designer and textile artist Natalie Chanin, the symposium’s 2025 edition focused on food, clothing, and shelter. The symposium also hosted a quilt-making workshop at the Kennedy-Douglass Center for the Arts in Florence. “Part of the experience of the Mt. Willing quilters is that they also sing as they work,” explains Barlow, who attended many of the in-person workshops. “So the singing is happening, and you have people scattered all throughout this historic house, sewing, learning to sew, learning about this story.”.

According to recent reports, by early 2026, the exhibition made its way back to the Jule for a more permanent place in the main gallery; as Barlow explains, this is an unusual trajectory for a curatorial project. “Most of the time, the curatorial side develops an exhibition, and then education responds to it,” she states. “However, this was a Museum in Motion initiative which eventually led to an exhibition. When you work that way, you have more input from community voices, who are part of the conversation from the very beginning.”.

Sources indicate that within the exhibition gallery, alongside featured quilts by Wini McQueen, Yvonne Wells, and Mercedes Braxton, other work by fellow Lowndes County natives was showcased. This included a painting by internationally renowned outsider artist Bill Traylor, a vivid three-dimensional collage by Noah Purifoy, a sculpture by Charlie Lucas, and a poster from the Lowndes County Freedom Organization. By pairing works from their permanent collection alongside quilts by the community, the exhibition emphasizes not only the variety of artistic forms across the region, but also the overt political nature of these practices; the Lowndes County Freedom Organization, for example, fought to empower Black voters during a time of extreme violence and intimidation.

Industry observers note that the exhibition soon became a focus of class visits from across Auburn University, drawing students in art history, philosophy, history, and even engineering. “A lot of Alabama-born students may not have a museum in their community,” explains Charlotte Hendrix, the museum’s communications director. “The Jule may be their first encounter walking into a space that can be intimidating; they might feel that they have to know a lot about art. When students participate in the process, you really can’t beat that, in terms of active, engaged learning.”.

#68665. Tech Report: So You Want to Run an Artist’s Estate?

Tech Report: So You Want to Run an Artist’s Estate?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1690 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hyperallergic

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, much has been written about the “Great Wealth Transfer,” a predicted $80+ trillion phenomenon that will enrich younger generations as their parents pass away in the next two decades.
  • For example, when the artist Sam Francis died in 1994, he left over 1,000 artworks, several businesses, extensive real estate holdings, ten cars, and a herd of cattle.
  • In a recent development, the following text, which touches on topics facing estates, was developed in consultation with experts in fields that serve estates and trustees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, much has been written about the “Great Wealth Transfer,” a predicted $80+ trillion phenomenon that will enrich younger generations as their parents pass away in the next two decades. For those who have inherited — or expect to inherit — the estates of visual artists, the challenges of this “transfer” can be especially complex. Works of art, which can carry both emotional and sentimental value alongside asset value, require special care and consideration. The resulting pressures and responsibilities can divide families and create legal challenges.

For example, when the artist Sam Francis died in 1994, he left over 1,000 artworks, several businesses, extensive real estate holdings, ten cars, and a herd of cattle. His will provided money for a foundation called “The Sam Francis Museum,” but his vague instructions did not specify its activities. Disputes among his heirs — Francis had four children and had been married five times — and the need to extensively document his artwork further complicated matters. Settling all parties' claims and establishing the Sam Francis Foundation took nearly five years.

In a recent development, the following text, which touches on topics facing estates, was developed in consultation with experts in fields that serve estates and trustees. There are also many organizations doing key work to advance this field, including the Center for the Preservation of Artists' Legacies, the Artists' Legacy Foundation, and Legacy Lab Newly introduced Mexico.

Sources indicate that ideally, estate planning should begin while the artist is alive, with someone available to guide the process and provide key information. Record contact information for key associates, including dealers and others, along with instructions for working with them. The estate will need access to digital assets, including archives, email correspondence, and computer files. Setting up a revocable trust can help the estate avoid probate, allowing assets and property to pass rapidly to heirs, and also provides great privacy.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to choosing trustees, Joe Oliveira, the sole trustee of the Nathan Oliveira Estate, mentioned, “Choosing trustees can be difficult, and they may not necessarily be family members. In my own case, I happen to be the most logical candidate. A single trustee like myself can make decisions efficiently and consistently, while still listening to and considering the ideas of other family members.”.

One of the most crucial challenges estate managers face is understanding and cataloging an estate’s full contents. This includes not only works of art but also related ephemera, such as correspondence and personal effects. Unique ephemera, like Joan Brown’s fingerprint-covered telephone on display at her SFMOMA retrospective, can strengthen future exhibition narratives.

Stuart A. Chase, a former museum director who now advises estates, suggests starting with an inventory. “In my experience, most heirs have no idea what they have. You can’t do anything without a catalog. You can’t approach anyone. It can be very simple: I use CatalogIt, which is straightforward to use and charges a nominal fee.”.

Recent findings suggest that when I took Chase’s advice and used CatalogIt to document my art collection, I looked under the bed and found a folder of unframed drawings a friend gave me years ago that I'd completely forgotten about. The app allowed me to print a copy of the completed inventory, which I added to my will.

An appraisal, an independent assessment of a property's value or condition, is essential to managing an artist’s estate because it involves the IRS. A Fair Market Value appraisal is typically required to file estate taxes and establish newly introduced cost bases for each work in the event of future sales by an heir. It will contain detailed reports for each object, including artist, title, date, dimensions, medium, provenance, condition, and the specific valuation method used. The IRS requires what it calls “qualified appraisals” for this, as well as for non-cash charitable donations to qualified institutions and other gifts.

Recent findings suggest that choose appraisers carefully, and select those who are highly recommended. Deborah Gerstler Spanierman, a longtime art advisor and certified appraiser, recommends engaging “qualified and trustworthy allied professionals: appraisers, archivists, estate and foundation attorneys to handle the estate tax filing. Empower them to do their jobs and to work with the artist’s gallery, if they have one, which will all eventually support the artist’s legacy.”.

Sources indicate that artist-Endowed Foundations differ from other philanthropic measures because they create programs that feature the artist’s work. These may include organizing and lending to exhibitions, developing and publishing catalogue raisonnés, or operating education centers.

Christine Vincent, the managing director of the Aspen Institute, an artist-endowed foundation initiative, explains: “Artists' estates and Artist-Endowed Foundations (AEFs) are entirely different things. Artists' estates are typically operated by private individuals and, as such, are not tax-exempt charitable entities. AEFs are tax-exempt charitable organizations with a mission to benefit the general public. An artist's estate may evolve into an AEF, for example under the estate plan of an artist's surviving spouse, but an AEF can never devolve into an artist's estate.”.

Recent findings suggest that checking an artist’s archive for condition concerns is essential. Identify which works need immediate care, which will need future restoration and/or repair, and act as promptly as possible. You might have to make difficult decisions about works that should be discarded or destroyed with the utmost consideration. Seek expert help — from conservators and other art professionals — when works require special treatment or present unique problems.

In a recent development, where you store work also affects its condition. “Know how to properly store works on canvas and paper in temperature-controlled spaces, and insure them to avoid any future or potential loss,” states Jamieson Grillo, the sole trustee of the Estate of John Grillo. “If the estate can afford it, make sure you get your artwork conserved by a professional conservator with past experience and a proven track record in conserving similar art. Also, share any conservation reports with galleries you are working with.”.

Industry observers note that galleries with long-term relationships with artists will likely want to continue that partnership after an artist passes away. But estates seeking upcoming representation should start by identifying suitable galleries, looking at those that handle works similar to the estate’s.

In a recent development, prioritize and prepare before contacting any galleries. Gallery owner Hollis Taggart swears by making it as easy as possible for the gallery by providing as much detail as possible. “The more organized an estate is, the more likely a gallery will be to take on the heavy lifting of representing that estate.” Taggart also advises a clear vision: “Be as supportive as possible by organizing an inventory list of the works so the gallery knows right up front what the estate holdings are, and how major a project is involved.”.

Placing works in museum collections helps enhance and maintain an artist’s reputation and legacy. But museums often hesitate to accept donations because of limited exhibition and storage space. Patti Smith, an art collections manager at the Stephenson Ceramics Studio, suggests approaching them thoughtfully and presenting only high-quality works, or collaborating with a gallery to develop a “gifting exhibition.” She says, “I helped develop one for the estate of artist Richard Wilt (1915–1981) that documented a body of his work and displayed it in the gallery. We approached latest museums as well as museums that already had his work. Since there was demand for purchasing the work, once the museums made their selections, the work was offered up for sale, and 100% of the proceeds went to the Richard Wilt Foundation at the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art and Design.”.

In a recent development, estates should have websites that include an artist biography, a timeline, a gallery of works, and contact information. This can help anyone doing research — including appraisers and dealers — and may also help locate lost works.

A social media presence, especially regular Instagram posts, keeps an artist’s legacy in the public consciousness. Mary Clare McKinley of the Richard Diebenkorn Foundation says, “When estates and foundations harness the power of social media, it can be a brilliant tool for education, legacy and community building. In my opinion, investing in research is always a good decision. Then, consider the platform a way to share information less formally than publishing a book, and creatively explore ways to use it: Enjoy the flexibility, interactivity, and immediate access to a wider public.” She shares that the Diebenkorn Foundation’s Instagram posts “highlight scholars making exciting discoveries, support museum exhibitions, feature [their] own intriguing archival finds, and suggest upcoming visual connections to Diebenkorn’s work.”.

According to the Center for Art Law, when an artist passes, their estate has two seemingly conflicting tasks: "to protect an artist’s work by exercising exclusive rights over them, and to disseminate their artwork to the public to establish a lasting legacy and placement in the art world.” But this dilemma runs parallel to another concern: Should estates prioritize revenue, or improve public access to art?

According to recent reports, auction results, now widely available through online databases, are key public indicators of an artist’s salability. Selling an especially strong work at auction is a gamble some estates take to establish a benchmark for an artist whose work lacks a previous auction record. Estates of recognized artists may want to partner with an auction house to mount a significant sale.

Recent findings suggest that to do so, an estate needs to meet certain standards. Wendy Battleson, senior vice president at Bonhams, notes, “Auction houses, in general, are looking for an estate with an established record of sales at relatively high values (five to six figures minimum), ideally sold publicly. We also look at the amount of inventory available in order to continue to tell the artist’s story over a period of time. The beauty of working with an auction house is that pricing is public, and there is rarely a concern that the art has been sold for less than market rate. With a dealer, the sales are typically private, so you don’t know if you could have achieved a higher price.”.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
