  • What $10,000 grows to at different rates over 30 years — the rate difference matters more than you think.
  • $10,000 invested for 30 years at 10% annual return.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that what's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

What $10,000 grows to at different rates over 30 years — the rate difference matters more than you think.

$10,000 invested for 30 years at 6% annual return.

$10,000 invested for 30 years at 8% annual return.

$10,000 invested for 30 years at 10% annual return.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Recent findings suggest that future value (FV) is the projected worth of an investment at a specific point in the future, based on an assumed rate of growth. It answers the most practical question in investing: "If I invest this money today, what will it be worth in 10, 20, or 30 years?".

Future value calculations rest on compound interest — the principle that your returns earn their own returns over time. Albert Einstein reportedly called compound interest "the eighth wonder of the world," and while the attribution is debatable, the math is not. The difference between simple interest (returns on your original investment only) and compound interest (returns on your investment plus accumulated returns) becomes enormous over long time horizons.

The basic future value formula for a lump sum investment is:.

For example, $10,000 invested at 8% for 20 years:.

FV = $10,000 x (1.08)^20 = $10,000 x 4.661 = $46,610.

Industry observers note that the table reveals two critical insights. First, small differences in return rates produce massive differences over long periods — $10,000 at 6% grows to $57,435 over 30 years, while the same amount at 10% grows to $174,494. That 4-percentage-point difference triples the outcome. Second, time is the dominant variable. At 8%, your money doubles roughly every 9 years — so 30 years gives you more than three doublings, turning $10,000 into over $100,000.

It has been revealed that most people do not invest a single lump sum and walk away. They invest regularly — monthly or per paycheck — over decades. The future value of a series of regular contributions uses a different formula called the future value of an annuity:.

FV = PMT x [((1 + r)^n - 1) / r].

Where PMT is the periodic contribution, r is the periodic rate, and n is the total number of periods.

It has been revealed that in practice, you do not need to calculate this by hand. The insight that matters is this: regular contributions are far more powerful than most people realize because each contribution starts its own compounding clock. Your first $500 contribution compounds for the full 30 years, while your 360th contribution (at month 360) compounds for just one month — but together they build wealth that dwarfs a single lump sum.

Sources indicate that A person investing $500 per month at 8% for 30 years accumulates $745,180 — from total contributions of only $180,000. That means $565,180, or 76% of the final balance, came from compound returns rather than your own deposits. This is the engine of wealth building.

Industry observers note that every future value calculation should be done twice — once in nominal terms and once in real (inflation-adjusted) terms. The nominal return is the raw number your investments earn. The real return subtracts inflation, showing you what your money will actually buy.

Sources indicate that historically, the S&P 500 has returned roughly 10% nominally and 7% after inflation. The difference matters enormously over long periods:.

In a recent development, that $1.13 million in nominal terms has the purchasing power of roughly $610,000 in today's dollars — still excellent, but nearly half less than the headline number suggests. When planning for FI, always use real returns (6-7%) rather than nominal returns (9-10%) to avoid overestimating what your portfolio will actually support in retirement spending.

Recent findings suggest that the Rule of 72 is the simplest and most useful mental math tool in investing. Divide 72 by your annual rate of return to estimate how many years it takes for your investment to double:.

This works in reverse too. If you want to know what rate of return you need to double your money in 15 years: 72 / 15 = 4.8%. The Rule of 72 is an approximation — it is most accurate for rates between 5% and 12% — but it is remarkably precise within that range and far faster than pulling out a calculator.

The FI community uses future value calculations as the backbone of retirement planning. The process works in three steps:.

The table indicates how starting balance and monthly contribution interact. Notice that increasing your monthly contribution from $1,500 to $2,500 (a $1,000 increase) with a $100,000 starting balance cuts 3.5 years off your time to $1 million. This is the savings rate lever in action — the amount you save each month matters more than any other variable you control.

In a recent development, A common question is whether it is better to invest a lump sum now or spread contributions over time (dollar-cost averaging). The math is clear: lump sum investing wins approximately two-thirds of the time because markets trend upward over the long term. However, dollar-cost averaging reduces the psychological risk of investing a large amount right before a downturn and provides a behavioral advantage that keeps many investors on track. For most FI-seekers, the question is academic — you invest each paycheck as it arrives because you do not have a large lump sum sitting on the sidelines.

Sources indicate that when projecting your portfolio growth for retirement planning, use real (inflation-adjusted) returns of 6-7% rather than nominal returns of 9-10%. A $1 million nominal balance in 30 years has the purchasing power of roughly $550,000 in today's dollars at 2% average inflation. Planning with real returns ensures you are targeting a portfolio that can actually support your desired spending level.

Track your actual spending for 3 months and annualize it. Multiply by 25 to get your FI number using the 4% safe withdrawal rate. If you spend $60,000 per year, your FI number is $1,500,000.

Add up all retirement accounts (401k, IRA, Roth IRA, HSA), taxable brokerage accounts, and savings. Exclude home equity and non-liquid assets. This is your starting balance for the future value calculation.

Subtract your monthly spending from your monthly after-tax income. Include employer 401(k) match and any other automatic savings. This is your periodic contribution amount for the future value formula.

Recent findings suggest that use the future value of a lump sum plus annuity formula, or a simple online calculator, to project when your current balance plus monthly contributions will reach your FI number. Use 7% real return (after inflation) for conservative planning.

In a recent development, test what happens if you increase contributions by $200/month, $500/month, or $1,000/month. Seeing the concrete impact of a savings rate increase — often shaving 2-5 years off your FI timeline — makes the trade-offs tangible and motivating.

For long-term stock market projections, use 7% for inflation-adjusted (real) returns or 10% for nominal returns based on the S&P 500 historical average. For a more conservative estimate, use 6% real. For bond-heavy portfolios, use 3-4% real. Always specify whether you are using nominal or real returns — mixing them up is one of the most common planning mistakes.

Recent findings suggest that future value calculations show what WOULD happen if returns were constant every year. In reality, markets fluctuate — you might earn 25% one year and lose 15% the next. Over 20-30 year periods, average returns tend to converge toward historical norms, making future value projections reasonably useful for planning. Treat them as directional estimates, not guarantees.

In a recent development, future value asks: "What will $10,000 today be worth in 20 years?" Present value asks the reverse: "What is $50,000 in 20 years worth in today's dollars?" They use the same variables but in opposite directions. Present value is useful for evaluating whether a future payout (like a pension or annuity) is worth the cost today.

The Rule of 72 works for any compounding rate, including inflation. At 3% inflation, prices double every 24 years (72 / 3 = 24). This means $50,000 in annual spending today becomes $100,000 in 24 years in nominal terms — your purchasing power is halved if your income stays flat. This is why investing in assets that outpace inflation is essential.

Industry observers note that for FI planning, future value is more intuitive — it tells you what your portfolio will grow to. However, the most practical approach is to calculate future value using real (after-inflation) returns. This effectively gives you a future value stated in today's purchasing power, which is what you actually need to know for spending planning.

In tax-advantaged accounts (401k, IRA, Roth IRA, HSA), your investments compound without tax drag, so the standard future value formula works directly. In taxable accounts, capital gains taxes, dividend taxes, and tax-loss harvesting all affect your real return. A rough adjustment is to reduce your assumed return by 0.5-1.0% for taxable accounts to account for ongoing tax drag.

Future value calculations are the most practical tool in the FI planner's toolkit. They turn abstract concepts like compound growth and savings rate into concrete dollar amounts and specific timelines. The key takeaways are straightforward: use 7% real returns for conservative planning, always account for inflation by using real rather than nominal returns, and remember that your monthly contribution rate has a far larger impact on the outcome than chasing an extra point or two of return. The Rule of 72 gives you instant mental math for any investment decision — how long to double, what rate you need, and how inflation erodes purchasing power. Combined with a clear FI number and a disciplined savings rate, future value projections show you exactly when financial independence becomes reality. Run the numbers, test different scenarios, and let the math motivate you to increase that monthly contribution whenever you can.

Industry News: The Venice Biennale's Sham Awards Cannot Artwash Genocide

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This Sunday, the Venice Biennale will award its newly introduced “Visitors’ Lions.” But no matter who receives this poisoned chalice, the results are void.

Stripped of the silver and gold they wore in previous iterations of the Biennale, the latest Lions have been thrown to the tourists; “Best Artist” and “Best National Pavilion” will be decided by a popularity contest. Why this surprising democratic turn? The expert jury initially appointed to give these honors resigned en masse in April of this year. These resignations were, in part, the result of the Art Not Genocide Alliance’s (ANGA) nearly three years of campaigning to exclude the Israel pavilion from the art world’s most vital biennial. After the jury publicly stated their intention to omit Israel and Russia from consideration for the Golden Lions, they were visited by representatives from Italy’s Ministry of Culture. The contents of the meeting are not public, but we can surmise how it went from the jury’s subsequent unanimous resignation. Shortly after, the Venice Biennale Foundation declared the Visitors’ Lions, inviting ticket-holders to cast their vote for awards to be announced at the end of the show’s run.

Sources indicate that “Our exclusion has been thwarted, and the choice now passes to the general public,” crowed Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar, whom human rights groups accuse of orchestrating the siege of Kamal Adwan Hospital and the notorious imprisonment and torture of the hospital’s director, Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya, in 2024. Firmly siding with torture and against principle, the Biennale made it clear that both Israel and Russia were back in the running for the Visitors’ Lions. As Antonia Majaca observed, the jury dared to apply a criterion, and the Biennale responded by dissolving judgment itself.

Sources indicate that many artists have rejected this sham from the start. On the day the 2026 Biennale opened to the public, 54 artists in the international exhibition and 22 national pavilion teams withdrew from consideration in solidarity with the jury. In June, more than a hundred artists threatened legal action unless their names were removed from the ballot. Sunday’s ceremony awards a prize that few want to win.

Sources indicate that the massive public pushback against the Biennale also demonstrates how close we have come to actualizing the moral principle that a genocidal, apartheid state has no legitimacy on any international stage. This year, we participated in a series of unprecedented protests. Biennale artists and cultural workers went on strike three times in seven months — nothing on this scale has ever happened before (not even during the anti-capitalist protests of 1968, which put a stop to the Biennale’s prizes for 18 years). This year’s protests were also unprecedented in terms of the level of collaboration between ANGA — which comprises artists, curators, and precariously employed workers — and rank-and-file labor unions.

In a recent development, the Biennale is resolutely global, unfolding in the “anywhere or not at all” of the international art circuit. Against the false globalization of the art market, our internationalism was grounded in local organizing against Israel’s Zionist genocide.

According to recent reports, the first of this year’s strikes, on May 8, was built locally in Venice, with Biennalocene, Sale Docks, and other local grassroots unions whose participation provided legal protection for striking art workers. On May 8, 30 of the Biennale’s 100 national pavilions closed partially or fully, and thousands of people marched from Via Garibaldi to the Arsenale, where they were met with police brutality. Many artists in the main exhibition draped or altered their works.

Recent findings suggest that the second strike, on June 12, was national in scale. It was the result of a year of organizing assemblies and actions in about 20 cities all around Italy, with organizations including Mi Riconosci?, Vogliamo Tutt’Altro, Biennalocene, and grassroots unions through the Cultural Strike platform.

The third strike, on 30 October, responded to a call that emerged from outside the art world from the World Federation of Trade Unions and, in Italy, was taken up by militant dockworkers, including the Autonomous Collective of Port Workers, and the grassroots Unione Sindacale di Base. A network of port unions at 113 in 22 countries, including Italy, France, Greece, Turkey, and Morocco, refused to load weapons bound for Israel. This was the biggest ever coordinated action of its kind, and our role was to help build local participation in Venice.

Today, November 20, as this piece is being published, the International Student Strike brought further strike action to Venice, demonstrating the political convergence between students and the Biennale — students in the city are often employed in the cultural sector under precarious conditions.

Our ability to do this grew out of the work we began in 2024, in adherence to the guidelines of the Palestinian Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel (PACBI) and Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions (BDS), when our open letter demanding Israel’s exclusion from the Biennale was signed by more than 24,000 cultural workers. That year, the Israel pavilion closed.

According to recent reports, between 2024 and 2026, our campaign connected more substantively with the Italian labor movement. As the June 12 strike articulated, the political atomization of artists is a labor concern, related to the art world’s reliance on precarity, which shifts the risk of political action onto individuals. The Biennale provides no fees or production money to artists, leaving them to fundraise their participation. Those whose work is not sufficiently market-friendly to claw back payment in future sales have to content themselves with being paid in the false currency of prestige.

Recent findings suggest that ANGA refuses the oppressive logic that allows the Biennale to support genocide and profit from precarious labor while claiming to rise above politics. This year, we have made clear that the alliance we have created has the power to disrupt the Biennale’s functioning and change its nature.

Today, the contradictions of the present political order — the indigestible, white-supremacy-coded cocktail of Europe’s simultaneous opposition to Russia and support for Israel; the flailing, ever-dying economy; the oceans of money poured into technologies of death and destruction — explode messily into the supposedly morally hermetic market-world of the Biennale.

Industry observers note that the farcical “Visitors’ Lions” are the Biennale’s wager that the walls can always be painted pure white again. But this year’s massive actions have demonstrated that we will not allow Israel’s unspeakable assault on Palestine to be art-washed and ignored. ANGA’s members and supporters are no less steadfast than we were three years ago, when our campaign first began. It remains obvious and undeniable that Israel, the United States-backed abattoir-state, must not be allowed to bring its logic of butchery to be art-washed into neutral “complexity” at the Biennale. And we are now considerably more organized and better connected to the wider struggle against Zionism.

When we look back to ANGA’s beginnings, in early 2024, we remember a time when the shock of total Zionist impunity was still raw enough to feel unreal. We could not imagine that friends or colleagues could disagree with this basic principle. We were soon disabused, as many cultural workers washed their hands of blood in service of their careers.

Sources indicate that but our collective efforts have transformed this anti-political status quo. The new compositions of struggle made possible by the mass revolt against Zionism offer a model for how the art world can reach beyond the isolated precarity of cultural labor into new alliances — with students, with dockworkers. The power of boycott as a tool has never been greater. We continue to remake the Venice Biennale, the modern world exhibition, from Walter Benjamin’s “place of pilgrimage to the commodity fetish” into a site of struggle.

In a recent development, “Inspired by the fairy tale, The Frog Prince, I had an idea to tell the story in the faerie kingdom. I wanted to depict this encounter as a moment of enchantment between two characters.”.

Industry observers note that “I created this artwork during a phase of obsessive reading. After struggling to find inspiration and wishing to be back in my books, the concept for this piece emerged organically.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I used my subject matter to create a border for the scene. I’ve recently been inspired to experiment more with shape and design; to not always have my compositions so confined within borders.”.

You can see Lavera's work in progress on her YouTube channel.

#68660. In a Midtown Office, Artists Sift Through the Junkspace of Capitalism

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1625 w)

In a Midtown Office, Artists Sift Through the Junkspace of Capitalism

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1625 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hyperallergic

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A few hours before 260 Madison opened on September 24, I trekked to its namesake address in Midtown to meet the curators.
  • The three artists-turned-curators, Shaina Tabak, Dayana Matasheva, and Edson Niebla Rodríguez (the latter two of whom make up the duo DemonLovers Inc.), organized 260 Madison as an intergenerational, “inter-everything” show with work by over 50 artists, including self-taught and non-traditionally educated practitioners.
  • According to recent reports, upon entering the first room on the left, I was immediately met with artist Jon Kessler’s towering nine-foot-tall sculpture, in which four plastic male dolls in Adidas tracksuits dangled from a weighted contraption somewhere between a carnival ride and a torture device.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A few hours before 260 Madison opened on September 24, I trekked to its namesake address in Midtown to meet the curators. A security guard directed me to the 14th floor of the 1950s office building, where drop ceilings, an exposed HVAC system, and two people I assumed were the exhibition organizers dressed in corporate drag greeted me. They promptly clarified they were not; they were from AmTrustRE, the real estate company that offered the derelict 23,000-square-foot office space to the artists for free while preparing it — and three other unoccupied floors — for their next corporate tenants.

The three artists-turned-curators, Shaina Tabak, Dayana Matasheva, and Edson Niebla Rodríguez (the latter two of whom make up the duo DemonLovers Inc.), organized 260 Madison as an intergenerational, “inter-everything” show with work by over 50 artists, including self-taught and non-traditionally educated practitioners. On view through this Sunday, November 22, the show arrives just as the Whitney Museum of American Art opens artport: A History of Internet Art, signaling a new wave of institutional recognition for internet-grown art. With 260 Madison artists Maya Man, Rachel Rossin, and Eva and Franco Mattes among those included in the Whitney’s 25th-anniversary exhibition for its net art commissioning platform, the Midtown show feels especially urgent, if only because it takes place at the precipice of a paradigmatic shift within the art world.

According to recent reports, upon entering the first room on the left, I was immediately met with artist Jon Kessler’s towering nine-foot-tall sculpture, in which four plastic male dolls in Adidas tracksuits dangled from a weighted contraption somewhere between a carnival ride and a torture device. Titled “It Takes a Global Village Idiot” (2018) after philosopher Marshall McLuhan’s early ’60s theory that information-age technology “recreates the world in the image of a global village,” the sculpture forces viewers to confront the fact that the quick fixes of amusement proffered by technology rely on the same methods of data extraction that undergird systemic violence. It’s an unsettling introduction to a show where, even in its more humorous, delusionally conspiratorial, or enchanting moments, discomfort is always in the periphery.

It has been revealed that “We don’t want to make a show or art that tries to be some form of escapism,” Rogríguez told Hyperallergic during an interview the week after the opening. “It’s like the [Werner Herzog] quote, ‘The poet must not avert his eyes.’ If some art in the show seems depressing, it’s because we live in what seems a depressing time.”.

Rodríguez and Matasheva, who are also a couple, began making work together seven years ago while studying film in Montreal. Their video-art duo is named after Olivier Assayas’s 2002 film Demonlover, where multiple global corporations compete for a fresh immersive Japanese hentai company through extreme methods of espionage, exploitation, and blackmail.

“DemonLovers is about the libidinal economy and how algorithms are weaponizing our very basic instincts and desires,” Matasheva told Hyperallergic, echoing Rodríguez’s interest in what he calls “financial Freud,” or the psychoanalytic dimension of digital capital flows.

It has been revealed that both DemonLovers’s own two works in the show and those they curated certainly don’t shy away from the degradation associated with extractive economies, be it of the self, physical infrastructure, or the proverbial global village. Nearby Kessler’s work, Theresa Tomi Faison’s “The Long Tail” (2026) climbs up one of the floor’s load-bearing columns. Across the curved sculpture’s six screens, images of memes, forum screenshots, and phrases ruminating on contemporary capital flow all accumulate and dissolve downstream. The river of digital spam ends at the viewer’s feet, inculcating the audience, but also the space itself, which the curators characterize as shaped by "junkspace” — architect Rem Koolhaas's term for fallout that “remains after modernization has run its course.”.

Among works that are either readymades or play with the form’s history — including Anthony Discenza’s windowsill pile of unopened credit card and loan offer letters in “Offers” (2026) and Eva and Franco Mattes’s distended taxidermied cat, “Longcat” (2026) — the corporate detritus can be difficult to parse from the artistic interventions. At one point, I mistook a few square feet of wallpaper with the Champion logo for a newly introduced work. The curators clarified during a later conversation that it was actually kept from the office’s previous tenants, HanesBrands, which owns Champion.

Sources indicate that having also inherited the space’s trove of gutted bathrooms, broken drywall, and stripped concrete floors (in short, its junkspace), the curators stated they view 260 Madison through “layers of site responsiveness” more than anything. With some works, that connection emerged during the eleventh hour of installation. With others, the site occasioned the work itself. Ivana Dama used exposed air vents for “The Air Was Already Here” (2026), a sound work that channels air through reeds, transforming the invisible, inaudible rhythms of the space into what the artist describes as a “sculptural presence.” Pictures Generation artist Matt Mullican took a 47-foot span of unused wall space as an opportunity to reflect on his five-decade practice of constructing, deconstructing, and classifying systems of representation and perception with largely nonverbal symbols.

It has been revealed that “He spent three days here drawing his entire practice on the wall, right from the beginning to the end,” Matasheva stated regarding Mullican’s monumental graphite piece, “Representing The Work” (2026). “He said he will give a lecture about it and that it's a very crucial work for him. It's kind of a conclusion of his practice.”.

In a recent development, meanwhile, the show’s video works are lodged into broken columns, ceiling alcoves, liminal backrooms, bathroom plumbing, abstract paintings, and even a hanging pink punching bag, a veritable reunion of the last decade of post-internet art movements. Alumni from Joshua Citarella’s publishing platform Do Not Research, the Latest Museum-affiliated Rhizome, and the traveling video and film screening series Open Secret, including Faison, Dana Dawud, Yehwan Song, and Ruba Al-Sweel, have contributed works. Many of them feature themes of surveillance, internet-induced conspiracy, and social media performance, as well as the technological, often AI-abetted methods of production that have come to define such enclaves.

In a recent development, yet, for all the immateriality and speculative knowledge that flows through these works, 260 Madison equally plumbs an idea of technology with a long, craft-driven history. Tabak, a sculptor with a background in furniture design, is the driving force behind this facet of the show — and the currents of divination, enchantment, and even sublimity that come with it.

“My practice is very handmade and material-focused, so I always know that that’s what I would contribute to the curatorial vision,” Tabak told Hyperallergic. “And just being in Midtown, you shouldn’t separate a show from what’s happening around it.

Sources indicate that tabak was particularly interested in curating works that “blur the line between the hand and technology,” inviting artists who “haven’t had a lot of chances to show in art contexts, whether it’s because they are in the design world or have nine-to-fives,” to participate in the exhibition. She explains that many of them complicate the very notion of technology and its use, citing Brian Oakes’s “Vessel 9” (2025), which gathers 3D-modeled circuit boards into a suspended “techno-Gothic” chandelier, and Ryan Decker’s “The Wavemaker Falters” (2026), which uses a motorized, rudder-like instrument to swoosh water through a raised vessel resembling a spaceship.

“We view technology not as something that has arrived in the 20th century, but something that has made humanity possible,” Matasheva remarked, expanding on Tabak’s comment. “Language is a technology, a chisel is a technology, everything is a technology.”.

Sources indicate that while many of the show’s craft-driven works conjure the anthropologist Alfred Gell’s idea that art is a technology that enchants, and in turn, becomes enchanted, others wield technology in the service of care. Kylie Mitchell repurposes a light-seeking solar robot and discarded electronic parts to move a found bird’s nest and egg toward a life-sustaining heat lamp. A few dozen feet away, Gregory Kalliche’s installation “Black-tailed gull nest; Ring-necked Pheasant Nest; Mallard Nest” (2016) suspends an LED light over three metal folding chairs printed with images of bird egg nests. Ben Gould’s “Ark II” (2026), on the other hand, augments a hospital gurney with eight aluminum armatures that hold fresh red roses inside coil-shaped glass vials. Doubling as a literal manifestation of Shakespeare’s “this mortal coil” phrase in Hamlet, the sculpture’s sterile infrastructure butts against the transitory visual comfort proffered by its flowers, mirroring a healthcare ecosystem wherein privatization, optimization, and tech automation have whittled medicine’s promises of care, healing, and empathy into mere aesthetic veneers.

It’s no coincidence that many of the works in 260 Madison position technology as both a pathogen and cure for today’s cultural ailments. In fact, when the real estate developers initially contacted Columbia University’s School of the Arts, it was to invite artists to “activate” a 36,000-square-foot gutted Duane Reade on the building’s ground floor. The developers eventually retracted their offer and moved the exhibition to the 14th floor, citing ongoing construction. Meanwhile, the original initiative for 260 Madison to occupy the husk of the Duane Reade will be realized in a different form next month. Now serving as the building’s fresh temporary lobby, the former pharmacy will play host to a different group exhibition curated independently by Tabak. Opening December 3, HOW I FEEL will feature artists working across sculpture, social architecture, photography, painting, performance, and programming, including Jessica Vaughn, Quay Quinn Wolf, André Magaña, and 260 Madison’s Grayson Cox and Luke Murphy. How the forthcoming Duane Reade show contends with this moment of tech-induced economic entropy, so intense that even an entity as extractive as a real-estate company cannot commit to its own speculations, remains to be seen.

Breaking: Conservation of the ‘Sistine Chapel of the Andes’ nears completion

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of Bolivia’s oldest churches, known as the “Sistine Chapel of the Andes” due to its impressive murals, is nearing completion of a conservation project focused on its roofs, stone buttresses and adobe walls—a process that began in May.

Recent findings suggest that the US Department of State’s Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation (AFCP) financed the work at the Santiago de Curahuara de Carangas church, located in the Andes mountains at almost 4,000m above sea level. Approximately 170km west of the city of Oruro, the church was declared a National Monument in 1960.

“The Curahuara church has great value because of its paintings, so it’s essential that the roof is in good condition to prevent leaks that could compromise the murals,” Josefina Matas, the architect in charge of the project, tells The Art Newspaper. This work follows restoration that took place more than a decade ago, funded by the German embassy in La Paz.

The restoration team has had to learn the church’s unique roof-building technique from locals, placing straw on top of hollow cane mats using a method that makes it more resilient. Hollow cane is hard to find in the highlands, so they needed to bring it in from Bolivia’s southernmost region of Tarija.

Working on the church’s upcoming roofs Courtesy US Embassy in Bolivia.

According to recent reports, during the previous restoration, corrugated metal sheets had been added to extend the lifespan of the roofs, which cover 800 sq. m. This time, workers replaced the damaged sections. The project was delayed because of proteststhat blocked roads across the country in May and June, preventing the arrival of materials and postponing its completion by one month—from the end of October to the end of November.

Industry observers note that built by Augustinians between the late 16th and early 17th centuries, the church houses paintings of the Nativity, the Last Supper, the Crucifixion and the Last Judgment in a display of religious syncretism. “It’s a complete catechesis,” Matas says of the murals, which were made using natural dyes and finished in 1777.

According to recent reports, there are also representations of the apostle Santiago (James), the church’s patron saint. Local Indigenous people identified him with Illapa, the Inca god of thunder. The style of the paintings ranges from Mannerism to 18th-century Baroque, with depictions of birds and flowers—an example of mestizo art.

According to recent reports, “It’s very striking when you enter the church, because there isn’t any empty space,” Matas states. “Everything is painted.” The paintings even cover the baptistery and sacristy. “Most of the churches in the region have murals. Here, they have been well preserved,” she adds.

Restoration underway at Santiago de Curahuara de Carangas Courtesy US Embassy in Bolivia.

The building has a single entrance through a side wall, similar to other churches in the area, and is surrounded by an atrium with two gates. “Indigenous people weren’t used to entering the building for religious activities, so the atrium was spacious enough to accommodate those who wanted to be evangelised,” Matas says.

The bishop of Oruro, Krzysztof Białasik, was the one who submitted the restoration project to compete for US funding. Since 2001, the AFCP has financed more than 30 projects in Bolivia, including the restoration of colonial paintings, the protection of Baroque musical manuscripts and the creation of a digital catalogue—including archaeological artefacts, pre-Columbian textiles and colonial art—available to customs services to curb the illicit trafficking of these goods.

To celebrate the completion of the conservation of the church, a mass will be held in Santiago de Curahuara de Carangas with the bishop and the apostolic nuncio on 15 December.

  • Industry observers note that A portmanteau of the Spanish words mal (poorly) and vestir (to dress), Malvestir features creatives across the Americas who probe the historical and contemporary resonances of Latin American dress.
  • Curated by MoMA PS1 director Connie Butler and associate curator Elena Ketelsen González, Malvestir will include a range of artists, from Newly introduced York City designers to textile artists reinvigorating intergenerational weaving traditions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Patricia Belli, Troy Montes Michie, Willy Chavarria, and Camila Falquéz are among the 20 artists and designers who will be featured in Malvestir, MoMA PS1's upcoming exhibition on the visual lexicon of Latin American fashion, opening in April 2027.

Industry observers note that A portmanteau of the Spanish words mal (poorly) and vestir (to dress), Malvestir features creatives across the Americas who probe the historical and contemporary resonances of Latin American dress. Western appropriations of Indigenous crafts, exorbitant textile waste, and the fetishization of Latin American styles are just some of the key concerns that will be interrogated in the exhibition.

Curated by MoMA PS1 director Connie Butler and associate curator Elena Ketelsen González, Malvestir will include a range of artists, from Newly introduced York City designers to textile artists reinvigorating intergenerational weaving traditions.

Several designers are striving to reclaim styles and symbols co-opted by mainstream Western markets. Known for his oversized proportions and street-style designs emblematic of the Mexican-American fashion tradition, Latest York designer Willy Chavarria is showing Safe From Home (2024), a film that expanded upon themes of love and the right to safety explored in his Autumn/Winter 2024 collection. Malvestir will also include the work of designer Carla Fernández, who nurtures collaborations with local artisans in Mexico to preserve Indigenous motifs against corporate reproduction and profiteering.

Sources indicate that works from multimedia artists who use photography, drawing, painting, sculpture, and textiles to preserve intergenerational customs will also be on view. New Mexico-based artist Josh Tafoya revitalizes his family’s weaving tradition through the centuries-long practice of Rio Grande loom weaving. David Ramirez Cotón pays homage to Guatemalan fashion with a series of hyperrealistic acrylic-on-canvas paintings cut to resemble articles of clothing hanging from a rack in a second-hand shop.

In a recent development, the exhibition comes at a time when Latin American communities are facing regressive crackdowns from multiple parties — the federal government, exploitative corporations, and immigration enforcement. Yet it has also prompted many to recognize the importance of Latinx artists through displaying the full range and power of their respective cultures, as mainstream appropriation and demands for assimilation reach new, threatening extremes.

In an opinion for Hyperallergic this month, Arlene Dávila, a professor of anthropology and American Studies at New York University, positioned the current political climate as a rallying cry for Latinx visionaries.

Within her essay, she referenced Chavarria and Raul Lopez (founder of LUAR), two of the artists whose work will appear in Malvestir, underscoring how they "frequently use street-cast Black and Brown models to communicate a richer, more inclusive vision beyond traditional, Eurocentric runways.".

"Across these fields, artists are choosing to create work that is deeply rooted in their communities, drawing directly from vernacular traditions, oral histories, and family memories that were once pushed to the margins," Dávila wrote. "While they recognize there are no guarantees of commercial or institutional rewards, their work stems from a shared conviction: We have rich cultures to offer, and we will tell our stories by any means necessary.".

These 8BitDo Tomb Raider controllers have made me rethink collectable gaming hardware

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1009 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I've never really been one for collectable controllers.
  • This is proper packaging design, crafted as much for the fan experience as for protecting the controller.
  • The controller sits on a sliding shelf, so even getting it out is part of the experience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I've never really been one for collectable controllers. I'm a fairly practical gamer, I suppose, and while I appreciate nice hardware design, I'm usually more interested in how a controller feels than how it looks, whether it has an on-brand D-pad or decals, for example. But opening the Tomb Raider 30th Anniversary Edition of 8BitDo's Ultimate 3 Controller has changed my mind a little, and I think it's largely down to the box.

This is proper packaging design, crafted as much for the fan experience as for protecting the controller. The Ultimate 3's box changes shape, opens, slides and reveals its secrets, almost like Lara Croft discovering some long-lost treasure, and I found myself enjoying the whole process far more than I expected. There's even a little golden envelope, almost hidden away, containing the instructions and a month of Xbox Game Pass Ultimate. It's all very Tomb Raider, and yes, I know I'm getting excited about a cardboard box.

The controller sits on a sliding shelf, so even getting it out is part of the experience. Then you start noticing the little design details. The faded brown-and-gold colourway features Lara silhouettes across it; there's a lovely golden metallic D-pad, and the whole thing looks like something recovered from an ancient tomb. The D-pad itself reminds me of a lost coin or compass face, which is a nice touch.

The metal D-pad disc did fall off once, but clipped back in fine. Do I expect that from a $120 controller? No, not really. Do I expect it from a $120 collectable controller where brand and design dominate? Yeah, probably.

Industry observers note that I like that 8BitDo hasn't gone overboard with the branding; it feels like a well-made piece of gaming hardware, with the Tomb Raider design integrated rather than simply plastered on. The buttons are solid black, the sticks feel responsive, and the controller has a reassuring weight. The triggers have a nice solid feel, not too light but with a little flick as they snap back into place if released.

In a recent development, then there's the stand, which I think is my favourite bit. The controller sits snugly in place, with a matching decal underneath, and it looks like you're slotting an ancient stone artefact into some sort of polar key and lock from the games. A soft orange LED glows when the controller charges, and suddenly I've got a little Tomb Raider shrine on my desk. I didn't think I needed one, but here we are.

What's clever about the design is that it gets at the look and feel of Tomb Raider without relying on Lara's face everywhere. The original games had such a distinctive visual identity: those angular environments, sandstone ruins, green foliage and Lara's turquoise costume, and it's a look that's stuck with me. The Ultimate 3 is more of a celebration of Lara across the series, but the colours, materials and little relic-like details bring back some of that atmosphere.

The less expensive Pro 3 Bluetooth Gamepad takes a more direct route back to the original game. Its design is inspired by the Lost Valley, with a jungle and ancient temple scene, and the charging stand picks up that weathered stone look. It's a different approach, and I rather like it. There's something about the Pro 3's shape, too, that reminds me of the old PS2 DualShock. It's lighter and a little more plasticky than the Ultimate 3, but still comfortable to hold, with a nice tactile feel to the buttons.

Sources indicate that this is the one I'd look at if I were playing on Switch 2, especially if you want to revisit the Tomb Raider: Definitive Survivor Trilogy on Nintendo's console. It's a good-looking pad; the Lost Valley artwork is lovely, and the included stand gives it personality when you're not playing. It's also a capable modern controller, with TMR sticks and Hall-effect triggers, so you don't feel like you're buying it purely for the artwork.

But I keep glancing back at the Ultimate 3. The Pro 3 is perfectly good and arguably has a stronger connection to the original 1996 game, but it doesn't quite have the same sense of occasion. Its unboxing is much more straightforward, and I never thought I'd say this, but I'd happily pay the extra for the Ultimate 3 packaging. The fact that the controller feels better made is a bonus.

According to recent reports, I've always thought of collectable gaming hardware as something that looks nice in a display cabinet but doesn't necessarily earn its place in everyday use, and I think that's what has surprised me most about these two pads. The Ultimate 3 has made me reconsider my somewhat cynical approach to collectable controllers, as it’s a gamepad I actually want to use, but I also like having it on my desk, and the whole thing was designed with that in mind.

Switch 2 players shouldn't feel left out. The Pro 3 is a lovely alternative, and if you're particularly fond of the original Tomb Raider, there's a lot to like about its Lost Valley design. But if you're after the full treasure-hunter experience, the Ultimate 3 is the one that has me reaching for my wallet. And that's something I really didn't expect to say about a controller.

Visit the 8Bitdo Tomb Raider website for more info.

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

Is GTA VI the Art Miami Deserves?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4281 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hyperallergic

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • SIGNIFICANTLY less cars on the road.” The text was from Miami-based artist, educator, and organizer misael soto, sent yesterday, November 19, a few hours after the release of Grand Theft Auto VI.
  • The premise of GTA VI is simple on the surface.
  • Industry observers note that to help make sense of these tensions, I got on a phone call with soto and Leo Castañeda, two Miami-based artists whose work I admire.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Driving at rush hour. SIGNIFICANTLY less cars on the road.” The text was from Miami-based artist, educator, and organizer misael soto, sent yesterday, November 19, a few hours after the release of Grand Theft Auto VI. We’d come full circle: The bumper-to-bumper traffic that Miami, the city I once called home, is now notorious for — in no small part due to overdevelopment, climate change, and strained infrastructure — was being alleviated by a video game that keeps people at home, inside a simulation of the same city locked in time.

The premise of GTA VI is simple on the surface. The game follows Lucía Caminos and Jason Duval in the criminal underworld of Leonida, a fictionalized state based on South Florida: Miami becomes Vice City, the Everglades are the Grassrivers. But its portrayal of real-life hardships, socioeconomic inequality, and even Lucía and Jason’s love story, among other elements, has elicited deeper reflections and responses across our increasingly blurred online and physical worlds.

Industry observers note that to help make sense of these tensions, I got on a phone call with soto and Leo Castañeda, two Miami-based artists whose work I admire. Castañeda is an artist and video game designer exploring Latin American Surrealism in the digital age, and soto co-leads Artists for Artists: Miami, which is leading a boycott of Art Basel next month, and works in the overlapping arenas of labor rights, public infrastructure, and conceptual and social practice.

Recent findings suggest that our conversation was edited and condensed for clarity. I hope you enjoy it.

Left: Leo Castañeda playing GTA VI, with a mural by Ahol Sniffs Glue included in the game. Right: misael soto's selfie in front of the inside of the clock tower in Assisi (photos courtesy the artists).

Industry observers note that hyperallergic: Before we even get into GTA, I was hoping each of you could tell me a little bit about your relationship to Miami — how long you've been there? How do you feel about living there now?

Leo Castañeda: I moved to Miami first when I was 11. My parents first moved to New York [from Colombia], and then they thought it was too cold, so they moved to Miami. I went to middle school and high school here, then I moved to New York for college, and I moved back in 2015. When I first moved back after college, it was mostly because of the cost of living in New York. And then, within the 10 years that I've been here, it became the same cost of living as New York, except with Florida salaries.

Sources indicate that I do feel grateful, though, to be part of the Bakehouse Art Complex, where I have an affordable studio. I live in the North Beach area, and I was able to find a sustainable rent. Miami has a lot of arts nonprofits that help over time. I do feel that, as complicated as the Miami arts ecosystem is, it is pretty supportive — but at the same time, it is tied to all the different layers of money that have come in and dominate the arts, which are very present here.

It has been revealed that misael soto: I moved here right after undergrad. I grew up in South Florida, originally from Puerto Rico, and Miami was always la locura, down south. We would visit my cousins and whatnot from time to time. As I became more and more interested in starting my own practice, I moved down here and have continually been sucked back in. I try to leave, and it pulls me back for whatever reason. Since COVID, everything's changed. Miami became the second most expensive city in the country. The influx was palpable: All of a sudden, there were Texas and California and Upcoming York license plates, Teslas zipping around town, and rent just started skyrocketing. There's more flooding. But at the same time, it's gorgeous, and it's special. I live in Mid-Beach. I can go to the water, I can breathe in some sea air, I can hear 10 different languages at once.

It's a really complex relationship with Miami. Especially, I think, both of us make complicated art — we both make art that is unconventional and perhaps even, you could say, difficult to collect. I don't know if you describe yourself that way, Leo, but I definitely do. And making this kind of work in a hyper market-driven neoliberal city like Miami, on the one hand, it gives me a lot of fodder, a lot of material, a lot of things to talk about, as we're doing right now. But at the same time, it can be really frustrating and alienating and lonesome, ultimately.

Recent findings suggest that H: I moved from Argentina to Miami when I was little because my mom got a job there. We lived in the Doral neighborhood, where most people I knew were also from Latin America, until I left for Chicago for college at 18. I've lived in Fresh York for over a decade now, but I still feel a strong pull to Miami, I feel seen, surrounded by people whose identities are a bit fractured the way I feel mine is.

According to recent reports, and on the note of nostalgia, GTA is a game that was made over the last 13 years, so it chronicles a Miami that’s partly gone. For example, customers say Lucía's home is based on a cute salmon-pink, 13-unit condo in Edgewater that was demolished in 2022 to build a 55-story tower, yet it lives on in the game. What does it mean for a video game to preserve a place that no longer exists?

LC: Well, a few thoughts. During that 13-year development, I would assume the map design was one of the first things they did. But there are also aspects of the chronicling of Miami, or Miami becoming this satire through the game, that have evolved in a shorter time period. For example, this morning I woke up, and there was a Miami Instagram influencer saying that in the fictional version of the Cuban coffee shop Versailles, which is called Antoinette, the bakery has a sign posted outside that says something like, “any politician must pay for all the food when they leave.” That's a reference from a few years ago, when Trump reportedly went to Versailles, ordered food for everyone, and then didn't pay and just walked out.

Recent findings suggest that so it does seem like a video game takes a long time to make, and this one is probably the most ambitious one ever made — 4,500 people working really, really hard, to the point of even having the union situations that they have in the UK branch of the organization. But at the same time, I feel like they studied Miami extremely well, and the integration with some local businesses and local artists in particular — I've seen a few street artists like Ahol Sniffs Glue, Soak, Tatiana Suarez, Typoe, as well as musician Nick León. One restaurant is based on Juvia on Lincoln Road, which doesn't exist anymore — they got priced out, and now there's a record of it. The game takes so long to make, but it lives in an ever-present, because it doesn't matter if you made an asset 13 years in the past, like Lucía's apartment, or now; they feel like the present. It's an interesting amalgamation. I would have to spend more time with it to really know: Does this feel like Miami in 2014 or Miami in 2026, or a hybrid?

H: To get into the politics of the conversation around GTA, I have a lot of icky feelings about one narrative that's taking hold online, which is that the game is “Woke 3.0,” and that the incels and Trump supporters are pissed about it. I only played for a few hours last night, and I went into a gun shop and bought a shotgun. That, to me, panders much more to the NRA hawks and the pro-gun community than to anything that could be considered woke, you know?

MS: Hmm. I see it the other way around, actually. To me, it's like pretending in order to pacify, in some ways. It's a very complex thing. On the one hand, I remember seeing the woman twerking on the top of a car as the sun came up over the MacArthur. Now that's in the game. And I remember the “face eater” on the MacArthur. I see a man in a thong skateboarding weekly, and now there's a character like that in the game. I teach art history, and I do a whole week on postmodernism and poststructuralism and simulacrum, and the consequences of that, which I think have led us into some really dangerous flattening territory in terms of the role of the artist in the late 20th to early 21st century. I see this game and the way that it's taken over the city in real life and in gameplay, and it makes me think about how much of this is pacifying the role of the artist, or is it pushing through to the other end and becoming a meta-modernist critique that has some gems in there, if you're willing to find them?

It ultimately makes me feel a bit sad in terms of what we deserve. I texted you yesterday, Valentina, when we were talking about having this conversation, and I said, “Well, maybe this is the kind of art the city deserves.” It's not the art that I want for Miami. But in so many ways, Miami is the perfect place. It's been the city for continual use by image makers, from Hollywood to video games.

In a recent development, H: There is some talk about the fact that the game does seem to have an awareness and sensitivity around identity. Cygnus, the curator at the Vice City Museum of Art, is the first non-binary character in Grand Theft Auto history. The actor cast for the role, Jesse James Rose, stated that to prevent anti-trans violence, GTA made it so players would not be able to harm their character. Does this feel like an honest gesture, though?

It has been revealed that MS: I was just talking to a friend who's been playing it, and she was like, “Where are all the Haitians?” I remembered there was this huge lawsuit against GTA and Vice City, the one set in the ’80s, from about 20 years ago. Haitian groups sued Rockstar over their portrayal. I did some research, and it seems now the company has shifted. They're saying, “We now punch up as opposed to punching down.” That feels, once again, so uncanny in comparison to the ways in which corporate America has shifted. It makes me think of the phrase, “Black faces in high places won't save us.” I don't want to be lobbing grenades at Rockstar. I think it's fantastic that these changes have been made, especially with such an influential game. But at the same time, it feels like the video game, in its attempt to replicate reality, is lagging in this area.

H: GTA has a long history of racism. We shouldn't forget that Black characters have been associated with criminality throughout all editions of the game. I haven't played enough to say whether that's the case in the latest version. There is also the question of how the organization actually treats its workers, and the labor disputes that are going on behind the scenes. Nestor Uriarte, an animation programmer for Rockstar, wrote an opinion piece for the Guardian where he asked, why is it that with this game that generated billions of dollars, we are still fighting to get union recognition?

It has been revealed that MS: I'm curious, Leo, as someone who has been playing games for as long as you have, how you feel about this. I'm a cinephile — I've been one since I was 18, and watched my first Kubrick film the summer before college. And I am dying to see Avengers: Doomsday (2026). I've been following the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) and have been consistently floored by the way they built out this world and the interconnected films. It's history, and it's been making history. But we all know how terrible Disney is. And even with the MCU, they tried to bring in more diversity, and the public didn't respond, so they backtracked on it. I don't know if that analogy holds. But it feels pertinent. It feels similar.

LC: Of course, I have to play more to fully understand it. There's the ads of the game and the game itself. I would say that the Netflix special did feel like it was perpetuating some of the stereotypes of the Haitian community. But at the same time, having played, or seen the range of minority characters so far in the first couple hours, it feels like they have a wide range of personalities, body types, and interests. It's not like they're all criminals. And I also found out that local Haitian muralist Serge Toussaint has his work featured in the game, which I think is an amazing thing. But in terms of artworks in other mediums that really relate to this, this is kind of like, let's say, South Park, or Euphoria — indicates that are a mirror to the world that's very explicitly showing you both the best and the worst, and it's making fun of and critiquing everyone. But then how does it flip to show a new perspective or a solution?

Recent findings suggest that I've seen a lot of people, especially women game critics and game developers, celebrating the relationship of Jason and Lucía being a central situation in the game, as opposed to a cast of different men from different backgrounds, or, in GTA IV, the Eastern European guy in the seedy underground. Having the relationship and the cultivating of the relationship be a core mechanic, almost in a Sims-like way — and even the learning of emotional labor, or doing kind things around the house, or the game having a really interesting reward mechanic for the nonviolent interactions ... At least in my experience so far, three hours in, I haven't shot a single shot.

H: Wait, how did you save Donnie in the first mission without shooting people?

According to recent reports, LC: Oh, by hiding. It was saying, “Crouch around to make sure no one sees you.”.

In a recent development, H: I think it's fascinating how different players can make these different decisions. I'm not very good at gaming, so I gave my husband the controller. I was like, “Get us out of here as rapidly as possible. I want to get to Vice City!”.

LC: Yeah, and usually my criticism of Rockstar Games and also Naughty Dog, two big companies that have these cinematic, movie-like games, is that the story missions often have a path where you fail if you don't take a violent action. The emergent gameplay — which happens just by walking around, the dynamic gameplay that's not in a story mission — is usually extremely layered and nuanced and can go in any direction, violent or not. Again, I'm only three hours in with GTA VI, but so far I appreciate that it is giving the choice of not using violence, and kind of rewarding it. There's something interesting about that. Because usually in those Rockstar games, I'm like, okay, there's this emotional tale, and now there's a mission, and I have to kill 20 minions.

MS: Leo, I'm thinking about your work and playing your pieces, immersing oneself in these worlds that you create, and there's a kind of mystery in the expansive potential that you create in your installations that at first can be a little overwhelming, but you have to just dive in. And this is the nature of games, or video games. There's a kind of trust fall. And I'm thinking about — let's just go there — the emancipatory potential of that. Because video games, to me, the potential in them as works is the building of awareness, the fostering of empathy, literally embodying someone who has a different way of life or a different body, a different perspective. Especially in our era of political correctness, and a lot of it is warranted, we're asked to speak from our own perspective and not assume things of others. And so this allowance — I wonder how you see the potential in that, especially in something like this game that is so immersive.

LC: I think games as artworks are, to a certain extent, some of the most affordably accessible. Yes, you need to have a PC or PlayStation or Switch or something, but they could be pieces of art that are globally accessible in an immediate way, and they really can affect culture. In terms of empathy, you're controlling a being that you identify as “I”: “I” drove the boat today, or in my game, “I” was camouflaging with the environment to gain energy. There's something there about the mutability of the body, or how one could shift one's self-identity into multiple beings, that is interesting in games, and also interaction and choice as a place that could be art, in a way that performance art also does, and maybe theater. And visual arts in general, maybe in a less touch-based way. But in terms of the empathy, I've been seeing a lot of reviews of GTA VI saying it's actually leading people towards that. Perhaps it is through the romantic relationship [between Jason and Lucía], or maybe by having so much freedom to do whatever you want and kill whoever you want, but then developing these characters and NPCs to a level where they feel like real people.

Recent findings suggest that H: There is one moment in the game that was very emotive in a way that might provoke empathy, and it certainly did for me. At the very beginning — so this is not really a spoiler — we're shown the backstory of how Lucía gets arrested. She's been sitting at a cafe, a little Cuban cafecito, and she's just ordering ice water. The server keeps coming up to her and asking if she wants something else, and she's like, “No, no, just ice water for me.” It's clear that she just can't afford anything else. So in an act of true desperation, and from a place of deep poverty, she decides to rob a payday loan store nearby, and she gets caught. At one point, you can hear the cops saying, “She's saying she left something at the cafe.” And then we see the owners of the coffee shop taking care of her baby, who is then taken by social services.

We're not shown Tomás, her little baby, at the beginning. It's something that the game surprises us with. To me, it was such a thoughtfully articulated moment.

In a recent development, LC: The beginning is so strong. And then having the tutorial on how to walk and use the camera be her nine months later in prison. Out of overcapacity, the prison is letting some people who have lower sentences perhaps have probation, so she's gonna be let go, but the woman who works there notes she doesn't know if or when Lucía will see her baby again. That works as a narrative tool, a teleology, giving purpose to the game beyond, “Oh, she's just a digital girlfriend.” Now there's this question of what the rewards of behavior are that the game's gonna have when one is part of the criminal underworld, but there is a child in foster care that could be taken back or not. That's gonna be so interesting if that ends up being a fork in the road within the narrative, because many of these games have multiple endings.

MS: This is so fascinating to me in regards to something we were talking about earlier — whether reality is informing the simulacrum and vice versa. It makes me think of how, living in Miami, it continuously feels like maybe the most neoliberal city I've ever lived in. But in so many ways, it oftentimes feels like when you're on the road or when you're at a cafe, you're alone. You really have to fend for yourself in this city. Of course, there are these moments where you break through, or if you're a regular at Enriqueta's, you know who to talk to, this and that. It makes me wonder how the game might change the way that we see ourselves. And, following that thread, how might it actually make us more united?

Sources indicate that I don't know if that's a bit of a stretch, but there are just so many people playing this game. And I think over time it's really going to show, as visitors come and reflect their years of gameplay back to the city. In the same way that folks experience Paris syndrome, what will the GTA Miami syndrome be? How might that change us? I was thinking about it for the worse, but how might it change us for the better? Because I don't know a Miami where that childcare situation in the GTA story would happen. Of course, I'm not a caregiver. I'm not a parent. But I don't know that Miami — and I've been here long enough and I have a lot of family here, chosen family. So that makes me, in a weird way, hopeful.

LC: I think it's interesting, let's say with Pop art and conceptual art — if you use a urinal or a fluorescent light, you think of urinal, Duchamp; fluorescent light, Dan Flavin, etc. These artists are claiming this thing from the world. And it's interesting to have this very fluid cycle of, let's say, the Only in Dade Instagram account becoming almost a live feed of GTA, or us within Miami filtering our experience — when there's a very special or odd moment, it being a rehearsal for the game, or the game getting reflected back in the world.

It has been revealed that if the game is marketing itself as this debauched, wild place, and that lures millions and millions of people in, but then it ends up being this profound story that actually highlights how South Florida has complications of income inequality and climate change ... There's a hurricane system in the game, so there's a very strong chance that there will be flooding. Will that situation, where violence and comedy, or things that are not explicitly telling people what the values should be, actually make them more subtle and implicit? Does that create change or not?

H: We've been speaking over an hour, we could probably talk for two more hours. This feels like a beautiful note to end on. But I want to ask if there are any burning observations you want to share.

MS: I feel like we should speak about the takeover of Miami in the real world, physically. Anybody trying to do anything — F1, Art Basel, all these people who come in and take over the city, as they've done for decades — if they want to gain favor with locals, just look at what they did with GTA. Because the amount of free advertising — I mean, I went to this GTA VI-themed drag night, and it was not sponsored by them. It was at Las Rosas. They had a pool table and some neons, and they had the beer from the game available for purchase, but the event itself was fully done just to hop on the bandwagon, and everybody was lapping it up. Morphine Love Dion was playing the video game while people were dancing. It layered some uncanny feelings for me. But at the same time, I'm just very, very impressed, and scared, by the power of putting it everywhere to the point where it was inescapable. It's been inescapable for the last week. It's very impressive.

Recent findings suggest that LC: Yeah. I've met at least two or three people who have been working on some of the release parties. So they're employing local artists and local musicians and local businesses, as opposed to, as misael was saying, these people arriving out of nowhere, renting a place for really exaggerated prices, and not giving back to the local community. At least through employment. We'll see over time if and how it leads to other forms of sustainability locally. I have a photographer friend who, similarly to that drag show, started doing GTA-style photos in front of one of the fresh signs and probably made some money through that, unofficially. So that's interesting.

MS: I think there's many ways to be a capitalist, or to do this kind of thing and take over the city in this way. And I've never seen something so thoughtful. It honestly reminds me to some degree of the first couple years of Art Basel, when they would do a lot of public programming and free concerts and they really seduced us ... But that's another conversation. I'll stop there.

H: Well, it's a perfect aperitif for Miami Art Week and the Basel boycott and everything else. And then the G20 summit hosted by Trump in Miami the following week.

H: Yeah, we're going from GTA VI to G20. It's just a perfect pipeline, really.

MS: It doesn't get any more Miami surreal than that. Truly Vice City.

#68655. Dezeen Awards 2026 interiors project of the year announced

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2132 w)
